- _ _ _ MY VA.LE:ts.TTINE. Oniv a bur.e.li of white sprint/ flowers, That some kind friend had sent; But who-can tell the influence sweet, These fragrant blossoms lent. They told me of a friendship true, Both lasting and sincere, One of the rays of sunshine bright, That on life's path appear. These lovely, fragile flowers of spring, Live here, but for a day; Their beauty and their fragrance charm, And then they fade away. But friendship will for over last, It des not fade or die, It's fragrance tills our hearts through life, And lives beyond the sky. ,

LORD BEACONSFIELD'S VALENTINE. Miss Isabella Fairlie, the grandniece of Lady Blessington, was a singularly beautiful and intellectually gifted child, though deprived of the faculties of speech and hearing. To this "Beautiful Mute," as he named the young lady, Mr. Disraeli address:cl the following lines : Tell me tam star from which she fall, Oh name the :lower From, out whose wild and perfumed bell, At witching hour, Sprang forth this lair and tdry maiden, Like a tee with honey laden. They say that those sweet lips of thins Breathe not to speak; Thy very ears, that seem so fine, No sound can seek. • And yet thy face beams with emotion, Restless as the waves of ocean. 'Xis well; thy face and form agree. And both are fair, I would not that this child should be As others are; I love to mark her in derision Smiling with seraphic vision, At our poor gifts of vulgar sense, That cannot stain Nor mar her mystic innocence, Nor cloud her brain With all the dreams of worldly folly, And its creature melancholy. To thee I dedicate these lines, Yet read them not. Cursed be the art that e'er refines Thy natural lot; Read the bright stars, and read the flowers, And hold converse with the bowers.

FEBRUARY.—A DREAM. I had a curious dream. A form appeared Amid dun shades his giant frame lie reared; There stood he, freezing me in every Vein, For, as I gazed, I wished him gone again. Bestrewn with snow and rnciled were his locks, His features dark, and hard as flinty rocks. His laboured breath was cold—so icy cold In hail-showers down his ragged beard it rolled. A mantle, like a shroud, the spectre wore, Resembling sackcloth, strewn with ashes o'er. Of fleecy clouds this vesture was composed, And fleath its folds valt pouches were disclosed. These all swelled out, like sails before the wind, For every pouch with rain was deeply lined! . '3long human throngs the apparition moved, And, grimly frowning, wheresoe'er he roved A chilling atmosphere around he threw, Whilst people, shivering, wrapped their cloaks anew ; As if 'mid lonely tombs of ghastly white They, fearful, roamed upon a boiserous night, Still strode this phantom forth; and, now and then, He'd shake his mantle o'er those throngs of men— As soaring eagles flap their pinions wide— Then biting blasts would rage on every side, • And still where'er 'mong men the monster passed Such gloom and discontent he seemed to cast That, sick at heart, I sighed, and stared aghast! • But now a gladdening change, divinely fair, Suffused the sea of human faces there ! in the spectre's hand a scroll was seen, Whereon was figured legibly 14." And where so late lurked gloom and discontent, Now sunny mirth an happiness were blent. 0, what a magic power had that" 11" ! A myriad missives sWift flew o'er the scene; A myriad maids and swains these, quick. unsealed; A myriad VALENTINES lay then revealed! Like summer-flowers they flashed in broad array, And, pinned to each, gleamed Cupid's arrow gay. But sundry valentines were spurious found, Grotesepte,—yea, hideous cumberers of the ground, Rough thorns in Love's own fragrant flower-world. • These at the spectre's feet were hotly hurled, Thence kicked to where oblivion's fog-fumes curled! Anon the valentines had lost their bloom ; And down, again, came discontent and gloom. And, yet, once more Mirth woke her jovial train; The phantom's scroll glad tidings bore again. With laugh and shout bright festive boards were spread, While Shrove-tide cakes their grateful savour shed. Like incense offered to some pagan god, A universal richness breathed abroad; And children, in ten thousands, sang the lay : " 0, pancake-Tuesday is a happy day !" And then the phantom thundered in my ear— "I'm FEBRUARY and— !"—I awakened here! And from my dream I trust this truth I learned— Although Life's frowns be often towards us turned, Yet, Hunan Life, like February, showers, In sweet surprises, scores of joyous hours. DAl'Wen, Feb. 4th, 1832.
JESSE.

A philosopher, who went to a church where the people came in late, said it is "the fashion for nobody to go till ' everybody has got there. YAH :—First Passenger: I travel third-claps on principle. —Second affable ditto : Do you, now ? Well, Ido it from I want of principal.—Judy. George Eliot says, " Openness is the sweet fresh air of our moral life," but there is something too much for that when the cold wind blows on a poor man who has ragged pants and no overcoat. THE POST-MASTER ABROAD.—enrate (to Suffolk labourer .down with fever and his wife away) : Well, James, and when is your wife coming home? Have you written to tell her how sadly you' are ?"--Jan3os : " Why yes, sir, thar 'a' hey',—but the latter come back two or t'rce days I arterwards from the ded h'us (Dead-letter Office, perhaps), I so then I sent her a poost-orfrce order (telegram, surely), I • as how she must come d'recly!"—Punch. HABITUAL POLITENESS.—A very amusing little incident —yet one showing the policy of habitual politeness—hap- pened (nye a correspondent) the other day. I was stand- ing by the telegraph office in one of our large institutions —I mustn't give its name—when there came up a very tall, thin, straight, gray-haired gentleman, with his hat on one I side of his head. This gentleman, addreseing the clerk in deerge, inquired the way to a certain office Or department.' The clerk, however, at that moment was engaged in sketch- ing caricatures on his blotting pad, and his assistant, a little esßena-er boy, was, in his tarn, amusing himself by pueh- leg the elbow of his superior at every attempt he made with his nen. Therefore it was that he was unable to attend to the tall, thin gentleman, who repeated his inquiry, which elicited the information, that " if he d look he would per- kers find it on the right hand side." "Do you know who ! kat is?" I aeked. " What, that old silamp•nosit--.No ?" sylid«,'s the Postmager-General," said I, and I think he's gone to his department to give instruclions for the increase of veer salary." The confusion of that poor youth was isomethiag painful to behold, and when I again saw him some twenty-four hours after it had not entirely passed away. The episode contains a special moral as to the beauty of civility. In his "MEDICAL HISTORY OF CHARCOAL," Dr. BelThc says 4. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &e.

The lectures on agricultural science being held in various districts of North Germany are already effecting beneficial changes. One lecturer has so far succeeded in his efforts as to influence fourteen landowners to drain their lands. LACK OF SKILLED FARN LABOUR.--Formerly in the northern counties ploughing matches were held in every district, where prizes were given for skill in ploughing, hedging, &c. These are gradually dying out, and so also is neatneee in work. If a-cu want a fence neatly and ju- diciously laid you have to seek out an old man for the work, or do it yourself. The introduction of machinery has much to do with this. Formerly, in hiring a servant, you never dreamt of asking could he do so and so—it was taken for granted; now you heai questions such as—Can yen plough; can you sow (broadcast) ; can you hedge; can you stack? These things cannot be learnt unless farmers will take the pains to teach them, and unless some stimulus is held out to promote excellence. AGRARIAN OUTRAGE IN PR.ANCE.—A very interesting account is given by Mr. H. M. Jenkins, the Secretary of the Royal Agricultural Society, in last Tuesday's razes, of a district in Picardy wherein the supposed rights of tenants had for generations been savagely asserted and defended against the landowners, so as to make the case an almost exact parallel to that of many a district in Ireland in the present day. This sutvived till 1864, but has since, under the ordinary administration of the law, almost entirely dis- appeared. Two things are admitted incidentally in the course of Mr. Jenkins' interesting statement. One is, that Ireland was in 18g4 even worse than Picardy at that time, and the other is that it has needed a quarter of a century of the firm administration of just law in the letter case to bring the "remarkable custom" to an end," even if it can be said even now to have actually expired." THE CENTRAL CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE.—A council meeting of the Central Chamber of Agriculture was held at the Society of Arts, on Wednesday. Colonel Paget presided. After the reading of the minutes, the election of Parliamen- t ire; committees was proceeded with. Several new members were elected, amongst whom was the Marquis of Salisbury. —A long discussion arose on the working of the Education Acts in rural districts, with special reference to the proposals for a new code. Mr. Owen dames moved "That the coun- CU views the proposals for a new revised code as tending to lessen the Governments grants and to increase the ordinary expenditure of the smaller schools in rural districts, and though their effect in many cases would be to increase the cost of education, which could only be jastified by a larger capitation grant from the Imperial funds." Several speakers supported the resolution, which was carried. PENNY WISE LANDLORDS.—A gentleman who farms ! well writes :—" In my own farm of 300 acres, the labour bill commenced to rise in 1873, and went up from £5OO to £700." "I have seen," says the writer, "many go through the fire of landlordism and get scorched, and I myself have not ezcaped. After my father and I having occupied one farm over half a century, I was offered 15 per cent. reduc- tion on a farm with no residence upon it, and the ground game reserved—for when I asked the landlord a question on the paint an answer was refused me. I have left the farm ; and after hawking the land about as accommodation land,l it has been re-let partly to five new, tenants at an average ! reduction of over 20 per cent. This is the rule now-a-days, to refuse an old tenant a reduction, to turn him out, and then re-let at a greater reduction than was asked to new ones. Further, the gamekeepere are dismissed ; and prob- ably, now I have left, the rearing of game, which was in full swing at the end of my tenancy, is stopped." At a meeting of the Bath and West of England Agricul- tural Society' Mr. Knoll, as chairman of the Implements Regulations Committee, reported upon the arrangements which are in progress for the trial of implements at the Cardiff Show. It appeared that as some difficulty in ob- taining suitable land for the trial of reapers occurred, the stewards resolved to secure a larger area of grass land, and to promcte an exhibition and trial of machines specially adapted for saving; and maturing grass crops. The atten- tion recently given to this question by agriculturists war- ranted the belief that if the various novelties, such as hay- driers, stack-suckers, grass-savers, &c., could be brought together and fairly tried, the results could not fail to be of interest and benefit. The co-operation of inventors and ' makers would be specially invited, in order to secure an ex- hibition at Cardiff as complete and representative as could be brought together. "MUCK'S THE MOTHER OF MotiEv."—A. correspondent of the East Anglian Daily Times, signing himself "E. W.," writes as follows :—The tenant of the beautiful farm in East Lothian, where I was once a pupil, used to be very fond of saying in broad Scotch, "Muck's the mother of money.'!l He died worth £60,000; he held his farm on a2l years' lease, he spent from £2,000 to £3,000 a year on cake and guano, and he paid £3 108. an acre rent. I mention these facts to show what a clever man on good land, with a lease, can do. We made farmyard manure here in perfection—no open yet-de, all the beasts stall-fed under cover, all liquid was saved, and not allowed to run into the horse-pond, as is -often the case round here, where the ponds near buildings are as black as ink. The Smithfield Club has decided to adhere to the rule in force with regard to the dentition of pigs exhibited at the Club's shows. The state of dentition :must agree "with the dentition test required by rule 22 of the Club," notwith- standing that the rule has been proved fallacious. It will be remembered that in two well-attested cases in connection 1 with the Smithfield Club Show last December, the pigs were right and the rule was wrong beyond the shadow of a doubt. Mr. J. Howard, M.P., publishes a letter to Sir Brandret'n Gibbs in which he shows very conclusively that in pigs which have been developed at an abnormally early maturity the dentition will also be abnormally early and otherwise irregular, and the action of the Club undoubtedly tends to the exclusion of the best and earliest-matured pigs freas their shows. At a farm near Melon experiments were made last week by M. Paeteur, in the presence of a host of specialists, on the duration of the action of anthractic vaccine as applied to sheep. It will be remembered that six months ago M. Pasteur vaccinated a number of sheep with anthrax vaccine, the immediate result being to preserve all these sheep from anthrax virus, whereas sheep not so vaccinated succumbed within twenty-four hours. The question was how long such vaccine would last, and the experiments proved that it lasts six months, and they will be continued from month to month to ascertain its exact duration. On Thursday week four utivaccinated sheep were inoculated with antbrsx virus, and also four of the sheep vaccinated six months ago. Two of the unvaccinated sheep expired within twenty four hours, , and the other two subsequently, whereas the sheep vacci- 1 meted six months ago resisted the action of the virus.l Another curious fact was ascertained. A lamb, the offspring! of a vaccinated sheep, was inoculated with the virus. It expired within twenty-four hours, thus proving that the immunity is not transmitted heredit Idly. The Seine.et- ' ltlaree Agricultural Society presented M. Pasteur with a gold medal, and a binquet was held, at which the great ser- vice remlered to agriculture by his discovery was warmly acknowledged. THE HOLKER Re:RD.—January 6, Grand Duchess of Oxford 32nd, a red and white bull calf, by Baron Oxford Bth (41,057). Jan. 11th, Grand Duchess of Oxford 47th, a red and white heifer calf, by Baron Oxford Bth (41,057). Jan. 23, Grand Duchess of Oxford 45th, a red heifer calf, by Baron Oxford Bth (41,057). Jan. 25, Grand Duchess of Oxford 39th, a roan heifer calf, by Baron Oxford Bth (41,057). Jan. 28, Winsome 23rd, a red bull calf, by Baron Oxford Bth (41057); named respectively Duke of Oxford 62nd, Grand Duchess of Oxford 62nd, Grand Do. Do. 63rd, Grand Do. D. 64th, and Baron Winsome 11th. Commenc- ing to breed at an early age, the "Oxford" females, as a rule, give a calf annually until well into their "teens." The great secret of Mr. Drewry's, success in this respect is, we believe' owing to his keeping the cattle in a natural state. The shippoes are such as any ordinary tenant farmer in these parts would have, and such as many have, due regard being paid to light and ventilation. The same applies to the buildings for calves, bulls, &c. The animals are com- fortably straw-bedded, and are cleanly kept. There is no pampering in diet, and they have healthful exercise, earn- ing their own keep in the paAtures when the weather is at all Et for them to be out. Pure water, pure air, cleardinees, ventilation, combined with a proper degree of warmth in the shippons, a comfortable bed, healthy but not stimulat- ing food, and watchful attention, are, we believe, the great essentials to success.—R., in Agricultural Gazette. INOCULATION FOR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES.—Blackleg has been discovered to belong to those several diseases which ! may be transferred by contagia consisting of minute or- ganisms, which propagate like the yeast of fermentation. We still want antidote for these virulent diseases; mean- while we have, as in the case of smallpox, the means of pre- venting or mitigating them by inoculation. M. Peisteur and his colleagues have used "benignant lymph" in the vaccination of more than 20,000 sheep with perfect success. The theory of vaccination is the subjection of the anithal to a weakened attack by the use of attenuated virus inocu- lation. At the outset of his experiments M. Pasteur inocu- lated with malignant virus taken from death-stricken ani- mals, which killed most of the subjects upon which it was employed. He then passed the virus on through several other subjects, till it lost its deadly character, and produced cnly a slight state of fever. If blackleg appears on any farm, the occupier can readily attenuate the virus, and can be his own operator. Following the example of the men of science, he should first inoculate a rabbit, mouse, or guinea pig. The first mouse would die in a few hours, and the virus would then be passed as in vaccination, which is an 'exceedingly simple operation, into the body of a second ! victim, and so on. It will be found that each animal operated upon in this manner will survive longer than its predecessor, as the transferred, virus becomes milder. The "lymph," or serum, from the extravasation in one of the milder cases, after two or three transferences, may be safely used in the inoculation of the young cattle of the farm, and, taking the disease in its mildest form, which is not ac- companied by any danger, they will thenceforward be exempt from attaak of blackleg. The " vaccine " will ulti- mately no doubt be as regularly Supplied and employed in veterinary practice as that which averts smallpox by the "medical profession." Blackleg is by no. means the only , disease which may be successfully dealt with by the means here described. Mr. Rutherford, of Edinburgh, states that pleuro itself will succumb to_ the treatment, "benignant lymphavng " fromf found efficaciouslung s o f n pleura-pneumoniaprotectfprotecting cattle f r osubjects h been d con- tagious pleuro. Fowl cholera is another disease which may possibly be banished by this same method of protective in- oculation, and among others which may be finally stamped out perhaps with the aid of inoculation are smallpox in sheep and distemper in dogs. Science has never promised more effective aid to agriculture than in the saving of life among the various animals of the farm.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1882
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1882

SCIENTIFIC NOTES. Some interesting discoveries of ancient Etruscan pottery , have recently been made at Corneto, the necropolis of the ITarquins ; also a bronze-chariot with strange figures of animals painted on it, and near this a quantity of metal chains, probably used as harness, and a'gilded helmet. BENT SPOKES FOR WHEELS.—TO mitigate the shock on carriage wheels, Herr Nordmann, of Dresden, gives the spokes a curving shape, so as to make them exert a certain resillience or resistant spring. After being cut the straight ashwood spokes are steamed and bent while hot in iron presses, then dried at a moderate temperature. The curva- ture is proportioned to the load and kind of cartiage for which they are designed. Mr. Pnoctor, a great astronomical authority, has repub- lished in his "Familiar Science Studies" an alarming pre- diction, to the effect that the comet of 1880 is in all proba- bility identical with the comet of 18-13 and that of 1668, i • and that if it is, it is almost certain to fall into the sun in I or about the year; 1597, causing a sudden conflagration in the great orb which will probably burn up all the animal and vegetable life existing on the planets of the solar sys- tem. A NEW ART DECORATIOi.—A new method for re-pros ducing oil paintings has been invented by Mynheer Bo- gaerts, a native of Holland, who has opened an exhibition of imitations of the Flemish masters in London. The speci- mens are remarkable for their fidelity to the originals, and copy even the marks of the painter's brush. The cost of the process is also low, a picture measuring 30 inches by 40 inches being prcduci Is for fifteen shillings, either on canvas or panel. In the decoration of walls and panels, the "Fein- ' ture-Bogarets" is, therefore, likely to find its own field. 1 In an article on "The Recent Weather," 21ratzfre remarks that the outstanding feature of the singular weather we experienced in January has been the extraordinarily high barometer which has accompanied it. With barometers equally, or all but equally high, the most diverse tempera- tures have prevailed, the conditions determining the tem- perature in any locality being the direction and force of the I wind, and not the height of the barometer. The highest barometer recorded dining the period was 30 970 inches at 8 a.m. on the 18th inst., at Oxford. The highest reading probably ever recorded in the British Islands was 31 046 at 11 p.m. on January 8, 1820, at Gordon Castle, Banffshire. Some letters have appeared in The Times as to recent ex- cavations in Asia. Mr. George Dennis denies the soft im- peachment that he has been exploring the tomb of Creams, since the last resting-place of that monarch is all unknown, but he is about to resume work on what he believes to be one of the royal men aments named by Strabo. If success- ful, some fresh light on Lydian arts and manners may be hoped for. Dr. Alexander Gonze writes to deny that the German explorers allow the carved stones they do not carry away to be used for building purposes. All that has been done is to allow some free stones of no scientific value to be used in the erection of a Greek school. The Danish Society for the Protection of Animals has offered two prizes of £BO and £4O respectively for essays on the possibility of replacing living by recently killed animals in physiological investigations. The society is well aware that it is not possible to obtain all the results which are desirable in the interests of humanity without the practice of vivisection, but it is desirous of limiting that practice as far as possible. In the adjudication of the prizes special prominence will be given to those essays which give previously unknown cases where dead may be Eubsti• tuted for living material without lessening the value of the results obtained. The essays may be written in the Danish, Swedish, English, French, or German languages, and for- warded before September 1 this year to the President of the Society, M. A. de Haxthausen, at the Society's offices, Copenhagen. THE THERMOMETER IN MEDICAL TREATMENT.—An ob- jection to the common thermometer is that the mercury takes some time to fullyeacquire the temperature of a part of the body. An improvement on M. Becquerel's applica- tion of the thermopile in this connection has been lately made by M. Redard. He applies one junction to the body and exposes the other to a temperature which is varied til the galvanometer shows no current; the temperature thus reached is the one sought.] The piece to be applied to the body consists of a small iron plate (with neck) having soldered into it, at right angles, an iron and a copper wire which pass to it through an insulating handle. This piece is attached by means of a belt. It is connected through binding screws, and iron and copper wire, with the other piece, or junction, and with a small sensitive galvanometer. This junction dips, along with a mercury thermometer, in mercury in a wide tube, and this tube is inclosed in another holding wood spirit, which is heated with water, or cooled by blowing air through it. THE WEATHER." GLASS," AND ITS REPORTS.—The old practice of marking the scales of barometers with words, which were taken to imply thd conditions of the weather that were to prevail when the top of the mercurial colnmn ranged near their position, was absurd. Thus the height 29 5, or 24, ' inches was assumed to be the midway line sepa- rating fair from foul, and accordingly was inscribed as "changeable," half an inch above it being marked "fair," and half an inch below " rain " an inch and a hs.lf above changeable was regarded as " very dry," and an inch and a half below it "stormy." In this arbitrary and altogether unwarranted formula, in which a fixed standard was assumed for a condition of nature that is itSelf literally as unstable as the wind, it was in some general sense conceived that the I Instrument was only to be used in situations which were about at the same level as the surface of the sea. Of course it was well understood by the makers of the barometers, although, unfortunately, not as certainly by their pur- -1 chasers and users, that one thousand feet of difference in elevation would at once shift "fair weather" into "rain." One thousand feet above the level of the sea corresponds with an inch less of pressure on:the barometer. Therefore, with two barometers of altogether similar quality and con- struction, one placed at the level of the sea would declare "rain" as imminent; whilst the other, upon a hill-side one thousand feet above, but under otherwise precisely similar meteorological conditions of the air, would be uncompro- misingly fixed at "fair." But there is a still more serious reproach than even this hanging over the old plan of scale• - nomenclature. From the mere difference of atmospheric pressure at different times in the same place, in temperate regions of the earth, the column of the barometer varies in height in extreme cases between twenttoeight and thirty- one inches; and in frequently recurring instances between twenty-niue inches and thirty inches and a half. Now, the " changeable " point may, in reality, correspond with any and every part of this extended range. A barometer which has been standing steadily for some days at thirty-one inches of the scale, if it fell to thirty inches within twenty- four hours, would give a most absolute indication of change, and intimate most certainly the approach of strong wind, and most probably also of rain, although at the lowest eleva- tion it was corresponding with "fair" upon the scale. And so, in a similar way, a barometer that had been standing at twenty-eight inches for some days, if it rose within twenty- f our hours to twenty-nine inches, would assuredly indicate that a cold dry wind was at hand, although the word on the scale with which it was then associated would be "rain." A barometer standing steadily at "changeable," as a matter of fact gives a more trustworthy promise of a continuance of fine weather than one which is descending rapidly from "very dry" to "settled fair." There is nothing, therefore, to be done wiSh these old arbitrary scale-nomenclatures but to reject them at once as unworthy of the attention of any one who pretends to turn the barometer to a serviceable and scientific use. This is now well understood by all meterolo- gically instructed people; but it is, nevertheless, a point of such paramount importance to the application of the instru- ment to any purpose of prognostication or forecast, that it is not possible to do otherwise than insist upon it here, even at the risk of seeming to repeat what, in this ace of improved scientific teaching, all educated people should be presumed o know.—Science for 411.

POPULAR MALAGASY HYMN TUNES.—For some few p are after the re-opening of Madagascar to Christian effort, the original hymns prepared by the first missionaries were used unaltered, and without any additions. There was a cmious mixture of old and new tunes; the former "survivals" of the early period, and a few of the latter taught by the mis- sionaries then commencing their work. But with these there came also a. number of other tunes, some picked up from barrel organs, and dance music learned from the mili- tary bands, often most incongruous and inappropriate to the words to which they were sung; and together with these were a few native melodies. From this strange mixture of tunes for religious worship a number of most elaborate pieces were composed by certain native musical geniuses. Some of these were of great length and complexity, occa- sionally not without considerable ingenuity and some merit In composition, but sometimes with a curious and almost comical bass accompaniment, more like the grunt of an animal than the sound of a human voice. Bat all were utterly unfit for congregational worship; indeed it often puzzled us how the singers themselves learned such lengthy and elaborate compositions. It was said that they some- times sat up all night practising these pieces, for which they paid a considerable sum (for Malagasy) to the teachers. The service of praise was thus thrown almost entirely into the hands of the singers, many of whom were slaves, and were often people quite unfit for the position they occupied as leaders of religious worship. The opening of new chapels in the country, and the united congregational meet- ings held on the first Monday morning of every month, were the grand times of display for these performances, so that this part of the service often became a mere singing con- test, in which parties of singers from different chapels vied with each other in producing startling effects.—The Quiver. div.head: ILT,TJSTRIOUS IRISH KEN,
div.p: ILT,TJSTRIOUS IRISH KEN,
No. VII.—HENRY GRATTAN.

Just thirty years are ending since first his glorious aid, Our sacred rights defending, struck shackles from our trade; To serve us still with might and skill the vet'ran now appears— That gallant man, who led the van of Irish Volunteers. He sows no vile dissensions,—good will to all he bears,
Ile knows no vain pretensions,—no paltry fears oseares, To Erin and to Britain's sons his worth his name endears, _ _ _
They love the man who led the van of Irish Volunteers. - -Ned Lysaght.

The "Act of Union" having become an accomplished fact, I Henry Grattan retired from the noise and heat of political strife. His health had been for some time unsatisfactory, and his spirits were greatly depressed, as well they might be. Regarding the " Act of Union" as destructive of the liberties of his country, he saw in it the overthrow of the entire labours of his life, and it unfolded to his piercing eye a leng vista of agitation, of disloyalty, of disaster. To use his own never to be forgotten words, he had "sat by the cradle and followed the hearse of the Irish Constitution." In 1803 an incident occurred which, as it illuetrates Grattan'e power of invective, we will mention. Sir Jonah Barrington, author of the "Rise and Fall of the Irish Nation," and Mr. Latouche, the opulent banker, were candi- dates for the city of Dublin in 1803, and were supported by the Liberal Party, in opposition to Messrs. Beresford and Ogle. Barrington, whose opposition to the Union had made him very popular, had reason to feel proud of his position— he was warmly supported. The four earliest who recorded their votes for him were Mr. George Ponsonby (afterwards Lord Chancellor), Mr. Henry Grattan, Mr. (afterwards Lord) William Plunkett, and Mr. John Philpott Curran (atter- wards Master of the Rolls), the four men moat remarkable for fidelity to the Irish nation. It was upon this occasion that Grattan pronounced his most vehement invective. Many years before this election, when the very name of Grattan operated as a spell to rouse the energies and spirit of his country, the Corporation of Dublin obtained and hung on their walls a full length portrait of him. His name graced their corporate rolls as an hereditary freeman, when the jealous malice of that rancorous and persevering enemy of every man opposed to him, the Earl of Clare, in a secret committee of the House of Lords introduced into their re- port some lines of a deposition by one Hughes (a rebel who had been made a witness, and was induced to coin evidence to save his own life) detailing a conversation which he alleged himself to have had with Mr. Grattan, wherein the ' latter had owned that he was a United Irishman. Every- body knew the total falsity of this. Indeed Mr. Grattan was, on the one hand, a man whose principles had been on certain occasions considered too aristocratic, and yet he was nowetienounced in the slang of the Lord Chancellor "an in- fernal Democrat." The Corporation of Dublin caught the sound, and, without one atom of inquiry, tore down from their walls the portrait which had done them so much honour, and unceremoniously expelled Mr. Grattan from the Corpo- ration without trial or even notice, thus proclaiming one of the most loyal and constitutional subjects of the British Empire to be a rebel and incendiary. He despised and took no notice of their extravagance, but nevertheless sorely felt their ingratitude. On the election in question Barrington was proposed by Mr. George Ponsonby, and upon Mr. Grattan rising next to vote upon his tally, he was immedi- ately objected to as having been expelled on the report of Lord Clare's Committee. A burst of indignation on one side, and of baisterous declamation on the other, forthwith succeeded. In the midst of the tumult Grattan stood silent, regarding with a smile of the most ineffable contempt ever expressed his shameless accusers. The objection was made by Mr. John Giffard, usually termed the "Dog in office"— a noted tool of the Orange clique, and who coined the term "Protestant ascendancy," an epithet which became very fatal to the peace of Ireland. On the first intermission of the tumult, with a calm and dignified air, but in that ener- getic style and tone so peculiar to himself, Mr. Grattan de- livered the following memorable words —memorable " be- cause conveying in a few short sentences the most over- whelming, although certainly hyperbolical philippic—the I most irresistible assemblage of terms imputing public de- pravity, that the English, or. I believe, any other language, is capable of affording :"—" Mr. Sheriff, when I observe the quarter from whence the objection comes I am not surprised at him who made it ;—the hired traducer of his country— the excommunicated of his fellow-citizens—the regal rebel —the unpunished ruffian—the bigoted agitator l—in the city a firebrand—in the Court a liar—in the streets a bully —in the field a coward !—and so obnoxious is he to the very party he wishes to espouse that he is only supportable by doing those dirty acts the less vile refuse to execute !" No wonder the object of this fierce onslaught was unable to reply. " Jack Giffard" for once lost his usual assurance. He was thunderstruck. When he did recover it was only to hiss out the vapid exclamation, "I would spit upon him in a desert." On examining the Roll it appeared that the I form of erasing M. Grattan's name had been omitted. The objection was therefore overruled, and Grattan recorded his vote. The erasure of his name from the roll was never after- wards attempted, and cn the dissolution of that Parliament he was requested by the very same body to stand forward as their most illustrious countryman, and elected by accla- mation in that very same Courthouse as the representative of the city and Corporation which had so recently endea- voured to debase and destroy him. This was in 1805. On the 25th of March of that year a petition was pre- sented to the English House of Commons by Charles Fox on behalf of Catholic Emancipation.' On that night Grattan made his first appearance in the English Parliament, and took him seat modestly on one of the back benches. This is no place for the "Irish Demosthenes," exclaimed the chival- rous Charles Fox, and he drew the Irish Demosthenes for- ward and placed him near himself. Fox opened the debate in a speech which, though long, was also a very generous, powerful, and enlightened one. Dr. Paddy Dengenam replied to Fox in a speech of more than three hours, and full of rabid bigotry and coarse invective. No soaner had he re- sumed his seat than Grattan arose. The House was breath- lees with expectancy. Would his maiden speech in the House prove a fail-ure, or would he carry captive the Eng- lish Senate as he had carried captive the Irish Senate? Was he "an oak of the forest, too old to be transplanted," or was he to give a refutation of his own elegant and compli- mentary excuse for his rival's failure? For a while the House contemplated with amazement his peculiar style—a style which Lord Byron designated "a harlequin style," but at length the " rnore then human eloquence" of the Irish Patriot touched the heart and intellect of the English Prime Minister, and Pitt made the first motion of applause. Soon he had the English Senate at his feet. His splendid speech —so novel in its style and manner, so vast in its concep- tions, its reasoning, and its force—produced in the House surprise and admiration. Pitt exclaimed, "Burke told me that Grattan was a wonderful man for a popular audience, and I see that he was right." Fox, in a private letter to Trotter, said, "I am sure it will give you pleasure to hear that Grattan's success in the House of Commons was com- plete and acknowledged even by those who had entertained great hopes of his failure." The Annual Register called the speech "one of the most brilliant and eloquent ever pro- , nounced within the walla of Parliament.' The saintly or ' rather sanctimonious Spenser Percival, while he spoke in complimentary terms of "the blaze of Mr. Grattan's elo- quence," endeavoured, as might be expected, to refute him in a narrow bigoted speech. The debate was adjourned, and was resumed on the 14th of April. At half-past four in the morning the House divided. Its intellects and principles were on the side of Fox and Emancipation. But bigotry carried the day. The ayes were 124, the noes 336. The majority against civil and religious liberty was there- fore 212, and so for a time vanished the hopes of Catholic Emancipation. Grattan determined to keep himself free from all parties. When Fox's Ministry came into office in 1806, he declined to accept office, and he also refused to accept £4,000, which the Roman Catholics subscribed in the same year to defray the expenses of his election for Dublin. In the following year he incurred much unpopularity in supporting the" Go- vernment Coercion Bill for Ireland," which he believed to be necessary on account of the disorganised condituen of the country. On the 31st of May, 1811, Henry Grattan once more pre- sented the Catholic Petition to the English Parliament. On this occasion he pleaded for the rights of his Catholic coun- trymen with his accustomed subtlety, power, and splendour yet he pleaded in vain. The ears of the English bigots were closed to the voice of the "charmer, though he charmed never so wisely." In 1819 he was again defeated, but it was bY a majority of only.two. On the accession of George IV. in 1820, Grattan proceeded to London to present the Roman Catholic Petition, but the exertion of the journey, though he travelled by easy stages and by canal, was too much for him, and he I died shortly after his arrival on the 6th of June, 1820. At i the request of the foremost men of the nation, he was buried in Westminster Abbey, two of the royal dukes being pall- bearers. He lies near the tombs of Pitt and Fox. The place is an honourable one, but it was the only honour that was bestowed upon him. Not a bust, not an epitaph marks the spot where the greatest of Irish orators sleeps. But one stately form seems to bend in triumph over that unnoticed I grave. It is the statue of Castlereagh, "the statesman of the Legislative Union," who amid the yells and cursings of ! the onlooking crowds was borne to that, his last reeting place, and to whom Lord Byron has given an unenviable !immortality in Don Juan, especially in the lines where he ! calls him "Carotid artery-cutting Castlereagh." We feel, however, with Shiel that Grattan ought never to have been entombed in the vaults of Westminster Abbey—that " the green cairn of the hills of his own country would have afforded a better monument." Truly it may be said, Ne'er to these chambers, where the mighty rest.

Since their foundation, came a nobler guest; Nor e'er was to the bowers of bliss conveyed A purer spirit, a more holy shade." We have thus followed Henry Grattan throughout his illustrious career. We have seen him emerge into public life, and finding his country without trade and without a Legislation. We have seen him give her both her commerce and her independence. We saw him call Ireland into exis- tence by his weed. We have watched him in those wonder- ful nights when Ire went forth to fight the battles of his country—contending for the liberty of .Ireland to her last gasp. We have seen him, like the heroes of the Illiad, still protecting her corpse from profanation, and seeking to obtain for her independence an honourable sepulture in the emanci- pation of her sons. We have seen him spending his life to its latest breath in the service of her country, and dying a martyr in the cause of civil and religious liberty. Is not his life a great moral lesson? He was a man of pure spirit and noble aims—an accomplished scholar—an orator un- equalled perhaps by the greatest speakers of any age or nation—a patriot inthe largest and broadest sense. He was the first Statesman inlreland who both aspired to national independence for his country, and perceived the impossibility of maintaining that independence even if established without

associating the mass of proscribed Catholics in the national aspirations and national triumphs. Wrapping his resolu- tions like a cloak around him, and forgetting the phrase- ology of cant and the badges of party, he t•levated great principles, not self, and in "the mighty sphere of his trans- parent mind embraced the world and breath'd for all man- kind." "I never knew a man," said William Wilberforce, "whose patriotism and love for his country seemed so com- pletely to extinguish all private interests, and to induce him to look invariably and exclusively to the public good." Well done! thou good and faithful servant of our sister isle! Having done thy work, and done it well, we will write thy name high up on the bead roll of those great men who have waged war with falsehood, who have fought for the rights of manhood, and who have urged on the cause of universal brotherhood. Men

Whose great thoughts possess us like a passion Through every limb and the whole heart; whose words Haunt us as eagles haunt the mountain air. Men who walk up to fame as to a friend Or their own house, which from the wrongful heir They have wrested from the world's hard hand and gripe. Men who, like death, all bone, but all unarmed Have ta'en the giant world by the throat and thrown him; And made him swear to maintain their name and fame At peril of his life—who shed great thoughts As easily as an oak looseneth its golden leaves In a kindly largess to the soul itirew on. The man who won a race with a mule in remarkably quick time understood mule nature. He kept tugging at the reins and shouting, "Back, back, you brute !" allthe way round the course, and the mule wentZahead for all he was worth.

Two young swells were making fun of a good country curate. The abbe, after standing it pretty well for a while, said—" Allow me to say, gentlemen, that I am not precisely fop, nor altogether a,fool, but betwixt the two." The young men departed. "What is the meaning of the word tantalising?' asked the teacher. " Please, marm," spoke up little Johnny Holcomb, "it means a circus procession passing the ichool- house, and the scholars are not allowed to look oat"— Chicago Journal. Dem what owe de firm will settle wid me, and cfern what de firm owe will settle wid Mose."

A clergyman in the country had a stranger preaching for him one day, and meeting the sexton, asked: " Well, Saun- ders, how did you like the sermon to-day ?" "It was rather ower plain and simple for me. I like thae sermons best that jumbles the joodgment and confoonds the sense. Ah, sir, I never saw ane that could come up to yours& at that." Professor Geiger sat in an easy chair on deck, looking very pale. The compassionate captain asked how he felt. "Miserable, miserable ; I'm sick, captain, I'm sick. I have paid tribute to Neptune till I have lost everything." "But," said the Captain, "I see you still have your boots left." "Yes," said the Professor, faintly, " but they were on the outside." A fellow stopped at ad hotel at Niagara Falls, and, on settling his bill, the landlord charged him 7dols. a day for five days. "Didn't you make a mistake ?" said the fellow. "No." said the landlord. "You did," retorted the wiry. looking fellow. " You thought you got all the money I had, but you are mistaken. I have a whole purseful in another pocket." As Mr. Walter Gilbey has indicated, draught-horse breed- ing has now become a profitable source of agricultural re- venue, indeed, one of the moat profitable. Landowners will scarcely believe it, but it is a fact, that many tenants of small moorland farms have sold yearling Clydesdale colts for 20 per cent. above the rental of the farm. One tenant, I be- lieve, sold a colt for four years rental cash a year or two ago. Waste hill lands in Jitorkshire are worth fortunes for such purposes.—Land. How TO TRAIN A CHILD MENTALLY.—ChiIdren think much more deeply than we imagine; we should, therefore, answer their questions to the best of our ability, unless evi- dently asked in a spirit of frivolity, and try to explain to them reasons for things they see occurring around them, and for the acts which you yourself perform. But gain their confidence' in every way in your power. A mother should be more of a monitor than a teacher, or rather she ought to be both combined. You like to see your boy clever, doubtless, but do not make a show-child of him. Do not even let him know you think him clever, and discourage all pertness in conversation, for this too often borders on impertinence. Never permit him to contradict you. If he contradicts his mother, may he not, when old enough to go out, be guilty at table of very great rudeness? At the same time, mothers should never deserve contradiction. When you have occasion to reprove, beware of doing so angrily. It is far better to speak gently, and make the child feel ashamed of himself, because shame breeds sorrow and contrition, and this in its turn the desire to behave far better in the time to come.—Cassell's Magazine. _ .

BAD WRITING.—There are degrees of badness in every- thing, and there may have been English writers who could have competed with the American about to be mentioned, but there is no record ot the fact. Horace Greeley, who at bottom was a most excellent man, was withal an oddity in many things and wrote vilely. Although in his own—the Tribune —office his printers might be supposed to decipher his handwriting after they had been in his service for several years, not one ever mastered it, and the first proofs had practically to be re-written. "Seldom," says one of his countrymen, "has the clearest and purest Saxon been veiled in such hieroglyphs." One of the numerous stories told of Greele3 's caligraphy is that sometime before the war he wrote a note to a member of the staff, discharging him. The expelled journalist went to California, and, returning after several years, encountered Mr. Greeley in Printing House- square, New York. The old chief recognised him, and in- quired, with his customary *affability, where he had been and how he had been getting along. "Let me see," he con- tinued, "didn't I get mad with you and send you off?" "Oh, yes. You wrote me a note telling me to clear out. I took it with me. Nobody could read it, but it was taken as a letter of recommendation, and I got several first-rate situations by it. lam r catty very much obliged to von." On another occasion, when Greeley was angry with one of his men, he sent him to the cashier with a note intended to indicate a considerable reduction of salary for the former. The cashier understood it to read, "Double --'s salary," and accordingly doubled it.

THE LAND QUESTION.
XX.

Speaking in London on the 17th December, 1345, daring the Anti-Corn Law agitation, the mild tempered Richard Cobden (the weight of whose opinions will excuse the length of the quotation) used the following words :—" I warn Ministers, and I warn landowners, and the aristocracy of this country against forcing upon the attention of the middle and industrious classes the subject of taxation. For great as I consider the grievance of the Protective system; mighty as I consider the fraud and injustice of the Corn Laws, I verily believe if you were to bring forward the history of taxation in this country for the last 150 years, you would find as black a record against the landowners as even in the Corn Law itself. I warn them against ripping up the subject of taxation. If they want another League at the death of this one; if they want another organisation, and a motive—for you cannot have these organisations without a motive and principle—then let them force the middle and industrious classes of England to understand how they have been cheated, robbed, and bamboozled upon the subject of taxation; and the end will be—if they force a discussion of this question of taxation; if they make it understood by the people of this country how the land- owners here, 150 years ago, deprived the sovereign of feudal rights over them; how the aristocracy retained their feudal rights over the minor copyholders ; how they made a b again with the King to give him 43. in the pound upon their landed rentals, as a quit charge for having dispensed with these rights of feudal service from them ; if the coun- try understand, as well as I think I understand, how after- wards this landed aristocracy passed a law to make the valuation of their rental final—the bargain originally being that they should pay 4s. in the pound of the yearly rata'sle value of their rental, as it was worth to be let for, and then stopped the progress of the rent by a law, making the valua- tion final—that the land has gone on increasing ten-fold in many parts of Scotland and fivefold in many parts of England, while the Land Tax has remained the same as it was 150 years ago; if they force us to understand how they have managed to exempt themselves from the Probate and Legacy Duty on real property—how they have managed, I sweet innocents that taxed themselves so heavily, to transmit their estates from sire to son without taxes or duties, while the tradesman, who has accumulated with thrifty means his small modicum of fortune, is subject at his death to taxes and stamps before his children can in- herit his property; if they force these things to be under- stood, they will be making as rueful a bargain as they have already made by resisting the abolition of the Corn Law. Again and again I warn the aristocracy of this country that they do not force us into a discussion of the peculiar hea- thens upon land." Let us see what grounds there are for such strong lan- guage. By the feudal system introduced into this country by the Normans, the great landholders held their lands direct from the King, subject to the performance of certain military duties as the condition of their endowment. The King was still considered as in some sense the proprietor, and was called the lord paramount, while the services to be rendered were regarded as incident or annexed to the holding of the land; in fact, as the rent to be paid for it. The sub-tenants of these great landholders also held their lands on similar terms. The great landholders were also subject to very considerable payments to the Crown on account of their estates by means of certain Feudal Customs such as Purveyance, Aids, Relief, Primer Seizin, Wardship, Alienation, Escheat, &c. For instance, Purveyance and Pre-emption were sources of revenue to the Norman Kin4s, by which their servants were permitted to take provisions, horses, and carriages for the use of the Royal household at a certain price, whether the owner consented or not. Under Edward 111., this sys- tem was reduced within reasonable bounds, small sums were to be paid on the spot, larger sums within four months. Relief was a fine payable by an heir on coming to an estate. Primer Seizin was the right of the King, when any of his tenants died siezed of a knight's fee, or fief (i.e., laud held by military or feudal tenure), to receive of the heir, pro- vided he were of full age, one whole year's profits of the lands, if he were in immediate possession, and half a year's profits if he had not yet entered into possession. In the reign of James L, 1603-25, when the income from the above sources contributed one-half of the public revenue of the country, there was some talk of substituting "a Com- petent yearly rent to be assured to his Majesty, his heirs and successors," of greater amount than he or any of his predecessors had received, but it ended in talk only, and in the reign of that "most Christian monarch," Charles 11., the Convention Parliament, largely composed of cavalier landlords, by a majority of two only (151 to 149), passed an Act (Stat. 12, car. ii., a. 24) by which all this was done away with, i.e., so far as the great landlords were concerned all these liabilities and obligations to the Crown were to be abolished, and instead of the rent or equivalent of rent, which the great landlords had previously paid or performed, excise duties—but only on liquors brewed or distilled for sale—should be granted to the King and his successors for ever—" in full compensation." This Act, which thus con- verted the landlords from tenants into owners, provided, however, that there should be no change between the great landholders and their tenants, who were to pay as usual, because as was said that would be very "prejudicial to the lords of the manors," or what would be called now•a-days "the landed interest," i.e., tile landlords, not the people who are dependent on the land for a living, as farmers or labourers. The rank and file of the nation had then very little controlling power over Parliament, and it was a com- paratively easy task to shift, as above described, such a burden from the backs of the landlords to the backs of the people, or, in other words, to tax labour instead of capital. In 1692, the first Parliament of William and Mary, over- coming the landed interest, imposed a lind tax of 4s. in the pound upon the then annual value of all landed property. Since the reign of William and Mary, however, the land- holders have been the dominant power in Parliament, and they have taken care that "the landed interest" has not suffered. By an Act passed in 1793, the 38 George M., c. 5. the tax was fixed as a perpetual charge of 4s. in the pound, as up to that time it had been continued by annual Acts.

_ So late as 1816, according to Oldfield in his "Representa- tive History," out of 658 members of the unroformed House of Commons, 213 were returned-by 87 peers in England and Wales, 31 by 21 peers in Scotland, and 51 by 36 peers in Ireland—that is, just 300 in all, or nearly half the whole. As 123 "commoners," who were generally at one with the landed aristocracy, or coukl easily be bought by it, com- manded 171 other seats, and the Crown disposed of 16 more in its own right, there were thus 171 so-called " indapenti- en t" constituencies.

To-day, when we are under the impression the: Liberal Party is in power, 402 members of the House of Lords hold (we will not say own) over 14 millions of acres, while the "People's House" contains 186 members who hold over two millions of acres, and 165 members connected with the Peer- age either by birth or marriage, in addition to which the Conservative members. returned by boroughs invariably go with the landlord party. From a consideration of the foregoing, is it any wonder that to-day the Land-tax of 4s. in the pound is assessed on the valuation made in 1692 ?

Some very interesting information is given on this sub- ject by the Financial Reform Almanac, which publication everyone taking any interest in politics should possess. Ac- cording to tables there given, it appears that in Great Britain for 1878-9, a real 4s. in the X would have yielded £11,865,062, instead of the amount which was received for Land-tax in 1880-1, viz., £1,050,467. In Lancashire, for instance, the Land-tax is only a fraction over a farthing in the £ As another instance, in the reign of William 111., the Land-tax contributed more than a fifth papt of the public income, loans included, whereas in 1880-1, the Land-tax supplied only an eighty-fourth part, exclusive of money raised by creation of debt. Succession Duty is another illustration of the manner in which the "landed interest" have taken care of themselves. In 1780 Mr. Pitt introduced a Legacy Bill, providing that where a person died possessed of property, whether land or money, or both, duty should be paid upon it by his bene- ficiaries. The "landed interest," however, managed that the two classes of property should be dealt with by separate bills. The House of Commons passed both bills all rights but when they got to the House of Lords, the one relating to personal property was passed, but the one relating to , land, which would have affected their pockets chiefly, was rejected. The result was that until 1853, where a man I —say a thrifty, industrious tradesman—died leaving £l,OOO in cash, or stock, or shares, a considerable sum in Probate, or Administration, and Legacy Duty, was payable to Govern- ment ; but if a man died leaving £lOO,OOO worth of land, there was nothing payable on it. Was that fair ? A table at page 184 of the Financial Reform Almanac for the current year, shows that from 1797 to 1881, personalty paid in the shape of Probate, Administration, and Legacy Duties, front which Realty is wholly exempted, no less a sum than £193,408,330! In 1853, Mr. Gladstone, as the then Chancellor of the Exchequer, attempted to remedy this gross injustice by the imposition of a Succession Duty on real property, which, however, is not estimated on the total value of the property, but is valued as a Life Annuity—viz., by reckoning how many years the person who succeeds to the property is likely to enjoy the rental, and even the duty so ascertained is I made payable by easy instalments. Its annual yield under such circumstances, so far from realising the expectations formed of it, only amounts to something between £600,000 and £BOO,OOO. The Right Hon. G. J. Goschen, M.P., having made the subject his especial study, published the result of his labours in 1872, under the title of "Local Taxation." Speaking of this country, he says—" With respect to amount, land by itself pays only £3,000,000 out of the £65,000,000 of taxa- tion, and the percentage is 5 per cent." But taking foreign countries, he says—" In Holland land alone pays 9 per cent., in Austria 17.- per cent., in France 18A- per cent., in Belgium 20,i per cent., and in Hungary 321 - per cent." What is required in this country is a re-valuation of lands for the more equitable imposition of the Land Tax, and also for the Land Tax to be levied on a scale so graduated as to press most heavily on excessively large holdings. Further, it is only fair, also, that the real or landed pro- perty of a person dying should furnish the same amount of taxation that the same value of personal estate does, so as to do away with the present inequalities between the two classes of property. This would require the abolition of "life estates," so that when the heir succeeds a great land- holder he. may succeed him as a real owner, and not simply as a "life tenant," drawing the rents, or rather the balance of rents remaining after the annual incumbrances in the shape of mortgage interest, jointures to widows, and annui- ties and rent charges to younger children, are paid off. If all the landholders were landowners, there would be no diffi- culty in devising a scheme by which real property should pay the same duties to Government which personal property now does.

div.p: THE ADDRESS.—The adjourned debate In the report of the Address was resumed by the ATTORnEY—GENERAL for IRELAND, who replied to the speeelres of Lord Randolph , Churchill and Mr. Sexton, and 'c's:posed the treasonable action of the Land League. He tubmittecl that there was sufficient reason for the decision come to by the Executive to arrest the leaders of the Land League, and said the Go- vernment would not have deserved to retain office if they; had hesitated to arrest Mr. Parnell and his colleagues. In the course ef his speech the Attorney-General read a letter from the Chairman of the Prisons Board denying that Mr. Sexton had suffered solttary confinement at any time during his imprisonment at liiimainham' but explaining that when he was threatened with typhoid fever the other prisoners were not allowed to visit him, and that this order was not given in any sense as a punishment.—Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN complained that the objects of the leaders of the Land League had been misrepresented, and on behalf of the League he repudiated any connection with the 'crime and outrage that had been rife in Ireland.—Mr. GEORGE 13'zrnicK ex- pressed his opinion that by recent legislation Ireland had been brought to the condition that nothing but the procla- mation of martial law in the disturbed districts would suffice to restore tranquility.—The debate was continued by Sir J. Hay, Mr. G. Beutinck, Mr. Labouchere, and Mr. J. Lowther.

div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE,
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE,

.Queen Elizabeth of Roumania is reported to be seriously The semi-official National Gazette says that the political horizon in Germany is said to be clear. Several hundred Turkish troops have left Constantinople for Yemen to repress the insurrection in• Arabia. It is reported that the position of the National party in Egypt is viewed with marked displeasure by the Porte. It is officially stated that the Pope desires the proposed pilgrimage from Spain to Rome to be conducted under the exclusive supervision of ecclesiastical functionaries. The French Council of Ministers has agreed to take into consideration the question of modifying the law of 1849 relating to the expulsion of foreigners from French terri- tory. It is announced in a telegram from Vienna that the Ser- vian officers studying at the military school in that city have received orders from Belgrade to return home imme- diately. A St. Petersburg telegram announces that intelligence has been received that more than 100,000 inhabitants of the new Chinese territory iu Kuldja have expressed a wish to settle in Russian territory. It is reported in Cairo that the Egyptian Ministry intead to take steps to effect the abolition of the slave trade, as it is thought that this will make a favourable impression on public opinion in England. A body of Tunisian insurgents, numbering about 1,200, have arrived outside the city of Tripoli and asked the Governor to send some Turkish troops to accompany then, back to their districts in Tunisian territory. Advices from the Cape -state that the Hon. J. H. Hofme- yer, who recently retired from the Capetown Ministry, will be invited to assume the presidency of the Transvaal Republic—a nomination which would be very acceptable to the Dutch. _

A Collective Note addressed by England and France to the Powers expresses the desireto come to an understanding with them in regard to Egypt, on the basis of the mainten- ance of the statew quo and respect for international engage- ments. President Arthur has sent to the Senate the official corres- pondence regarding the proposed congress of American States, And it is found to .confirm all the suspicions enter- tained as to the design of Mr. Blaine to recognise no authority of the European Powers over the American continent. Commander Selby, of Her Majesty's gunboat Falcon, has been seriously wounded by an Albanian at Artaki. On hearing of the outrage, 'Lord Dnfferin at once despatched his dragoman to the palace of the l'rime Minister, Said Pasha, who issued orders to have the offender arrested immediately. A curious symptom of feeling in connection with the Culturkamiff in -South Germany is reported from Munich, where the Chambers, by 111. to 60 votes, have carried a motion for the abolition of undenominational schools, which were supported, one speaker urged, by all atheists and champions of modern revolution, and which were hotbeds of unbelief. The "31inister of Public .Worship did not take part in the debate. The Rome correspondent of the Times states that the references made in Parliament to .Mr. Errington's sojourn in that city have necessarily been read with much interest there. On the Liberal side the Capitale twits the Clericals with having been rather too hasty in declaring that even Protestant England had bowed down before the Vatican ; while in the 'Vatican circles Sir Charles Dilke's replies have been, in the circumstances, equally well received, as being a perfectly truthful and straightforward statement of the case.

div.head: JAPANESE GOVERNMENT.
div.p: JAPANESE GOVERNMENT.

Adyicef.3 received at Plymouth on Thursday, announce that the Mikado of Japan has decided to resign the absolute governance of his dominions, and proposes in future to rule as the head of a constitutional form of Government. An edict has accordingly been issued for the necessary electoral preparations to be made for the appointment of a National Assembly in 1890 aed for a representative House of Peers THE PERSECUTION OF THE JEWS IN RUSSIA.

An official communication is published in .the Russian press reiterating the assurance that the Government of the Czar cannot permit foreign interference on the subject of the anti-Jewish disturbances. It points out that the Hebrews who are Russian subjects at present enjoy the full protec- tion of the Government. The Golos speaks in terms of high approval of Mr. Glad- stone's reply to Mr. Simon's question as to the persecution of the Jews in:Russia.

THE REVOLT IN THE BALKAN PROVINCES. A telegram received in Vienna from Zara, and published apparently with serni-oilicial authority, states that the con- dition of affairs in the revolted Austrian provinces has I greatly improved, the disaffected part of , the population showing a disposition to submit -to the imperial troops. The force employed in the suppression of the revolt in the "occupied provinces" is said to comprise one-fifth of the Austrian army. The troops are suffering great privations from the severity of the weather and the constant attacks of the insurgents-upon their lines of supply. The official news from the " occupied provinces" by way of Vienna is highly favourable to the Austrians. The pacification of Crivoscia itself is declared almost complete. "The positions gained have been fortified, and the transport of building material and provisions from the coast into the interior is proceeding without opposition. Same arrests have been made at Stolac. Finally, the whole of Bosnia and the northern and central portio as of Herzegovina are , described as perfectly tranquil." On the other hand, the correspondent of the Standard at -Serajevo states that a band of insurgents have appeared on the railway at Zenitza, in North Bosnia, and .have torn up the rails. He adds that the plan of the insurgents is to surround and capture Serajevo, and adds :—" The insurgents have already rendered the roads to tile south and west of .Zenitza unsafe, and if they ever succecd-in interrupting the railway communications with Austria, Serajevo, the capital of I3,)snia, would, for a time at least, be lest, and the entirt garrison, who would be un- able to procure provisions, could hardly fail to be captured."

div.head: EMPRESS OF AUSTRIA.
div.p: THE EMPRESS OF AUSTRIA.

Three constables who went into a Ladies' Land League meeting on Monday at Middleton, county Cork, and attempt- ed to seize some documents, were expelled by the members with the aid of young :nen. The Lord Lieutenant has issued a proclamation declaring five baronies of the county Roscommon, and seven baronies of the county Waterford, to be in a state of disturbance re- quiring additional establishments of police. Lord Cloncurry, on Tuesday, obtained at the Four Courts 27 verdicts against as many tenants of his estate in county Limerick in actions of ejectment which he had brought against them for non-payment of rent. A man named Ryan, who gave evidence before the Land Commissioners a week ago, has mysteriously disappeared from his residence at Carron Cloughty, county Tipperary. Fears are entertained that he has been murdered. A Cork correspondent states that sub-constable Welsh, whose conduct on a Whiteboy trial was recently the subject of inquiry, he having suppressed important facts in his evid- ence and communicated them to the solicitor for the defence, has been dismissed the force. A pamphlet is on the point of being issued by the Com- mittee of Irish Landlords giving statistics concerning the working of the Land Act down to the 31st January. It shows that by the decisions given up to that date the average reduction of rent was a fraction over 21 per cent. Parliamentary returns issued on Saturday, dated February 11, give the total number of arrests under the Coercion Act as 512. Of these 93 are at Clonmel, 89 at Naas, 82 at Kil- mainham, 73 at Galway, 48 at Limerick, 43 at Dundalk, 39 at Armagh, 23 at Omagh,.2l at Monaghan, and 1 at Cork. On Saturday evening a farm servant named Kelly, in the employ of Mr. Coleman farmer, Groom, county Limerick, was fired at and wounded while ploughing his master's field, two shots taking effect in his leg and arm. Kelly had been threatened with death if he did not leave the service of Mr. Coleman. _

..... A return was issued on Wednesday showing the number of agrarian outrages in Ireland specially reported in each year since 1854. The number last year was 4,439, as against 2,535 in 1880, and 863 in 1879. There were 17 agrarian murders last year, against 8 in 1880; and 66 cases of firing at persons against 24'. ' As Mr. Wilford Lloyd, brother of Mr. Clifford Lloyd, R.M., was driving from Scauff, county Clare, to Tulla, on Scisday evening, accompanied by a party of police, five or six shots were fired at bins about a mile from Rodyke. One bullet struck and wounded a policeman sitting on the box. Mr. Lloyd and the police returned the fire. Six arrests have since been made. The Daily .37-c-ws New York correspondent telegraphs that enormous estimates are published of the amount of money sent to Ireland from America. One places the total for two years at two millions and a half of dollars, another at one million and a half. Both include the quarter of a million levy voted by the Chicago Convention, of which only 110,000 dollars has as yet been paid. The ladies of the Liverpool Land League forwarded to Mr. Parnell, on Monday, a valentine in which the symbol of remembrance was a cheque for £lOO. This sum, which is one of several similar instalments sent from Liverpool dur- ing the last six months, is to be devoted, it is understood, to the Prisoners' Sustentation Fund at the wish of Mr. Parnell.

In consequence of the Queen's letter to Lord Aberdare on the multilation of cattle in Ireland, the Dublin Society for the prevention of 'Cruelty to Animals on Friday considered the matter, and, believing that an appeal to those guilty of such barbarities would be useless, resolved to ask the Pr- otestant and Roman Catholic Archbishops to fix a day on which a remonstrance should be made in the churches against the cruelties which bring disgrace on the Irish people. The United States House of Representatives has refused to consider a resolution on which the Foreign Affairs Com- mittee had reported adversely, asking the Attorney-General to state whether, in the event of an American citizen, "guiltless of any crime," being arrested through the sus- pension of the Habeas Corpus Act, the British Government could detain him without trial, and whether the United States could demand his release. THE LOUGH MASK MURDER. The men charged with being concerned in the murder of the two bailiffs whose bodies were found in Lough Mask were again brought be- fore the magistrates at Clonbur on Tuesday. The Crown Solicitor made an affidavit that it was necessary in the in- terests of justice that the inquiry should be conducted in private, and the, magistrates having acceded to this course he then asked for another remand. The magistrates said they granted a remand with reluctance, and it must be understood that on the next occasion evidence would have to brought forward. Mr. Patrick Egan, who" takes charge " of the Land League funds, has been adopted by the Roman Catholic priests as a candidate for the representation of county Meath. The priests assembled on Tuesday by direction of and under the chairmanship of Bishop Nulty, who had requested them to first ascertain the wishes of their flocks •before making a definite choice of the candidate "whom it would be their duty to recommend to the electors." . "The illustrious bene- factor of the Irish farmers, Michael Davitt," would, one of the resolutions declared, have been selected had he been in a position to accept the trust. I THE EXPLOSIVE LETTER TO Mn. FORSTER.—Further disclosures have been made respecting the explosive letter sent to the Chief Secretary at Dublin Castle. The authori- ties have submitted the material to Professor Hartley, of the Royal College of Science for Ireland, for analysis. Mr. Hartley states that the material consisted of iodine of nitro- gen in its pure state, the quantity being about 15 grains. He states that even when wet the material would explode on being subjected to friction or pressure ; while if it were to Ito dry it would explode without friction or pressure. It ap- peared that the letter bore the arms of Trinity College, and that it was posted in the College Green Post Office, a few yards from the College gate. It is surmised,on this account, that the stuff, which is only used in chemical laboratories, may have been surreptitiously obtained from the laboratory in Trinity College by one of the students.

Her Majesty the Empress of Austria had a most enjoyable day's sport with Sir ViTatkin Wynn's hounds on Saturday, I being rendered all the more enjoyable on account of the "royal " weather. The Empress left Combermere at 12 o'clock, and rode the whole way to Broughton Hall. The field was not only large but a very brilliant one, the com- pany including a greater number of :ladies than has been seen out for a long time, and the popular master of the hunt j —Sir Watkin Wynn—was also present. Her Majesty ! hunted on Monday with the -Shropshire hounds, and had a I rather tame day. On Tuesday the knowledge that the Elopress would hunt with the Cheshire hounds attracted an ; enormous crowd to the neighbourhood of the inn at Burley- dam, where they met. This is always a favourite meet, but I the residents had never previously witnessed such a sight. The horsemen numbered considerably over 200, and carriages, broughams, traps, ac., were al-so very numerous, I to say nothing of the crowd of pedestrians. The weather j was delightful. The EMpress and suite arrived at eleven, and Her -Majesty was evidently struck with the crowd and the brilliant field, which included ladies and gentlemen of considerable note.. A smart run of 40 minutes' duration, I and a brilliant run of an hour and a half, were enjoyed, but there was no kill. The Empress hunted on Wednesday with the North Staffordshire hounds, which met at Ma-deley. Snow and rain fell af- intervals during the day. —Thursday's meet was a close secret, there being a doubt, indeed, whether Her Majesty would hunt at all. At ten o'clock, beneath a louring sky and in drizzling rain, the Empress left Combermere Abbey cc Fomte for some trysting place in Captain Park Yates's district, anal at Church Minshall the master of the South Cheshire Hunt, Captain -.Park Yates, was once more seen wearing the the green cap. There was a goodly field. Though the weather gave no sign of clearing up the hounds went to work with a good heart, and a fox was soon found. There was capital going for nearly an hour, with no mishaps, but the grass land was sloppy, and the rain continued to fall. In the end, however, the fox got safely away. The Imperial party cantered to Calveley for home.
