THE EXAMINER SATURDAY FEBRUARY 18, lBB2. THE STATE OF IRELAND. -- I MISCELLANEOUS. Eteven men were arrested under the Coercion Act on Sun- day night, near Swintord, county Mayo, charged with being concerned in murderously beating three men. A number of incendiary fires have taken place between Michaelstown and Knockling, in County Limerick. Outrages have been principally committed on the tenants paying rents.

It is reported that much damage has been caused in some parts of Scotland by the gale and floods of Monday. It is officially announced that Prince Leopola's knee is nearly well, and that his Royal Highness will shortly return.

• Some boats were capsized during the gale on Lough Erne on Sunday, Lieutenant Smith (of the 105th Regiment), his servant, and two boatmen being drowned. The Rev. Lionel Brown, of Worcestershire, committed suicide on Saturday by shooting himself. Pecuniary dill'', c alties are believed to have induced the act. The execution of Robert Templeton, for the murder of Betty Scott, at Lower-house, Burnley, on the 3rd January, took place an Monday at Manchester. Marwood was the executioner.
The arrangements which have been in progress between The O'Donoghue M.P., and his creditors were completed on Monday, and Le hon. member will resume his seat in the House at once. _ _ _ _

At a meeting of the City of Glasgow Bank shareholders, on Tuesday, Mr. Boyd, Edinburgh, presiding, the liquida- tor's report, showing a surplus of £119,000, after paying everything, was taken as read. A special meeting of the Liverpool Liberal " 900" was held on Tuesday night, and a resolution was unanimously adopted in support of the Government proposals on Parlia- mentary procedure. Lord Cranbrook opened the new Mechanics' Hall, at Horsefrith, in Leeds, on Saturday, and dwelt upon the value iof mechanics' institutes in promoting culture and cultivat- ng higher ideas of the dignity of labour. At the usual periodical banquet of the English commer- cial community in Paris on Saturday night, there was a strong opinion expressed as to the necessity for a treaty and closer commercial intercourse between the two countries.

The exchequer returns from April 1 to February 11 are £72,223,981; expenditure, £73,184,667; balances, £4,747,310. In the corresponding period last year the receipts were £70,790,366 ; expenditure, £70,111,323 ; balances, £7,381,791. A lamentable accident occurred at Blackpool on Monday. The outer wall of a house in course of erection was blown down, and three brothers named Turnbull, who were play- ing near it, were buried in the ruins. Two of them were killed on the spot and the third was very seriously hurt. At the Derby assizes, on Saturday, Mr. Justice Hawkins passed sentence of 20 years' penal servitude upon William Goddard, a slater, for kicking his wife to death at Chester- field— At the same assizes, George Bestwick, a collier, was sentenced to penal servitude for 15 years for the man- slaughter of Samuel Falconbridge at Belper. The Earl of Cavan, father of Lord Kilconsie, the Liberal candidate for Taunton, has published a letter, stating he wishes it to be distinctly known that his principles are Con- servative, lest anyone should be misled to vote Liberal through personal regard. It would be a great sorrow to him if the principles prevail which aim at destroying the bulwarks of the Constitution. _

Lord Salisbury, acknowledging receipt of a resolution passed by the Shrewsbury Beaconsfield Club, says he earnestly hopes that Conservatives will see in the present deplorable condition of affairs a powerful incentive to do what in them lies to counteract the principles which ani- mate the policy of the Government. In conseqaence of the answer of Mr. Gladstone to Sir Wilfrid Lawson, asking him to wait for the Local Govern- ment Bill (which would have certain bearing on the ques- tion of licensing), the Executive Council of the United Kingdom Alliance on Tuesday night addressed a circular to members of Parliament urging them to press upon the Government 'the importance and the urgency " of the question. A meeting at which the Lord Mayor presided was held, on Tudday, at the Mansion House in support of Lady Bective's movement for promoting the prosperity of the British woollen trade. The Marquis of Salisbury made an eloquent appeal to the arbiters of fashion—a power of which he con- fessed he had the vaguest notions—and to the women of England, as patriots and humane persons, to do all they could to encourage native industry. An emphatic warning to persons who presume to marry wards in Chancery without the consent of the Chancellor had been obtained, was given by Mr. Justice Fry, on Tues- day. The learned Judge stated that in one day two cases had been brought before him, in each of which a man had married a ward of Court without having obtained the neces- sary sanction. In each case he had committed the bride- groom to gaol, and directed an inquiry into the validity of he marriage. Addressing a crowded audience at the Hall of Science, London, on Sunday morning, Mr. Bradlaugh said what he intended to do, with regard to the refusal of the House of Commons to allow him to take his seat, was that, unles the house vacated his seat or arrested and detained him in custody, or a bill of attainder was passed depriving him of all his civil rights, he would take his seat as member for Northampton this session, though on the question by what means he would effect this he would keep his own counsel. At the Leeds assizes, on Saturday, William Bray, a comic singer, sued the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany for damages for injuries sustained in a collision a t Norrnanton on tha sth January of last year. The plaintiff had been ill ever since, and it was stated to be doubtful if he will be able to resume his professional duties, at all events not for twelve months to come. He kept a beer- house, in addition to which lie earned, before the accident, from one to two guineas per night. The jury found a ver- dict for the plaintiff, and he was awarded £l6OO damages. TERninLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—An extraordinary and terrible explosion occurred in the Coedcae New Steam Col- liery, in the Rhondda Valley, on Saturday night., Two men went down the shaft a short distance for the purpose of re- pairing some damage which had been done. An explosion took place, and both perished. An exploring party proceeded to descend soon afterwards, but the cage had only been lowered a few yards when a second explosion happened, The cage and the men were blown to the surface, but the poor fellows, except one, then fell down the shaft. The per- sons at the top saw one man clinging to the gearing, and began to try to save him, but, a dense volume of smoke then issuing from the pit, he lost his hold, and, like the others, fell down the shaft. In all, it is said, six men were killed and many injured. The houses near the mine were shaken as though by an earthquake, and the shock of the explosion was felt at a dietance of three miles.

THE NEW RULES or PROCEDURE.—The committee of the National Liberal Federation have issued a circular to the Federated Associations on the new rules, asking them to con- sider the deitirability of at once offering Her Majesty's Ministers their support in passing the rules, which, after anxious and mature deliberation, they have submitted to Parliament as absolutely necessary for the purpose in view. Not only, they say, are the Tories opposed to these rules, but at the instanca of a Liberal member who has given notice of an amendment opposition is threatened from another quarter. It seems imperative that Liberal organisa- tions throughout the country should in the strongest manner, and without a moment's delay, express their determination that the whole strength of the Liberal party should be put forth in support of the Government in the present crisis. MILITARY OPINION OF THE CHANNEL TUNNEL.— General Lord Chelmsford, Genettl Sir John Ayde, and Baron Henry de Worms were present on Saturday night at the presentation of prizes to Rifle Volunteers, at the Wool- wich Royal Arsenal. Lord Chelmsford, in testifying, his appreciation of the value of the Volunteer force as a means of national defelce, referred to the Windsor Review, and said that never uring" his military career had he been more gratified then when he witnessed that most splendid sight. From a soldier's point of view the conduct and discipline of the Volunteers Was most admirable. As to the Channel Tunnel scheme, it was possible it might become a danger to be at all events watched and guarclod. Sir John Adye, Surveyor-General of Ordnance, remarked that he had in- spected the Channel Tunnel within the last few days, and walked half mile through it from the Dover end of the channel, and certainly it did not present to his mind the prospect of any great danger to this country. A narrow channel terminating with small hole did not seem to him difficult of defence or distruetion.

THE SLEEP OF INFANTS.—The infant should sleep in its I own little bed or cot, should be allowed to sleep when it likes, and may pass three parts of its life in sleep. It should be • put to bed at regular hours, and the bed should be so soft , that the little body finds rest in every part. The infant shoullbe kept warm while sleeping. The atmosphere of the room should be pure and comfortably warm, and the air should not be excluded. All artificial methods of causing , sleep are bad. Walking about with the child and rocking and jogging it are bad habits. Once taught these habits • children fail to go to sleep without them, and they create disturbed sieep, dreams, and startings which load to feverish fretting the next day. Soothing syrups, laudanum, poppies, and all sleeping drugs are most injurious as a means of pro- ducing sleep, and should only be used under competent medical advice. They ought to be excluded from the houses of all persons who call themselves respectable, except, when prescribed, under medical direction. The sleep of the child should never be disturbed by noises and sudden surprises. It is most hurtful te take up an infant from its quiet repose to show it to strangers, .or to amuse it in e-aslight, candle- light, or lamplight. The bedroom should he airy, light and ciean, and while the cot should be shaded, sunlight when present should be freely admitted.—Dr. B. W. Richardson, in House and Horn!. Mns. GLA.DsToNE.--The writer of a biographical sketch of Mrs. Gladstone in House and Home, an excellent publication for the household, speaking of her solicitude for the people, says :—" It is for the rural population of Ha.warden she is concerned. Then their attention is directed to their culture, to their moral and physical elevation, and to their spiritual progress. She encourages floriculture and horticulture among them, and stimulates in the cottages a spirit of rivalry re- garding the neatness, order, and cleanliness of their homes. It is thus that she exerts her influence in improving the houses and homes of Hawarden ; and in all these beneficient and benevolent works she is heatily suppotted by her family, while her distinguished husband delights to take part in local efforts for the common good. Her kindly sympathies are also evoked in aid of the dwellers in large centres of popula- tion and industry, who have none of the natural advantages of air and sunshine, trees and flowers which are the common property cf villagers. In London, Mrs. Gladstone's name is associated with such benevolent movements as homes for working girls, convalescent homes, hospitals, and other in- stitutions for the relief of the suffering, or the amelioration of the condition of the people. Mrs. Gladstone is in svm- paty with all the more prominent movements for increasing the well. being of the people. But her philanthrophies ex- emplify the adage—' If you want anything well done, do it yourself; ' and probably her best work for humanity has been done under her own personal direction and supervision."

Snow fell in considerable quantities in several parts of the country on Wednesday. It is stated that Major Bond has commenced an action for libel against Mr. Jesse Collings. M.P., claiming £5,000 as damages. Between thirty and forty persons were injured by a pas- senger train and:a goods train coming into collision atreter- head on Wednesday._ _ _ _ _

_ Messrs. Ciowes and Johnson, the released farmers, on Wed- nesday, each received a cheque for £5OO from the Home Office by way of compensation. At Plymouth, on Tuesday afternoon, the Rev. H. Wheeler was hurrying home to prepare to officiate at a funeral, when he fell dead on the steps of his house. Mr. Wheeler was grand chaplain of England of the Order of Good Te mplars. Eleven of the crew of the ship Bosphorus have arrived at Liverpool, and report the loss of their vessel op the coast of Tripoli. The mate and eight seamen were drowned through the capsizing of a boat. The imprisonment of the Rev. S. F. Green was discussed on Wednesday in the Upper House of Canterbury Convoca- tion, and a very carefully worded resolution condemning the course taken by the promoters of the suit was passed. An inquest was held at Tipton, on Monday, on the two boys who were drowned by their brother, a youth named Hindelong. A verdict of wilful murder was returned against the prisoner, of whose insanity scarcely a doubt can be felt. Esther Pay was again charged at Westminster Police Court, on Wednesday, with having murdered the girl Georgina Moore. A woollen scarf found in the Medway was identified as belonging to the prisoner. The case was further adjourned. On Wednesday the Barnsley magistrates committed John Charlesworth, miger, of Thorncliffe collieries, for two months, for wilfully removing a lead plug from a safety lamp, and lighting it with a naked light in workings where over 70 men were employed. Thomas Harvey has been sentenced, at the Thames Police Court, to two months' hard labour for unseemly disturbance in a Wesleyan Chapel in Stepney. He spoke loudly and roughly, swore freely, and assaulted a sergeant of police and others who interfered to preserve orde rand decency. An important conference of poor law guardians and over- seers was held in London on Wednesday on the subject of local assessments. Resolutions were adopted in favour of a more equitable assessment of rates, so that outgoing occupiers may be liable only for a period proportionate to the term of their occupancy. At the Liverpool Police Court, on Tuesday, William Shimming, a warehouseman, was committed for trial, charged, on his own confession, with having set fire to a cotton shed on the wharf of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Company on Sunday evening, the sth inst. The fire des- troyed 1,000 bales of cotton and 4,000 sacks of wheat, the damage being estimated at £4,000. . It appears from a Post Office Savings Bank return, issued on Wednesday, that the amount of deposits have increased from £1,300,000 in /880 to £1,600,000 last year, while the depositors have increased in the same period from 400,000 to 700,000. The average amount of each deposit has fallen from .-.C3 ss. in 1880 to £2 ss. in 1881. The inquest on the bodies of the two men who were killed by the explosion of a tank on board the flat Leader, in the Brantley-Moore Dock, Liverpool, on the 4th instant, was concluded on Wednesday. Evidence was given that an indiarubber washer between the escape pipe and tank had not been cut out in the centre, and had stopped the escape of steam. The jury found that the deceased were acciden- tally killed through the neglect of John Nisbet t, the man who fitted the pipes.

At Marylebone Police Court, on Wednesday, David Atkins and James Harris were again charged, on remand, with stealing the picture "Monarch of the meadows." A statement by Atkins was read, in which he threw the blame on Harris, and also a statement by Harris who declared that the picture was really stolen by a man named Dehore. The magistrate committed both prisoners for trial. A meeting of the General Council of the National Reform Union was held on Tuesday at Manchester. A resolution was unanimously passed recognising the neces- sity that had been forced upon the Government of so alter- ing the forms of parliamentary procedure as to adapt them to the present condition of the House of Commons, and call- ing upon the Liberal party both in Parliament and in the country to give the Government such support as will enable them to carry out this most important work. Other resolu- tions were passed protesting against the unconstitutional action of the majority of the House of Commons, by which Mr. Bradlaugh is debarred from taking his seat and North- ampton is deprived of half of its electoral influence, and relating to the city ftanchise and corrupt practices at elections.

CONVOCATION OF THE PROVINCE OF Yonx.—On Wed- nesday the Archbishop of York, replying to the gravamen adopted by the Lower House on Tuesday relative to the Rev. S. F. Green's case, explained how matters with re- ference to that case at present stand. Mr. Green, he said, should submit himself to his Bishop—a step which a clergy- man who had made a solemn oath to obey the monitions of his Bishop might very consistently take. That was the only feasible mode apparent to him by which Mr.' Green could extricate himself from his present position. His grace -quoted a letter from the Home Secretary with reference to the matter, in which the opinion was expressed that " the powers of the Crown to discharge persons from custody could not be rightly or even constitutionally exercised in the case of a person impriSoned for contempt of Court and com- mitted for persistent disobedience to the lawful commands of a competent tribunal." It was not possible for the bishops, as wfis desired, to appeal to Her Majesty in person to effect the release of Mr. Green. Notwithstanding what had occurred, the bishops were anxious to embrace any feasible method of releasing Mr. Green which would be consistent with the duty of the Crown, the Church and the country. A resolution was afterwards carried in both Houses declaring "that to avoid unseemly litigation it is desirable to make provision by canon for appeasing diversities of ritual and teaching by the pastoral authority of the Bishop, and no suit chould be commenced in the Ecclesiastical Courts without the permission of the Bishop after exercising the powers so accorded to him." —Both Houses of the Convocation of the Province of York met on Tuesday for the transaction of business. The Prolo- cutor brought under notice the case of the Rev. S. F. Green in the form of a gravamen declaring that the continued im- prisonment of a clergyman of that province for not acknow- ledging the spiritual authority of a Court which is now under consideration by a Royal Commission was a per- plexity and scandal to that House and the Church at large. This proposition was subsequently moved in the Lower House by the Dean of York, and seconded by the Rey. Canon Owen, and on a division was declared carried by 38 votes to 18. A further resolution declared that while the Lower House did not feel called upon to commit itself to any expression of opinion on Mr. Green's conduct, it requested the Upper House- to take some united action, either by an address to the Queen or otherwise, which might lead to the removal of the scandal complained of by the release of Mr. Green. At the joint meeting of the two 'Houses, a motion was agreed to requesting the President to direct the appointment of a committee to consider and report upon the constitution and management of Queen Anne's Bounty.

A WOMitN'S STUDY OF HUSBANDS.—We hear much about the art of winning a husband. Let us take a step further and make a study out of keeping a husband. If he is worth winning he is worth keeping. This is a wicked world, and man is dreadfully mortal. Let us take him just as he is, not as he ought to be. In the first place he is very weak. The wife must spend the first two years in discovering all these weaknesses, count them on her fingers, and learn them by heart. The fingers of both hands will not be too many. Then let her study up these weaknesses, a mesh for every one, and the secret is hers. Is he fond of a good dinner? Let her tighten the mesh around him with fragrant coffee, light bread, and good things generally, and reach his heart through his stomach. Is he fond of flattery about his looks? Let her study the dictionary for sweet words, if her supply gives out. Does he like to hear her talk about his brilliant intellect? Let her pore over the encyclopmlia to give variety to the depth of her admiration. Flattery is a good thing to study up, at all hazards, in its delicate shades; but it must be skilfully done. Is he fond of beauty? Here's the rub—let her be bright and tidy, that is half the victory. Next, let her bang her hair (metaphorically) and keep up with the times. A husband who sees his wife look like other people is not going to consider her "broken down." Though it is a common en eer that a woman has admitted that her sex considers more, in marrying, the tastes of her, friends than her own, yet it 4 must not be considered ludi- crous that a man looks at hi wife with the same eves that other people do. Is he fond of literary matters? Listen to him with wide•open eyes when he talks of them. A man doesn't care so much for a literary wife if only she be literary enough to appreciate him. If she have literary in- clinations, let her keep them to herself. Men love to be big and gteat to their wives. That's the reason why a helpless little woman can marry three times to a sensible, self-reliant woman's none. Cultivate helplessness. Is he curious? Oh, then, you have a treasure; you can always keep him if you I have a secret, and only keep it carefully. Is he jealous? ; Then, woman, this is not for you; cease reading; cease tor- turing that fretted heart which wants you for its own, and I teach him confidence. Is he ugly in temper and fault;•find- ing ? Give him a close of his own medicine, skilfully done. Is he deceitful? Pity him for his weakness, treat him as one who is born with a physical defect, but put your wits to work—it is a bad case. It is well not to be too tame. Men ; do not waste their powder and shot on hens and barnyard ; fowls; they like the pleasure of pursuing wild game—quail I and grouse and deer. A quail is a good model for a wife— neat and trim, with a pretty, swift way about it, and just a ; little capricious. Never let yourself become an old story; ;be just a little uncertain. Another important fact is, don't be too good; it hurts his feelings and becomes monotonous. Cultivate a pleasant voice, so that this very mortal man may have his conscience prick him when he is in jeopardy; its pleasant ring will haunt him much ,more than a shrill ; one. It is hard to do all this, besides taking care of the babies and looking after vexatious household cares, and . smiling when he comes home; bat it seems necessary. At ; ; the same time, gade-wife, keep from trying any of these , things on any other mortal man bat your own. These rules iare only evolved in order to "keep a husband." The poor, weak creature would rather be good than bad, and it is ' woman's duty to help him by every means in her power.— San Francisco Argonaut. MILL BROW GENTLEMEN (RUNCORN) V. NEWTOWN.— The above clubs met on Saturday last, and after a close and exciting game the match was won by the Gentle- men. The scores were—Mill Brow Gentlemen : 1 try, 8 touchdowns, 4 minor points. Newtown : 1 try, 4 touch- downs, 3 minor points. OCGIITRINGTON PARK V. NEWTON•LE-WILLOWS (ASS°. cuTioNl.—A very enjoyable game was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, which resulted in favour of Oughtrington Park by three goals to nil. The game was chiefly alkound. play, Dudgeon playing well for the visitors and Tunnicliffe for the home team. NEWrOWN VICTORIA. V. RUNCORN ROVERS.—Thie match was played on Saturday last, and resulted in a victory for Newtown. Score, 2 tries, 7 minor points, to 1 try, 7 minor points. LATCHFORD V. WARRINGTON FREE WANDERERS.—The return match between these clubs was played on Saturday on the Latchford ground, and resulted in a decisive victory for the home team, the score being—Latchford: 1 goal, 3 tries, G minor points: Wanderers : 2 touchdowns. •

•At the Eastern Police Court, Glasgow, on Thursday, James Elder was remitted for 43 hours on a charge of having been found in Clyde-steeet, Calton, with a coffin containing a dead body in his po.:.,session, of which he could give no account. On Wednesday night Elder was seen to go into a cemetery in the east end of the city, having under his arm what appeared to be a coffin. He is sexton of the cemetery, which is closed except for the laitholders who have obtained permission to use it from the authorities. The police having been apprised of the circumstances took Elder into custody, and a coffin found in his possession was placed in the mor- tuary at the Eastern police office. The coffin contained the dead body of a female child, about two years of age. Elder declined to explain how the body came into his possession, and for the purpose of making inquiries into the mystery he was detained by the police. The affair has created a great sensation in the east end of Glasgow. . .

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

The angle-iron smiths, platers' rivetters, and holders-up connected with the Liverpool and Birkenhead Boilermakers' and Iron Shipbuilders' Society are agitating for an advance of V; per cent. in wages. The Royal Commission on Mines is still engaged upon the investigation of the South Wales coalfields. Com- menced at Christmas, the inquiry was interrupted by the necessity for putting up fresh apparatus. This is nearly finished, and the commissioners expect to return to South Wales in the course of the present month.' The best proof of the continued revival in the iron in- dustry, so far as the Wigan district is concerned, is shown by the increasing production at the works of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company. At the close of the directors' meeting a week ago the, the blast was put on an ad- ditional furnace, which makes seven out of ten in opera- tion. An interview took place on Tuesday afternoon between a deputation from the operative cotton spinners of North and North-East Lancashire and the Central Committee of the Masters' Association, at Manchester. The operatives with- drew their recent application for an advance of wages, and put forward one in favour of substituting payment by indi- cator for payment by weight as at present, but this was re- fused by the masters' committee. Colonel Albert D. Shaw, United States Consul in Man- chester, in his annual report to the Department of State, gives the result of the exhaustive inquiry recently made by him into the complaints of the extensive adulteration of American cotton. Colonel Shaw, whilst of opinion that the great bulk of cotton from his country is honestly placed in the market, yet finds the complaints well grounded to a lamentable extent, and suggests as a clank upon fraudulent practices that every bale of cotton should contain evidence of its source, in order to afford a prompt means of tracing any malpractices. IRONWORKERS' WAGES. - On Monday, at a meeting in Wolverhampton of the Iron Trade Wages Board, the em- ployers' offer was accepted to give the ironworkers in Staffordshire, Shropshire, Worcestershire Lancashire, Derby- shire, and South Yorkshire the same Worcestershire, as bad been conceded to the Cleveland men, namely, 9d. per ton for puddling and 7-1 per cent, for mill work. This puts an end to the sliding scale, but it was understood that before April 30 the Board will re-assemble with a view to arrange a new scale.

DANGERS IN COALMINING.—Mr. Crawford has received a 1 letter from the home Secretary to the effect that he fears the deputation which attended the Home Office on February 2nd misapprehended some remarks he made on that occa- sion. He certainly did not think it right to encourage too sanguine expectations that all the objects desired could be accomplished by legislation, but he did not intend to convey an opinion that no legislation was required. On the con- trary, he thought the subject capable of considerable amend- ment, and they might rely upon his giving it most careful consideration, with a view of obviating the terrible risks to which the lives of miners were exposed. THE LABOUR MARKET.—The labour market has entered on few important changes during the week. Owing to the continued mildness of the weather the household collieries have not been so busy, but steam and gas colliers as a rule continue well employed. A national conference of em- ployers and employed in the coal trade will probably soon be arranged in London. The iron and steel trades at tile lead- ing centres are well engaged, and at Sheffield, Barrow-in- Furness, and Middlesborough there is special activity. At Wolverhampton most of the works are well under contract. At Birmingham the hardware branches show some dulness, but the miscellaneous trades of the town are generally well employed. THE MINERS AND THE HOME SECRETARY. A corres- pondence has been issued by the miners representatives of Great Britain, relative to a recent interview with the Home Secretary regarding the proposed amendment in the Mines Regulation Act. The deputation, after the interview, wrote to the Home Secretary telling him his reply had given general dissatisfaction. The deputation were fully aware of the great difficulty there must be in making any extensive changes in the Mines Regulation Act, but considering the great loss of life and injury to limb inflicted is connection with mining operations they expected the Home Secretary would have been enabled to hold out some hope that the subject would be dealt with, in order that loss of life and injuries might be reduced to a minimum. The Home Secre- tary replied, promising the matter his attention. THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE: MANCHESTER, Wed- nesday.—The coal trade of this district continues very de- pressed. In the Manchester district the pits are still being kept on full time, but stocks are accumulating heavily ; whilst in the West-Lancashire districts, with a large number of the pits not going more than three or four days a week, supplies are also in excess of regairements. The return of milder weather has tended to check the slight improvement in the house-fire coal trade, and in other classes of fuel for ironenaking, locomotive use, and trade purposes generally there has been a less active inquiry. The leading Manches- ter firms are still holding for their late rates, but there is a good deal of underselling, and where stocks have to be forced upon the market very low prices have to be taken. Conces- sions of about 6,1, per ton upon round coals have been pretty general since the commencement of the month, and Os. represents the average figure at which best coal can now in most cases be bought at the pit mouth ; second qualities average about 75., and common round coals from ss. upwards. : Burgy is quoted at 4s. 63. to 55., good slack 3s. 91 to 45., and common sorts 3s. to 31. 31. per ton. In the shipping trade there has been rather more doing, but supplies both at Liverpool and Garston are still plent4l, and low prices are quoted. Coke for iron-making purposes is in fair demand, at about late rates.

THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE : MANCHESTER, Wed- nesday.—There is still only a very limited amount of buy- ing going on in the iron market of this district, and prices during the week have been decidedly easier. Both consumers and dealers, as a rule, hold so much iron that their require- ments are generally covered for the present, and although the large deliveries which makers have still to complete enable them to be fairly steady in their quotations second- hand holders display a good deal of weakness, and there is underselling going on to a tolerable large extent. Lancashire makers of pig iron are now sellers up to the end of June at at about 51s. to 51s. GI per ton, less 2, for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, but they are unable to secure new orders. Lincolnshire brands are this week quoted by makers at 50s. Gd. to 515., less 4., delivered equal to Manchester, and there are sellers at quite is. per ton under these figures. Local finished iron makers are so well supplied with work that they are generally indifferent about further -orders at present, and £7 per ton remains their nominal quotation for bars delivered into the Manchester district, but second-hand lots are offered at £6 155., and hoops are now quoted at £7 to £7 ss. per ton. There is no material change to notice in the condition of the local engineering trades ; toolmakers, machinists, millwrights, and founders continue generally well employed, and in the heavier branches—such as -locomotive builders and boiler makers—there is plenty of work stirring.

The contest for the vacant seat at Taunton was decided on Thursday. Mr. Allsopp, Conservative, was returned by a majority of 227 votes over Lord Kilcoursie. The result does not affect the relative strength of parties in the House. A pretty girl told her beau that she was a mind reader. "You don't say so!" he exclaimed. "Yes," said she, "you have it in mind to ask me to be your wife, but you are just a little scared at the idea." Their wedding cards are oat. Some people are so very auxioas lezt men should be spoiled by the possession of too much money that they strive to get it all themselves. This kind of philanthropy is not uncommon.

Information received from Lloyd's on Thursday, states that the steamer North Eastern, of Hull, 1070 tons register, has foundered in the North Sea with all hands, 25 in num- ber. She sailed from Granton for Copenhagen on the oth , January, and has not been heard of since, and, as the passage , is usually made in about four or five days, all hopes of her , arrival have been given up. . At the Rotherham Police Court, on Thursday, Messrs. Steel, Toozer, and Hampton, Limited, Phcenix Bessemer 1 Steel Works, Rotherham, pleaded guilty, and were fined the 1 maximum penalty of £5 and costs for an offence against the Factory Act. The defendants had allowed a youth, 17 years of age, to work for 40 consecutive hours, at the end of which perio I he was instantaneously killed by the accidental break- age of a fly wheel. The Queen, accompanied by Princess Beatrice, arrived at Buckingham Palace, London, on Thursday from Osborne. While driving from Victoria Station to the Palace, through , St. James's Park, one of the out-riders preceding the Royal carriage was thrown from his horse, sustaining some in- : juries. A crowd speedily assembled, and cheered loudly , when it•was found that the accident boded no harm to her , Majesty. Nevertheless it was reported through London that the Queen had been injured. A question was put on the subject in the House of Commons, when Lord Harting- ton gave a prompt contradiction to the story. The ninth annual conference of the Licensed Victuallers' National Defence League was commenced on Wednesday at I Chester. The report of the Council referred in detail to the ' measures affecting the liquor trade announced to be brought before the House of Commons, and urged that efforts should be made by the licensed victuallers to secure their just rights. It was pointed out that the small income at the command of the League, compared with the vast sums subscribed to carry on, the work of the United King- dom Alliance, made the battle between them a most un- equal one. Two outrages were perp'etrated in Edinburgh on Wednes- day evening by means of infernal machines. Two box( s , were consigned to different houses, and on each being opened 1 there was an explosion, resulting in injury to eight persens. 1 Charles Costello, alias Johnstone, a mason, was taken into custody in connection with the outrages the same night, and it seemed that the prisoner had written threatening letters to both Miss Barron and Mr. Macdonald, to whom the boxes were sent. It is feared that Alexander Macdonald, one of the injured, may lose the sight of one eye, and a girl named . Galloway has been seriously burned. div.head: EXTRAORDINARY FRAUDS BY A WOMAN.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY FRAUDS BY A WOMAN.

The further the investigation proceeds the more startling does the career of the adventuress now in custody at Bk. raineham for frauds committed while ;personating Lord Arthur Pelham Clinton, appear. The frauds already discovered exceed £15,500. It is believed that the womah has a large amount of the proceeds invested, and efforts are being made to ascertain where the money has been placed. The police have received a letter from a near relative of the late Lord Arthur Pelham Clinton, giving full particulars of that person's death. One result of the ingestigation of the correspondence seized has been to cause the authorities to intimate to Gething's relatives that no further opposition will be offered to an application for his release on bail. Mrs. Ward was induced to furnish the story of her daughter's engagement to Furneaux while she was masquerading as a man at their house. The subject was introduced one after. noon by Furneaux remarking that her daughter wanted but one thing to make her complete, and that was the wedding ring. "He" offered to . supply the deficiency, and the girl, who was of age, accepted the offer with hesitation, because of the difference in their position. Furneaux banished her scruples by asserting that " he" should never again marry a lady of position. The wedding ring was purchased, but the wedding being impossible until "his lordship's" period of hiding was at an end, the ring was pledged. The poor girl was led to believe that the Prince of Wales was taking a deep interest • in the engagement, and Furneaux produced numerous letters "from the Prince." In one the Prince was made to announce that he had placed a monument over the grave of Lord Arthur Clinton's first wife, Annie, who was drowned in the Serpentine, and to express the hope that the wife he had arranged to marry was neither poor nor ugly. The pseudo lord wrote a reply to this epistle, assuring the Prince that Miss Ward was neither poor, old, nor ugly. The letters to the Prince, which were often entrusted to the Wards to post, are described by Mrs. Ward to have been so saucy at times that she often rebuked "His Lordship " for his impel*. tinence. Upon one occasion when Furneaux returned from a pretended visit to the Queen, for which purpose she had assumed man's attire, she showed them a wills formally drawn up on parchment, bearing immense seals, and having Her Majesty's aname written upon it, as attesting its provisions. By thisßocument the sham lord bequeathed -£5,000 to Mrs. Ward and " his "intended wife, with various .other legacies to members of the Gething family. Furneaux complained that the neighbourhood in which they were then living was not fashionable, and Mrs. Ward was persuaded to relinquish a lucrative business and remove elsewhere. Her means soon became exhausted, and the loans for which she had become surety falling due a distress was levied. Furneaux became unable to meet the bills of exchange she had negotiated -with a Birmingham builder, and was compelled to leave town. She removed to Liverpool, whither Miss Ward accompanied her. The ad- venturess appears to have been so sorely pressed that she was afraid to go outside the house, but Miss Ward was de- spatched every moruing to a post-office for letters, Furneaux professing to be in daily communication with the Priece of Wales. Mrs. Ward ultimately was unable to find a penny to support them, and she ordered her daughter to return. Furneaux then took the situation of attendant at the Prest- wich Asylum, notwithstanding their denouncing " his" conduct in moving among a number of women. Mrs. Ward and her daughter were almost starving in the meantime, and Bishop and Gething fetched Furneaux from the Asylum, and she went on to Bristol and Oxford "to see Lord Cole- ridge," afterwards acting as a governess at Preston Bissett, and eventually settling down at Liverpool. Furneaux here made the acquaintance of Miss Horan, a lady of property, and Miss Ward was very much slighted in consequence. Miss Horan declared that Fred, by which name Miss Fur- neaux was generally addressed, had never cared for the girl. This was repeated to Miss Ward, and subsequently Furneaux wrote announcing that she was married. Miss Ward, who. had been so devoted to her lover that she had even pledged her trinkets and clothing to find the adventuress money, became affected in her mind. She was painfully excited by the impression that Fred was taking away her character, and at last her reason entirely gave way, and she has since been an inmate of the Rubery Hill Asylum. When the Prince of Wales visited Packington Hall a few years ago Miss Ward was taken there by Furneaux, who borrowed the best articles of dress the family could find him. The woman pretended to have an interview with the Prince, and returned with the news that "Jenny pleased him very much, as he could see honesty written in her face." Among the documents which have come to light is one relating to Furneaux's dealings with a Liverpool phrenologist. In one of these the phrenologist gives an opinion of Furneaux's character. He says: "Your integrity is ngicloubted, and perseverance unceasing. You are clever in carrying out whatever you undertake. You are refined and courteous in manner." Miss Horan, the young lady in Liverpool to whom the prisoner was paying her addresses, was a teacher in a Sunday-school, but fell ill some time ago. The super- intendent wrote to Miss Horan congratulating her on her restoration to health, and requesting her to take charge cf her old class and bring Furneaux with her. The superin- tendent expressed a with that Furneaux would take charge of one of the lower classes. In another letter prisoner is specially invited to attend a prayer meeting. The most striking proof of her hypocrisy is to be found in a long letter on "the future state." The writer says :---" In an- swer to Miss loran's question, Do the dead ever visit the earth ? I must first explain that immediately after death the soul separates from the body, goes either to heaven or hell, or purgatory. Then St. Paul says in his epistle to the Philippians, i. 23 desire to be dissolved in Christ.' And again we read of the soul going to hell immediately after death, in Luke xvi., 22d verse, 'The rich man also died arid was buried in hell.' Now in direct answer to the question I have to say that according to,the natural course of things souls cannot leave their place of sojourn after death, and they are entirely cut off frem their converse with the living, but by a special disposition of Divine Providenca. they may leave their place of abode for a time and appear to the living to benefit them. They continue in their pre- sent state of punishment or happiness, which is not interrupted by their appearance to the living. We have several instances of apparitions in eccle- siastical history. Then St. Augustine refers to Felix the Martyr when he appeared to the inhabitants of Nola when they were besieged by the barbarians. St.. Martin of Tours commanded one of the damned souls to ap- pear, as we read in the Lives of the Saints,' by Butler. So far for theology. Sometimes apparitions of this kiad happen during sleeping or waking hours, by the operation or agency of good or evil spirits for the instruction of the-liv- ing. As a rule we must be very slow in believing that any apparitions of persons dead are real." The forged letters of Lord Cole, idge are of a most audacious character. In one letter she makes Lord Coleridge sag, "Your sister is toler- ably well. I expect her home shortly. She is very stu'n- born, and will not come unlees she thinks proper. She is very eccentric I assure you, but in the main she is good. I am not at all well myself. as I have got rheumatism in the body and limbs." Sonic of the letters are written upon forms of the High Court of Justice, Queen's Bench Division. How the woman obtained possession of these forms is a mystery. On Saturday, two letters were discovered in which the name of Sir R. A. Cross, the late Home Secretary, had been forged. One of the letters runs as follows:—" Case is under special jurisdiction, and no doubt a speedy settlement may be relied upon. You will hear again from the Court directly any steps are ordered, and will give freedom In your trying cases." A letter was received on Sunday from a Liverpool gentleman named Pettitt, stating that he is also a victim Of the frauds. Furneaux bad reported hsrself to be an heiress, and had nearly ruined him and his family. Messrs. Burman and Rigbey, the Bit minaham solicitors, who are prosecuting the woman Furneaux ou behalf of one of the dupes, Edward Bsynon, of Selly Oak, are in commu- nication with the Treasury, and they have no doubt the prosecution will be undertaken by the Home Office. Upon searching the papers handed over by their client they fora:id bn Wednesday a " security " for £5OO bearing the forged signature of the late Lord Justice Lush, in addition to the names of Lord Coleridge and the Earl of Lanesborougb, whose forged signatures appear on so many of the docu- ments given as security to most of the victims. The solici- tors also discovered a promissory note for £6,000, given by the adventuress to their client. The "consideration " paid by Mr. Beynon for the promissory note did not represent more than £2,000, the extra £4,000 being the interest he expected to receive. At the Birmingham Police Court, on Thureday, Miss Figneaux, alias "Lord Clinton," 43, and James Cretheing, 42, engineer, Clark-streeti.Birmingliarn, were charged with forgery and fraud at Birmingham and Liverpool and other places during the past eight years. There were at least a hundred nersons present who had suffered directly or in- directly from the pseudo "Lord Clinton." Many of them had corns expressly from Liverpool and other distant places to see " his lordship" in the dock. The appearance of the woman was greeted with a suppressed hiss, but she bore her self with much greater composure than during her previous appearance before the court. She is above the medium height, and wore a fashionable Newmarket coat of a peculiar cut about the chest, and it was evidently intended that tI g garment might be the more readily convertible when re- quired to complete her assumption of male attire. Her features are altogether unprepossessing, and are rather signid- c int of craft and cunning than of intelligence. Her face is thin aud angular, and her upper teeth slightly project, leaving the lips partly open. Her chain recedes d the jaw hears an e lower raw bears a • strong resemblance to the published portraits of the potoyops Lefroy. The partly open mouth is a pehuliarety distinctly to be recognised throughout the entire series of her ortraits which are in possession of the police, i and s spech ly marked in the photograph of the woman in her convict dress ten 3-ears ago. Mr. Rigby, of the firm of Burm.an and Rigby, the, prosecuting soliciters for Mr. Ben- yon, in replying for a remand, said that since last week the case had assumed a greater magnitude than was at first anticipated. It covered a large area, and a larger number persona had bsen defrauded tan was previously .believed.. He had, in consequence of this discovery, considered it necessary to- put himself in communicat.ion with the Home Office, and on Thursday morning he received a reply stating that the public prosecutor would take up the case. A large bundle of forged documents were handed in to the magisa trates' clerk as already haying been discovered, Mr. Rigl y added that he lead in his hand a document purporting to le shined by Iler Majesty thee Queen, Lord Straithnairn, Lord Litton, Colonel Collins, Sir Thomas Biddulph, Lord Gran- ville, and Lord Coleridge; and another bearing the signaa tares of Lords Coleridge and Lush, Sir John Bennet, and Frederick Earl of Lanesburgli. The remand was unwed. An application. was then made for Gething's liberation on bail. The police did not oppose it, and two sureties of £5O were accepted for his appearance.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

The breach of promise case against John James Water- worth, landlord of the Egerton Arms, Bridge-street, Run- corn, has been the topic of the week in that town. The question of whether Waterworth would be called upon to pay his former servant's legal costs in the suit has greatly exercised the local quid-nucs. As they appear quite unable to arrive at a conclusion on the point, I may inform them that Waterworth will have the exquisite satisfaction of pay- !ng both his own and Miss Banner's costs. The value of a good supply of water is something like that of money—one only needs to be without it to know how extremely useful it is. The Runcorn Waterworks' Com- pany have had many difficulties to contend with since the concern was started, but managed to steer their commercial barque into comparatively still waters, and the outlook, as far as dividend is is concerned, seems to be very good. An unexpected difficulty in the company's path has, however, made its appearance within the last few days. This arises from the fact that the Mersey Salt and Brine Company are now pushing forward their works with considerable rapidity, and some of the officials, or friends, of the Waterworks' Company have made the discovery that the pipes in which the brine is to be conveyed, will be placed within about 100 yards of the splendid well from which the supply of domestic water for Runcorn and the two adjoining township is obtained, it is feared that if any of the pipes belong to the Salt and Brine Company should at any time leak, the liquid from them may percolate through the adjoining soil into the well, and so render the water belonging to the Runcorn com- pany impure, and consequently useless for some purposes. The Waterworks Co. directors have, I understand, carefully considered the question, and they have come to the decision that it is of such importance that they are compelled to take immediate action with the object of seeing if some engineering plan cannot be devised which will render such a contingency impossible. lam sure that all your readers in Runcorn and the neinghbourhood will wish them every success. There has been some talk in Widnes concerning the style in which many of those present at the Parish Church con- gregational tea party conducted themselves. Mr. H. Wade. Deacon kindly, presided, and it must have proved very annoying to those connected with the place who are lovers of good manners, to hear the sharp roproof which the Vicar (the Rev. J. Wright-Williams) had to give to those who ought to be more under the control of their spiritual teachers. I understand that the Vicar's appeals for better behaviour, based on the ground that a gentleman of standing in the town had taken the chair, were met with cool con- tempt. The School Board and other educational agencies in Widnes have, apparently, a very heavy task set before them.

Within a short period the members of the Whines Local Board have had several meetings, to which reporters have not been admitted, at which the solemn subject of debate has been the conduct of the ts% o surveyors in their service. It seems that for several years past Mr. Higginson, the old sur- veyor, worked pleasantly with the Board, but some four years ago anothergentleman was introduced upon the scene in the person of Mr. Copland, who, at first, was understood to be that gentleman's assistant. By-and-bye little un- pleasantnesses cropped up, showing that the two surveyors did not work very harmoniously together—probably, on the old principle that two of a trade never agree. Mr. Copland is no doubt a gentleman of undoubted abilitiv, and it is to be hoped that the insinuations that his wishes towards Mr. Higginson are not of the most friendly character are not well founded. At last the matter in dispute reached what Mrs. Malaprop would call a " cripus ; " and the Beard agreed, at their meeting on Wednesday, that the representatives of the fourth-estate should be allowed to remain whilst the ques- tion was thoroughly considered. Mr. Kershaw, chairman of the Highway Committee, began the attack by telling the Board what a good friend he was of Mr. Higginson's, and then, I suppose as a proof of his title to this dear name, he weat on to dissect the surveyor, and presented the members with a map, PO to speak, drawn on a large scale, in which they could see what pro- fessed to be an account of that gentleman's pecadillos. Dr. O'Keeffe maintained that Mr. Higginson had not had fair play for some:timed, and urged that if Mr. Copland was his assistant, the Highway Committee ought to put him in his place, and see that the old surveyor had the privilege of his position accorded to him. Mr. Eustace Carey—a gentleman with the critical faculty very largely developed—whilst acknowledging that Mr. HigginsoWs business abilities did not strike him as by any means pro- found, admitted that he believed they were capable of improvement, and that the work he had done for the Health , Committee had been fairly carried out. Mr. Benjamin ; Brown proved a stout friend of Mr. Higginson; and on the motion of Mr. Kershaw, that that gentleman be asked to re- sign, being put, it only received three votes in a well attended meeting, whilst Mr. Sbuttleworth's amendment, that no , change be made, for the present, in the surveyor's depart- I ment, was carrried by a large majority. At a time when" miscarriage of justice," is appearing with disquieting frequency at the head of items of news, it is 1 reassuring to find that there are still empanneled from time ; to time juries having as trong sense of the responsibility rest- I ing upon them. So strong, indeed does it occasionally appear as to lead to ludicrous results. I was rather amused by the action of a Bristol jury, for instance, who at the assizes on Monday, sent to the Lord Chief Justice of England a mes- sage to the effect that "they wanted to look for themselves at the law," a request which elicited from Lord Coleridge, I whose direction was inferentially disputed, the remark that the message was "the most extraordinary which a judge ; ever received from a jury." The circumstance to which this incident was due, was the indictment of a German named Charles Goes, of Manchester, for embezzling money belong- ing to his employers, who are millers aui biscuit makers at Bristol and Newport. The question Was raised whether the accused was agent or servant tp the prosecutors, and Lord Coleridge directed the jury to find a verdict of "Not guilty." This, however, a portion of the jury refused to do, and made known their wish to sift the law further. His Lordship discharged the jury, and as the prosecutors deter- mined not to proceed with the evidence on other indictments, Goes was set at liberty, the Judge remarking, however, that there was abundant evidence that he had mis- conducted himself and appropriated his employers' money. When there was such evidence before them, I cannot blame the jury very much for the course they adopted in their desire to prevent one whom they believed to be guilty escaping punishment for miscon- duct, especially as his lordship had himself decided, in the earlier stages of the case, that if the prisoner were convicted he should reserve a question for the Appeal Court, while later, on being more fully informed as to the decisions in previous cases, he directed an acquittal. The lovers of music in :the district will be gratified with the intelligence that a stand is being made against a practice that has of late been growing amongst professionals, of neg- lecting to attend rehearsals prior to appearing before the public. As a consequence of the disposition thus manifested ; to make their own convenience paramount, patrons of con- ; certs have bad from time to time to be contented with the rendering of music, written with full orchestral accompani- ment, with no other instrumental embellishment than ; a pianoforte afforded, or, at best, with the orchestral accom- paniment played, far less effectively than under the more favourable circumstances of proper rehearsal, would have been the the case. Mr. De Jorg, of Manchester, is endeavouring, however, to strike a blow at the practice before it becomes too firmly rooted to resist attack. This led to an extraordinary scene at the last of his series of con- certs on Saturday evening. Amongst the vocalists engaged were a "concert party," cimprising Mdme. Sinico, Mdlle. Verdini, Signor Tecchi, and Signor Campobello—the last- named being the entrepreneur—with Herr Lowenthal as their accompanist. Madame Sinico's scena from " Der Freischiitz " was rendered, after some delay, in a way that showed there was a lack of sympathy between the singer and the orchestra,—due to the lady having requested the instru- mentalists at a moment's notice to play the scena a semi- tone lower than the key in which it is written—and consi- derable delay occurred in the appearance of Signor Campo- bello. When he emerged from the ante-room he displayed no immediate intention of ascending the platform. Mr. De Jong meanwhile occupied his position at the conductor's desk; and gradually signs of impatience began to be ex- hibited by the large audience. Presently the voice of Signor Campobello was beard calling Mr. De Jong by name, and then the latter turned and addressed the audience. He was understood to say that he had again to complain of the non-attendance of singers at rehearsals, and as Signor Cam- pobello declined to sing the composition in its integrity, he suggested that his services should be dispensed with. An almost unanimous response in the affirmative came from the audience, and Mr. De Jong was about to proceed with the " Faust " selection when Signor Campobello appeared on the platform and attempted to address the audience who, however, sternly repulsed him amid a storm of hisses. On retiring, Signor Campobello spoke to the different members of his party, and insisted upon their leaving the hall with himself. Bldlle. Verdini and Signor Tecchl were anxious to remain, but Signor Campobello would not permit this, and the whole party left at the conclusion of the first part of the concert. The only remaining vocalist was Mr. Barton M'Guckin, who sang some extra songs. Mr. De Jong, at the suggestion of the audience, sent for his flute and played several solos, and with this assistance a successful concert was given, the audience applauding every item vociferously. Mr. De Jong acknowledged the sympathy shown him in the difficulty, and announced his intention to give half the amount of the salaries of the absent vocalists to the funds of some local charity. Mr. De Jong will receive the semi-, pathy not only of concert goers in Manchester, but of all who are anxious for the most artistie, production of the best works; and I sincerely hope that he will continue to strive to secure that end.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY FEBRUARY 18, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY FEBRUARY 18, 1882.

Alter the recent sermon by the Bishop of Manchester, in which he put the end of the world before his hearers as a proximate event, and quoted Mr. Proctor as an authority respecting the possible mode in which this might be accom- plished, one is inclined to look forward to the year 1896 with some misgiving. With such a near approach of the end of all things it might be permissable to rest on one's oars, for what is the use of labouring from morn till night to.accumulate a little store of filthy lucre, to seek "the bubble reputation," or to provide for posterity, when at the close of 14 years the book of the worid's history is to be closed? Why should I seek by anxious thought and care- fulness to obtain means to educate the bairn who has not yet cut his first tooth when accepting Mr. Proctor's hypothesis, I have reason to believe that his brief career will be closed with that of the rest of mankind long before the time at which, in the ordinary course of things, his wisdom teeth would appear? A shadow of hope is given, however, in a letter on the subject of "Astronomical Portents," by the Rev. Thomas Mackereth, F.R.A.S., described by a writer in the Spectator as " at once an astronomer and a man of •faith." Mr. Mackereth, referring to the Bishop of Man- chester's sermon, states that the bishop's quotation from Mr. Proctor about a comet falling into the sun, "and forming , such an accession of heat that the earth and all that is therein will be burned up," is a pure speculation, and with little or no foundation in fact. Further, Mr. Mackereth states that "no one knows of what comets consist. They are not self-luminous, nor are they either opaque or solid bodies. In density they are not supposed to differ from the density of our atmosphere at the surface of the earth. If, therefore, we know not actually of what they consist,. and yet they are such flimsy things, we need not fear for any conflagra- tion they can cause." Thanks, Mr. Mackereth, for your reassuring comments. But, unhappily, another argument of a disquieting character, leading to nearly the same conclusion as Mr. Proctor's comet theory, has been recalled to my mind. Some years ago, in my voracity for literature, I read some- where, I don't know where, an argument to the effect that each thousand years of thc world's history is analogous to a day of the week, and that as there are only six week days and then a day of rest, so a great change—the milennium— , may be expected at the expiration of 6,000 years. Accord- ' ing to the chronological tables there were 4,004 years before Christ, and 1996 more will complete the 6,000, so that Mr. Proctor receives support from a quarter he has not looked to for confirmation of his conclusions that the world has almost run its course. FLACCUS.

THE WIDNES PARISH CHURCH TEA PARTY.—The sum I realised by this tea party, held last week, together with sub- scriptions, amounted to nearly £4O. Mn. MARE DOW, the American gift king, will give his entertainment in the Drill Hal!, Widnes, this (Saturday) evening, and also on Monday evening next. VISIT OF THE ROCK BIND TO RUNCORN.—OR Tuesday evening this company visited the Temperance Hall, and gave their musical performances on an instrument entirely composed of stones taken from Skiddaw and the neighbour- hood. The announcement may seem a little farcial to those who have not had the exquisite pleasure of hearing the band, who were received most enthusiastically by a delighted audience. The singing of the ladies connected with the company was of an exceptionally high character, and we feel sure that should they visit the town again, they will be warmly welcomed. HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL lAPROVEMENT ' SOCIETY.—A meeting in connection with the al,ove society was held in the Girls' schoolroom, on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. W. Haydock presided, and there was a good atten- dance. A paper entitled "Agricultural Depression " was read by Mr. T. Wright, at the conclusion of which a dis- cussion was opened, the following members taking part : The Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. J. W. Haddock, J. Haddock, T. Miller, R. Tandy, G. Crute, J. Lambert, M. Leach, J. Hancock, and W. Philips. THE FIRST MARRIAGE AT HALTON WESLEYAN CHAPEL. —The Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Halton, is now licensed for the solemnization of marriages. The first ceremony of this character within its walls took place on Wednesday, the officiating minister being the Rev. J. Bateman. The I couple united in the "holy bonds" were Mr. W. H. Brad- bury and Miss Martha Jane Haddock. In conformity with an , old custom, the pair were presented with a Bible and a I hymn book. Mr. R. N. Davies, on behalf of the trustees of the chapel, made the presentation. TEBAY v. THE MANCHESTER, SHEFFIELD, AND LIN. COLNSHIRE RAILWAY COMPANY.—On Monday, in the Chan- eery Division of the High Court of Justice, Mr. Badcock moved es parte before Vice-Chancellor Hall, for an interim injunction restraining the Widnes Local Board from raising the surface of a road over a railway bridge leading to the plaintiff's property. A motion was pending in the matter, and was to come on on Thursday, but in the meanwhile, the learned counsel stated the Local Board were rapidly pro- ceeding with the work of raising the surface of the road. His Lordship said he could not interfere at the present stage' I and refused to grant the injunction. THE LATE MISS E. H. JONES, OF HALTON.—OR Mon- day the remains of Miss E. H. Jones were consigned to their last resting place at Great Budworth churchyard. The de- ceased lady was the daughter of the late Rev. Richard Jones, a former incumbent of Little Leigh. Miss Jones, with her sisters, since deceased, came to Halton about 48 years ago, and conducted a ladies' first-class school at Sum- mer Hill. In consequence of advancing years, they gave up I the school several years ago. The deceased was also an lactive church member, and up to twelve months ago was the honorary secretary of the Halton Parochial Clothing Society. The funeral was conducted in the generally observed simple style. Preceding the hearse was a private carriage containing Dr. Carruthers. The first mourning I coach contained Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., Mr. A. Thomas, , J.P., and Mr. Thomas Wright. In respect to the deceased, I the residents of Halton drew their blinds down, and the I shops were closed. The coffin was of oak, covered with black cloth, with brass mountings, the shield bearing the inscrip- tion, "Eliza H. Jones, born July sth, 1798, died Jna. 9th, 1882." The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. Thomas Wright, of Halton.

MARRIAGE AT HALTON.—On Thursday, the village of Halton was gay with flags and bunting, notwithstanding the very unpropitious state of the weather, owing to the mar- riage of Miss Mary Elizabeth Wylde, oldest daughter of the late Mr. Samuel Wylde, ofHalton-road, to Mr. J. S. Nolan/ of Birkenhead. The ceremony took place at Halton Church, and the party were taken to their destination in nine carriages. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. J. W. Barran, of Sideburgh, assisted by the Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar of Halton. The bride was given away by her brother, Mr. Samuel Wylde; and her three sisters, Miss Louisa, Miss Ethel, and Miss Mabel Wylde, officiated as her brides- maids. Mr. Astley Cooper and Masters John and Edward Wylde were the groomsmen. The bride wore a satin dress trimmed with flowers and lace, with a wreath and veil; and the costumes of two of her bridesmaids—the Misses Louisa and Ethel Wylde— consisted of Gainsborough hats, dresses of nun's cloth, with cream-coloured skirts, pompadoured with blue and yellow brocade, and trimmed with May's satin bows. The third bridesmaid—Miss Mabel Wylde—wore a somewhat different but equally charming pink and ivory coloured dress, and pink satin hat trimmed with white lace. Each of the bridesmaids carried a basket of flowers. Among the persons present at the ceremony, including the wedding party, were Mr. and Mrs. Edward Bolton, Mr. and Mrs. Gillbanks, Mr. and Mrs. J.
