ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES.—About double the

amount required for the repair fund of this building, was produced by the bazaar held in November last. As the necessary amount of £250 has been raised, the church will now be consecrated by the Lord Bishop of Liverpool. It is expected that the ceremony will take place in April next. UNITED KINGDOM] ALLIANCE MEETING AT RUNCORN.— On Monday eveniag a meeting will be held in Bethesda Con- gregational school-room, Runcorn, under the auspices of the United Kingdom Alliance. Mr. John Paton will lecture on ! "The liquor traffic—a poacher on the domain of labour." No charge will be made for admissioa. THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY COM- PANY.—The report of the London and North-Western Rail- way Company states that the net profit for the half-year was £2,560,429, against £2,400,595 in the corresponding period of 1880, showing an increase of £65,834. Deducting in- terest on debenture stock and loans, the available sum is £2,127,081, out of which it is proposed to pay a dividend, as already announced, at the rate of 8 per cent. per annum on the ordinary stock, leaving, with £43,372 brought down, £69,979 to be carried forward. LACEY-STREET BAND Cc HOPE, WIDNES.—On Monday evening, a meeting of this society was held in the school- room. The Rev. J. Tesseyman was announced to preside, but was not able to fulfil his engagement. Among the prin- cipal items of the programme was a song entitled "Close the shutters," by Miss Lewis; a recitation, " Touch not the glass," by E. Webb ea dialogue, "The right road," in which H. Wright and F. 'Rowlands took part ; a duet by Messrs. Rylands and Travis;. a recitation called "The death of an inebriate," by J.. Barrows•; and other items of a similar char- acter'. In the cours3 of the evening several hymns were sung by the Band of Hope children. COTTAGE LECTURES-AT FARNWORTM—A series of cottage lectures have been commenced in the parish of Farnworth since the Rev. G. Bond has succeeded the previous incumbent in the cure of the souls therein. Their object is the religious education, if the term may be used, of the working classes, and it is hoped.- that by their means many who do not usually attend church may be brought within the sphere of religious teaching. A lecture is given each week ; and so far they have met with a fair measure of success. No doubt, as they become more widely fenown the attendance will in- crease. . RUNCORN YO,UNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.—A meeting of the committee of this association was held on the evening of the 10111 inst. Forty-five new members were propased-24 by Mr. Nickson, the newly appointed secretary. It was stated...that about £2B had been collected by various friends. This, with Mr. Robert Shaw's subscription of £lO, and other contributions, will enable the comnfittee to clear off the debt. This result, which has been brought about so speedily, is highly satisfactory, and reflects the greatest credit upon those who have been instrum:ntal in bringing it about. CATHOLIC BALL AT WIDNES.—The fourteenth annuli ! ball under the auspices of the Widnes Catholics took place on Monday evening, at the Volunteer Hall, and proved very successful. No attempt of any magnitude had Len made in the way of decoration, but the building was well lighted, and this, together with the charming costumes of the ladies and the captivating strains of Mr. C. Pow-ell's excellent ! string band, made up of a very brilliant and effective spectacle. The upper end of the hall was reserved for the dancers, and the lower was partitioned off by a screen, behind which light refreshments might be obtained. At eleven o'clock, there could not have been fewer than several hehadceds of people present, and the proceedings were kept up with the greatest liveliness until some bolus after mid- night. Mr. John Tallon, jour. was M.C., and the following gentlemen acted as stewards :—Messrs. A. Tracey, T. Smith, 'l'. Stoner, C. Flynn, W. Murphy, W. Hubbersty, J. Quinn, T. Mulvaney, J. Carrol, J. Carrolan, P. D'Arcy, T. Mullon, H. Loughlin, J. Tracey, P. Whelan, and R. Forster. The ball was under the auspices of the authorities at St. Mary's Church, and the preliminary arrangements were carried out by a committee of which Mr. John Quinn is president, and which comprised Messrs. P. Tallon, J. Whelan, senr., G. Brown, E. Gould, J. Fitzpatrick, J. Hewitt, Dr. O'Keeffe' J. Whelan junr., W. Atherton, J. Tansey, J. Donoghue, W. Gallagher, M. Quinn, —. Leatherbarrow, J. Jameson, J. E. Johnson, J. Newton, and J. Tilley. Mr. John Tr.llon, senr. acted as treasurer to the committee, and Mr. Samuel Quinn as secretary. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A WIDNES PLATELAYER,— On Tuesday, an inquest was held by Mr. William Hardy (acting as temporary deputy for Mr. Driffiald), at the Railway Inn, Waterloo-road, on the body of Samuel Taylor, platelayer, formerly in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Co. Evidence was given by the wife of deceased, who lives in Waterloo-road; William Dobson, railway porter; Thomas Jackson, platelayer; and Dr. McDonnell. Deceased was a very stout man, 56 years of age. On the 26th July last he was working under Jackson, who was his foreman, and as he was crossing the platform at the station, to go for his wages' he accidentally fell, hurt his thigh, and was very much shaken. He, however, managed to walk home, and followed his work until the 29th of the same month, when his foreman told him to go home and rest until he was better. Taylor was attended by Dr. McDonnell up to the time of his ' death. He complained of having been badly shaken, and I said he had a pain over the liver. There was no fracture, I and the doctor gave it as his opinion that the primary cause of death was diseased liver. No doubt the fall produced inflammatory symptoms. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." Rtis7CORN HALTON-ROAD WJSLEYAN TRACT SOCIETY.— On Thursday evening, a public tea meeting in connection ! with the above society was held in the Mill Brow Sunday School. The tables were presided over by several ladies,mem- bers of the congregation at Halton-road chapel. After tea, a public meeting was held in the same building. Mr. J. R. Frith occupied the chair, and was supported by the Revs G. I Hack aud J. Bateman, and Messrs. W. Shaw and R. Nor- man.—Mr. W. Shaw (secretary) read the report, which stated that for some months the society had been going down, and one object of the meeting that night was to give it a little impetus, and set it again on a substantial basis. ! Unfortunately, the attendance at the tea party had not been so large as was anticipated, and he was sorry to say that he I believed they would be compelled to appeal to the generosity ! of the congregation for funds to carry on the work of dis- tributing tracts.—The Chairman; in the course of a few re- marks, said the abject of the meeting was the ;eet_herance of the cause of God. He bel:eved the Gespel had been instra- mental in making a great number of people happy, and it was the duty of all who were f o,sessed of that great bless- ing to do their utmost to extet d its principles among the less fortunate of mankind. He thought the simple tract had often proved a wonderful means of winning people over ! to Christ. There were many people who were never at a place of worship, and who, but for the tract distributors, would never hear about the glorious news of salvation. The work was one on which God smiled approvingly, and if they ' would only look to Him for help and guidance he felt sure that great good would result from their labours.—The Rev. G. Hack made a few very encouraging observations to the members of Halton-roacf chapel, and said he believed there would be a lime, and that not far distant, when their chapel would have better congregations, and better days in every respect. He thoroughly believed in the efficacy of prayer. ! "More prayer" had been his song ever since he had come to Runcorn, and he should still continue to sing it. He was glad to be able to state that he had never but once preached in Halton-road chapel without havine several "enquirers," and that was a very encouraging state of things. However, all the magnificent success that had been obtained, and all they were hoping in the future to accomplish, had not been, and would not be by their own exertions, but merely in answer to prayer. In conclusion, he urged upon them the necessity of asking God's blessing and help on all they did, feeling assured that success would crown their efforts, as it was an immutable law that where faithful work was carried on success must be the result.—The meeting was afterwards addressed by the Rev. J. Bateman, and Messrs. B. Kniveton, R. Norman, S. Pope, and B. Smith. LANCASHIRE INDEPENDENT COLLEGE BAZAAR.—The preparations for the grand county bazaar to be held in Man- chester ha May in aid of the funds of the Lancashire Inde- pendent College, Whalley Range, are in an advanced state, and the bazaar seems likely to be a great success. It is intended, mainly, to remove a heavy debt under the burden of which the college has been working for several years. The increasing applications for admission to the institution compelled the committee in 1875 to undertake extensive alterations and enlargements. Amongst other improvements the students' rooms were made larger and more comfortable, and their number was increased to GO ; a commodious new library and assembly room, available for various purposes, was added ; three spacious' lecture rooms, with common rooms for professors and students, were built; the entrance hall was remodelled, better provision was made for cases of sickness, and the interior was completely repaired and decorated. The whole scheme involved an outlay of nearly £23,000, of which a little under £9.000 remains as a debt. It is hoped to raise by the bazaar at least £lO,OOO. Should this hope be realised, of which there seems little if any doubt, the balance remaining after the debt has been paid ' will be devoted to some useful purpose in connection with the work of ministerial education. But the anticipation of the promoters do not end here. They trust that the bazaar may be the means of very largely increasing the interest 'felt in the college, and generally in the training of ministers for the denomination, and that in future the churches will accord the institution more liberal support. The scheme has been taken up by the churches in the county with great heartiness. Not one probably will be unrepresented in St. James's Hall, when the sale opens on the 2nd of May. It was clear to the committee from the first that no ordinary building would be sufficiently large for their requirements, and they therefore secured the new structure in Oxford- street known as St. James's Hall, the vast proportions of which render it well suited for such a purpose. The interior of the hall will be transformed so as to represent a German medimval town. What has been called a branch of the bazaar will be held in St. George's Hall, Liverpool, in the last week in larch. The Liverpool churches have joined very cordially in the scheme, but it has been felt that, in- stead of sending their contributions to Manchester, it wauld be better for them to hold a sale in Liverpool in anticipa- tion of the greater event in this city. 211aRchester Examiner.
PROPOSED PENSION FUND FOR RAILWAY SERVANTS.-

A correspondent, writing last night, says the directors of the London and North-Western Railway are proposing to form a pension fund, for the bedefit of their faithful servants. The main feature of the scheme is, that a servant, after subscribing 2d. per week to the fund, for not less than 20 years, will be entitled, at the age of 65, to a retiring pension of 103. per week. Hitherto a man at 60 has been obliged by the rules of the service to leave it, and indeed so far as my experience goes, I have seldom seen an , employ 6 beyond that age fit to remain. The district delegates called a meeting at Widnes at six p.m. to night, for the purpose of puttinc, the propositions of the directors to the vote, and so touched were the .feelings of the work- men by the unwonted love shown them by the masters in this matter, that at meeting time they were still overcome, and only one man, appeared. He was too much " moved "to move a vote of thanks. "Ingratitude, thou marble-hearted fiend !',

RuNconx Courrs COURT.—At this court, on Tues- day, before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, Mr. Gratebatch, of Stoke-upon—Trent, claimed from the London and North- Western Railway Co. £3 12; being the value of 1 ton 2 cwt. 1 qr. of ochre which was short in a consignment of 20 tons sent.to Messrs. Tempest and Son, paper manufac- turers, Little Eaton,. near Derby. Mr. Richardson, barrister, Stockport, appeared for the plaintiff, and the company was represented by Mr. Preston. From the evidence it appeared that the plaintiff's agent at Runcorn consigned 20 tons of ochre to Messrs. Tempest and Son on the 7th. and Bth November. Previous to placing the material in the railway company's-wagons at Runcorn, it was weighed and found correct. On arriving at Little Eaton the wagons were run into Messrs, Tempests' works where they were weighed when, full and when empty. The difference of the two weighings showed that only 18 tons 17 cwt. 3 qrs. of the chemical had been received. The weight of one of the wagons, number 24,371 was stated to be 4 tons 18 cwt. 2 qrs. when empty. Mr. Preston, for the defence, contended that each wagon bad been incorrectly weighed, and be calle4 Samuel Arrow- smith,.weighing clerk at Earlestown Junction Wagon Works, who stated that the wagon 24,371, when weighed by him, on the 15th February, 1872, weighed 3 tons 16 cwt. 3 qrs. The weight of the wagon on the 10th inst., when he again specially weighed it, was 3 tons 18 cwt. 14 lbs. Mr. Richar- dson said as this accounted for a ton of the ochre, he would not further press the case. His honour gave judgment for the defendants with costs.

A YOUNG MAN DROWNED AT RUNCORN,-At tl- e- • Runcorn Town Hall, on Wednesday, Mr. Worsley, deputy coroner, held an inquiry into the circumstances of the death of a young _man named Theodore Eccleston, who was drowned on Saturday night in the Weston Point Canal.— Daniel Eceleston said the deceased, his son, was by trade a whitesmith, and on the previous day was 24 years of age. The last time be saw him alive was at half-past four on Sat- urday afternoon. He left home about five o'clock, and was perfectly sober and quite well. The deceased usually took a drop of drink on Saturday nights.—By a Juryman: The deceased was keeping company with a young woman at Weston Point, and had to return home by the canal.—Wm. Ainsworth, Wright's-row, Weston Point, said he was return- ing to that place on Saturday night about half-past eleven, and when about 150 yards along the canal bank he met the deceased coming towards Runcorn. Witness said to him, "Good night. Be careful and keep out of the cut." At the corner he passed two sailors who were intoxicated. Deceased had had some drink, but was .sober, . and could walk quite steadily. He told him to be careful because he saw he had taken something. It was not dark, and the lamps on the other side of the canal were lighted.—The Coroner: No doubt the lamps would be very misleading to the poor fellow. Mr. Croley : There have been several persons drowned at the place where deceased was found.—Mr. Blease : The deceased told me not long since that be was in the canal a few weeks ago.—Thomas Hulse, Lunt's-row, Weston Point, said he dragged the canal on Monday night, and found the body of the deceased in Parr's Lock.—Sergeant Walley deposed that he was at Parr's Lock when the bady was taken out. Eccleston was fully dressed, and there were no marks of violence on the body. He found in his pocket a necklet, a knife, the sum of 2s. 2d., and other articles. He had fre- quently seen the deceased the worse for drink on Saturday nights.—A juryman (Mr. Yarwood) asked whi•ther the deceased had given his wages to his parents on Saturday.— Sergeant Walley said he asked his mother whether be had given her any money, and she stated that be had paid her on Saturday as usual.—The Coroner said that from the evi- dence given the jury could only return a verdict of "Found drowned," as there was no evidence to show precisely how the deceased met his death.—The jury accordingly returned that verdict.

SAD ACCIDENT IT WIDNES.-011 Saturday an in- quest was held by Mr. T. W. Barker, deputy coroner, at the Simm's Cross Hotel, Widnes, touching the death of Edward Evans, a brakesman lately in the employ of the Alkali Co., which took place on the previous Thursday, from injuries received on the 3ri instant. Richard Bevan, engine driver, West-street, said he was in the employ of the Alkali Co. On the 3id instant, about a quarter past five in the afternoon, he was on his engine, shunting some wagons from the main line of the London and North-Western Railway Company, into a siding belonging to his employers. There were wagons both before and beside the engine, and they had shunted some into the siding, which were stationary. Evans went round the engine for the purpose of uncoupling some of the wagons which the engine was pushing. Immediately after he had lost sight of Evans, he heard a scream, and, on looking out, saw that he had been caught between the coal bunker of the engine and one of the, stationary wagons. Evans called out "I am done, Dick." Witness at once re- versed his engine, got off, and went to the assistance of the deceased, who was taken home, e;here he died the Fame day. Deceased was injured about the thigh.—By the Foreman : The wagons had been placed on the line by deceased, at an earlier portion of the day. It was part of Evans's duty to uncouple them.—John Whitfield, horse driver in the service of the Alkali Co., deposed that he lived in William-street, and was on duty when the accident occurred. He did not see deceased before it happened, bat, on hearing him say "I am done, Dick," he went to his assistance. Deceased said nothing to him about there haying been any negligence on the part of any one.—Mrs. Evans, wife of deceased, who lives in Charles-street, stated that when her husband was brought home he did not attach blame to any one. She was of opinion that the sad occurence had been quite accidental. —The Coroner, in summing up, said there appeared to be no doubt as to the manner ih which the deceased met his death. ne only question for the jury was whether or not there was any biaZ2c illtaehed any one. If Evans had been under the control of the engine blame might have been attributabte to him, but such case. Then, as to was noi utr, uncoupling the wagons whilst the engine xst.: ,t.?. ifl. motion, such might be a responsible practice, but no donbt ft was sometimes necessary, and they found that railway servants and others who became familiarised with danger, were in the habit of incurring all sorts of needless risks. It was very difficult for the railway companies, or any other bodies, to prevent their servants doing such things. In the present else, he did not see that blame • could he attributed to any one.—The Foreman was of opinion that there ought to be a Space left between stationary wagons and the next line of rails.—The engine driver was at this part of the proceedings, recalled, and, in reply to the Coroner, stated that not only was time deceased independent of him, but he was actually under Evans' order, being obliged to move when the deceased told him.—The Coroner : That alters the case.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," to which they added a rider in favour of a space being, in future, left be- tween the stationary wagons and the next line of rails.

ACTION AGAINST WIDNES MANURE MANUFACTURERS. —On Saturday, at the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Chitty, was heard an action, Adelphi Bank, Limited, v. Edwards, on a bill of exchange, and involved two other actions. Mr. C. Russell, Q.C.,. M.P., and Mr. French were for the plaintiffs; and Gully with Mr. Lumb appeared for the defendant. Mr. Ambrose, Q.C., and Mr. Kennedy represented the defendant in the other claims.—Mr. Russell, in his opening, said the defendant had been living at a place near Corwen, and on the 4th August last, he accepted a draft which had been drawn up by Messrs. John Knight and Co., and the circumstances of the case would be found to be similar to the following two cases in the cause list : G. C. Dabell and Co. al. Edwards, and Adelphi Bank (Limited) v. Davies and Edwards; in fact, the same question would decide all three. Messrs. Knight and Co. carried on business as manure manufacturers at Widnes, and the defendant, Mr. Edward Edwards, was a small farmer and agent for their manures. Not only that, but Mr. Edwards acted as collector to Messrs. Knight and Co., and from time to time he received money on their behalf, which he was in the habit of repaying to his principals by the form of an acceptance already alluded to, the different sums amounting only to between £2O and £3O. On the 4th August the sum of £22 2s. was due from the defendant to Messrs. Knight. The latter drew up a bill for that amount, which was accepted by the defendant. The next thing Mr. Edwards knew of the matter was after Messrs. Knight's representative had come into Liverpool and dis- counted a bill at 5 per cent. at the Adelphi Bank' the words of which ran as follow :—" Four months after date pay to our order at London two hundred and twentv-two pounds two shillings, for value received." These wor-ds were regu- larly written, and in unbroken lines, and in the corner of the bill were the figures £222 23. When the bill became due Messrs. Knightabsconded, and the bill was dishonoured, with others upon various other people in Wales, who had also been agents for the manures. The defendant refused to pay on the ground that he had only given the acceptance for £22 2s. It would be conceded by the other side that the first figure 2 had been placed on the note between the X and the second 2, and that where there was a blank on the bill, between the words " London " and " twenty," the three words "two hundred and" had been added. It might be mentioned that the bill was drawn up on paper bearing a 2s. stamp, which would carry a much larger amount than £22. The plaintiffs were willing to accept the defendant's explana- tion, but they urged that allowing such blanks to pass upon a bill of exchange was tantamount to great carelessness on the part of Mr. Edwards. For the defence it was submitted that the blanks on the document did not excite the defen- dant's notice, neither did the fact that there was a 3s. stamp on the paper, where a threehalfpenny one would have suf- ficed. Evidence was then taken, but as it became more apparent that the whole three actions involved important questions of law as well as of fact, it was agreed that his lordship should hear the arguments in London. The present and other cases were therefore withdrawn.

'TALTON MUTITAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—OR Monday evening, Mr. F. div.head: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS.
div.p: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS.

Under the presidency of the Lord Mayor of York, the annual meeting on behalf of the Wesleyan Home Missions was held in Bold-street Chapel, Warrington, on Thursday 'evening. There was a good audience, and amongst those on the platform were :—The Revs. R. W. Starr, of Liverpool (deputation), J. Eglinton, J. Agar Beet, and Thos. Rippon ; and Messrs. Lamplugh, D. Garnett, Bowes, egx. Devotional exercises having been engaged in, The Rev. J. AGAR BEET said the income of the society for the last year was over £34,000, whilst the expenditure had been £250 below that amount. The income had been spent in helping weak circuits which without that help could hardly be maintained; in supporting ministers in opening new ground—a most successful department of the work; in maintaining a certain number of district missionaries; and also in sending ministers to preach to the soldiers, to the sailors in the navy, and on mercantile ships. The War- rington circuit had contributed to the funds—from yearly collection made in the classes, £l9 4s. 8e1.; congregational collection, £27.;- public meeting, £ll 48.; juvenile associa- tion, £l2 10s.; making with other small sums, a total of I £73. Owing to the affliction in reference to their late dear minister Mr. Hagen, they had received from the fund £5O to enable part of his work to be done by supplies. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, im- pressed upon the audience the de,irability of missionary work being commenced at home, but, he said, it would be of no value if it were not undertaken in a right spirit. Their own spiritual prosperity and health depended greatly upon what they did for the Lord. He should have been a backslider that night, had he not been a worker in the vineyard of God. The Lord blessed his soul, and gave him a desire for the salvation of others, and in trying to help a brother or little child his spiritual strength and power were increased. (Applause.) There was a work for everyone to do, and if they only knew the joy and blessing that came from it, he was sure there would be many hearts laid upon the altar that night, saying" Lord, what would'st thou have me do?" (Applause.) If they were to be successful home missionaries they must join hand in hand with the temper- ance question. (Applause.) He hoped they had connected with the chapel a Wesleyan Temperance Society, and with the school a Band of Hope. (Hear, hear.) The number of cases brought before the magistrates through strong drink was very alarming, and as Christian people, when they saw a great evil in the land they ought to endeavour to reduce it. A home missionary when he went into the house of the poor found it necessary to take teetotalism with him hand in hand with the Gospel, and moderate drinkers had been compelled to join the temperance section on the question. (Applause.) TII9 Rev. T. RIPPON observed that the object of the home missions was alike patriotic and evangelical, and met in this country a great moral need. From the report they learned that 272 churches out of 723 in the Methodist con- nection were aided by this fund, and many other objects, and upwards of 15 missionaries were engaged in travelling from village to village. They who lived in towns were apt to overlook the villages, to which they were indebted. Their churches bad reaped from the villages their best divines, and the world its foremost men of thought, but they had been neglected socially, politically, and religiously. (Hear, hear.) For a long time the villager was under the heel of the landlord; to-day to a considerable extent he was under the foot of the priest. Popery, which was thought to be dead and buried as far as this country was concerned, bed shame a wonderful sense of vitality, and had come back to them home grown, nurtured within the national church. He could a tale unfold, even in fair Cheshire, of how the black ox trod on the foot of the poor, of how charities were denied the Dissentws, of how the parson formed the conscience of the landlord, who in turn formed the conscience of the tenant. He held that 'Metho- dism 4as well fitted to cope with error and superstition in the villages for the reason that other Nonconformist churches lacked lay agency. He hoped that the best minis- ' ters in the Wesleyan connection would be sent to country circuits—that they would seek them, and not shun them, as they did now. He noticed that it was considered going down hill to be sent to a country circuit. But why should it be so? Was it regarded as a lowering in status when a clergy- man of the Church of England was appointed to a country parish? No, if the living was a good one. (Laughter.) The difficulty with the Wesleyans was a financial one, and if they could meet that they would soon tide over the trouble. Having referred to the missionary help needed by the Shetland islands, Mr. Rippon commented on the religious , census taken in London and Bristol, comparing with them ' the number of persons who entered public-houses during a given time; and asked was not the demon they were called upon to fight strong drink? (Hear, bear, and applause.) It was darkening homes, blighting lives, hindering the churches, and sending more souls to hell than all the Wes- , leyan ministers were the means of saving. Let them get to work ; whether it was done by men or women, boys or girls, regularly or irregularly. In fighting the devil any weapon was legitimate. He thanked God personally for the work that had been done and was being , done by the Salvation Army. (Hear, hear.) One blessed result of their work had been to waken the Wesleyan and other churches to the necessity of adopting the means to the end in the evangelisation of the uncared-for outcasts of our , towns and villages. He mentioned this to say that the I'Vesleyans could do the work of the Salvation Army, and shame upon them if they did not. But it was being done in two parts of the Warrington circuit—in Buttermarket-street and in Silver-street. There men and women were going Sabbath after Sabbath, often amid showers of stones, to witness for Christ; but they must continue to do it one and all. Then let them get to work, right work, for Christ ; not talking so much about it but doing it. (Applause.) Rev. R. W. STARR then addressed the meeting., relat- ing in a graphic manner the conditions and manner of life of the lower class population in London and Manchester, ; where he had worked for some time as a missionary. He gave some stetis!ici of detected crime, and demonstrated, from a return published by the Chief Constable of Liyer-i pod, that in Chet town since 1375, the number of persons charged with drunkenness had decreased by one third. He attributed this improvelvent to the establishment of cocoa houses, of which there were 45 in Liverpool. On the proposition of Mr. LAMPLUGH, seconded by Mr. D.evin GARNET, a cordial vote of thanks was pissed to the Lord Mayor of York for occupying the chair, and to the Rev. R. W. Starr, the deputation. A collection was then made, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

WORKING OF THE IRISH LAND ACT.—Earl DONOEGITMORE moved for a Select Committee to enquire into the working of recent legislation with reference to land in Ireland, and its effects upon the condition of the country. He asFerted that fhe Land Act had been a failure, although it had been loyally accepted by the landlords, and that the rncie 91_ admintsi..".!!`2ll linthedlate and thorough enquiry. He contended that the decision of the Commissioners in favour of reducing rents had been based upon altogether im- proper grounds.—Lord CARLINGFORD defended the Land Act, and insisted that no inquiry info its operation was needed, as it had only been in force for four months.. He therefore objected to the appointment of a Select Comn;lttee. He contended that the Sub-Commissioners were well chosen, that they had done their work well, and fixed the rents fairly, and he defended the Commissioners in their reduction of the old rents. He hoped their Lordships would not , assent to the proposed inquiry.—The Marquis of WATER- FORD denied that fair rents bad been fixed under the Act. The landlords of Ireland repudiated Griffiths' valuation, on the ground that it did not represent the real value of the land.—The Marquis of LANSDOWNE said the Land Act was tending to gradually annihilate the only class in Ireland who had in good and bad times been loyal to the empire.
LATEST NEWS.
The Journal de St. Petersburg, yesterday denied the reports of an insurrection in Herat.

I Yesterday, the Earl of Wilton was reported 'to be in a very critical condition, having had a very serious relapse during the night. A St. Petersburg telegram of yesterday's date says:— "The formal transfer of Kuldja to China is definitely fixed for the 23rd inst."

Yesterday morning, six farmers' sons were committed for trial by Majot Bond, at Claremorris, for breaking into a farmer's house and threatening his life. Six officers of the Bradford Labourers' Accident and Burial Society have been committed for trial on the chai7e of stealing £127 belonging to the society and falsifying the books.

Intelligence from Lloyd's states that the iron steamer Cleveland, 538 tons register, has foundered in the North sea, and that her crew of 15 men have perished. She sailed from Grimsby on the 4th of last month.

On Thursday, Benjamin Bouch, charged with the murder of two of his children, whom he threw into the Rochdale Canal, at -Manchester, on the evening of the Bth instant, has been committed for trial on the charge of wilful murder. At an adjourned inquest, yesterday, in London, upon William Rowles, aged 52, who died from injuries alleged to have been inflicted on him by three boys on the 29th ult., the jury, after a long deliberation, returned an open verdict.

EASTER SIONDAY REVIEW.—The Mayor of Portsmouth received a telegram last evening from the Committee of Metropolitan Commanding Officers announcing that Ports- mouth has been unanimously selected for the Easter Monday review.

CONSERVATIVES AND THE CLOTURE.—The Council of the National Union of Conservative and Constitutional Associa- tions yesterday unanimously passed a resolution condemn. ing 'the attempt of Mr. Gladstone to suppress freedom of speech in the House of Commons."

Sir William Harcourt has written to Mr. Arnold Morley, M.P., announcing that baying had before him the applica- tion on behalf of Henry Westley, under sentence of death for the murder at Nottingham, be had, after further medical enquiry, advised Her Majesty to respite the capital sentence.

TEE WATERLOO Crr.—Yesterday at Altcar, in the de- ciding course for the Waterloo Cup, Captain Ellison's Snowflight beat Earl of Haddington's Hornpipe, and won, Mr. J. Cr: Winder's ad Macpherson beat Mr. W. Reilly's Princess Dagmar, and won the Waterloo Purse. Mr. L. Pilkington's Debonnaire beat Mr. M. Morrison ad Maid Marian, and won the Waterloo Plate. , PROGRESS OF TIM ELECTRIC LIGHT.—The British Electric Light Company have just completed experiments for light- ing Trentham Hall, the Staffordshire residence of the Duke of Sutherland. The machinery is worked by the engine in the building yard, from whence insulated wires are carried to the hall. The principal drawing-room is very successfully lighted by 16 candescent lamps, giving a most agreeable light. The conservatory and principal staircase are also similarly lighted. ColcvocATro-Nr AND TEE REVISED VERSION.-At the sit. ting of the Convocation of York, on Thursday, a resolution was proposed expressing thanks to the Revisers of the New Testament for "their sustained efforts in the great work entrusted to them," but it met with so much opposition that it was withdrawn. Canon Trevor denounced the Revised Version as an utter disgrace and a schism from the English Bible; and the Archbishop of York held that the substitu- tion of the new translation for the version now in use would be othing less than a disaster.

RENTS IN IRELA.ND. A Parliamentary return, issued yesterday, shows that 1,313 judicial rents have been fixed by the sub-commissioners, affecting 42,802 statute acres and reducing rents from £37,441 to £28,586, with a tenement valuation of £25,849, the former rent of £37,441 having been reduced to £28,586. In some cases it is notified that the judicial rent has been increased on appeal by the com- missioners, and in one case that it has been reduced, whilst in several it is intimated that the order includes provision as regards the labourers. THE EXTRAORDINARY FRAUDS BY A WOMAN.

Another victim of the adventuress was discovered yester- day, but in this case the victim did not live quite long enough to become cognisant of the frauds. The discovery *as made in a strange way. The executors, upon looking over the papers of a lady who died a week or two since, found that she had lent the adventuress £2OO, and. until in- vestigating the securities, the relatives of the deceased were under the belief that the security given for the loan was genuine. A Birmingham photographer states that about nine years since Miss Furnieux called at his studio in female attire, and that she, in response to his statement that he could take her in any costume, immediately altered her collar, put on a scarfe and moustache, and in this masculine transformation had a few carte de visitcs struck off. THE TERRIBLE COLLIERY DISASTER.-72 LIVES
LOST. [CENTRAL NEWS TELEGRAM.] TRIMDON, FRIDAY EVENING.

Up to six o'clock the total number of miners rescued alive is thirty-two, but it is feared that scarcely half those who were in the pit have been recovered. This morning an ex- ploring party went down, but their work was rendered extremely difficult by the heavy falls which they came across. Several bodies were, however, sent up, some of them burned to a cinder. It was ascertained that at the time of the disaster there were over one hundred men in the pit. Mr. Bell, Her Majesty's Inspector of Mines, headed a party of managers and others who proceeded to the bottom of the Trimdon Grange shaft early this morning, and they report at first having distinctly heard voices and knocking, which they believed was caused by the imprisoned men in another part of the mine. The greatest efforts of the search party were now turned in this direction, but to no purpose, and as time went on and the noises were no more beard tie last remnant of hope concerning the safety of a.ny of those still beIQW was dispelled, and it was feared that the dreaded after-damp had overtaken them. The total number of dead is to-night estimated at 72, and this number, it is thought. is only too exact. The colliery all day has been surrounded by thousands of people who have been kept in a state of the greatest anxiety by the various reports which have reached them from below. As day drew on the :press of people round the pit mouth grew so g7fat that the manager found it necessary to give orders to fence off the approac;ieg P!!". neighbouring pits have been laid idle during the work of exploration.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS AND LAND. Mr. JESSE COLLINS gave notice on an early day to move a resolution in favour of facilities being given to agricultural labourers and others, to obtain proprietary rights in land. EDUCATION IN IRELAND Mr. O'SHAUGHNESSY gave noti 2.e to call attention to the working of the Education Acts in Ireland, and to move a resolution. THE REPRESENTATION OF NORTRAMPTON.—The ATTORNEY GENERAL, replying to Mr. Labouchere and Mr. Newdegate, said from what had yet taken place the seat for Northamp- ton was certainly not yet vacant. THE COLLIERY EXPLOSTO:I.—Mr. HIBBERT said a tele- gram had been received from Mr. Bell, stating facts already published, relating to the colliery explosion yesterday. It , further stated that the exploration of the mine was going on ' satisfactorily. Mr. LABOUCHERE AND THE STANDING ORDERS.—Mr. LABOUCIIERE asked whether the resolution passed on February 7, with regard to Mr. Bradlaugh taking the oath, was not opposed to the standing order relating to the same subject.—The SPEAKER said he Saw no inconsistency be- tween the resolution and the standing order, and therefore, the resolution passed on 7th February was quite tegular. PROTECTION IN IRELAND.—Mr. FORSTER replying to Mr. Chaplin said it was intended to give protection to care- takers in Ireland, but the Government must be left to judge the best means by which they could do so. THE ADDRESS.—The adjourned debate on the reception of the report of the address was resumed. Sir W. BASTE- LOTT having criticized the working of the Land Act in Ire- land, passed to the depressed condition of agriculture in 'England. He said that if the ensuing harvest should prove a bad one the ruin of tenant farmers would be complete. Mr. FOWLER admitted that farmers required assistance, bu t he did not think further relief from local taxation would give anything like the relief required. If the land was freed from its trammels our farmers could then enter into compe- tition with America.—Sir B. Leighton, Messrs. Arnold, Pell, Storer, Gregory, O'Sullivan, Heneage, Chaplin, Goschen, Gorst, and other members continued the debate.

div.head: L A.TER'.
div.p: L A.TER'.

One of the bodies bronght up this morniny, has been iden- tified as that of William Jennings, 17, putter. He was found lying between two dead horses, and hill smothered with broken wood and debris. The ventilation is still very defective, but every means is being taken to restore it although it will probably be midnight before further bodies are reached. Water has commenced to accumulate at the bottom of the shaft, and this still further impeded work. The Coroner visited the. colliery to-day, and will open an inquest on the bodies of those recovered to-morrow.

div.head: FRODSIIAM.
div.p: FRODSIIAM.

FRODSIIAM DIY Soto°Ls.—The annual sermons on be- half of the Frodsham day schools were preached in the Iron Church on Sunday, in the morning by the Rev. D. Howell, 8.D., vicar of Wrexham, and in the evening by the Rev.H. B. Blogg, vicar. The collections amounted to £ll ss. 2d., a decrease of upwards of compared with last year.

- . VOLUNTEER SUPPER AT FRODSHAM.—On Saturday even- ing, at the Town Hall, the members of the I Company 2nd C.R.V.C. were entertained to supper by Lieutenants Henry and Harrison. The guests, about GO in number, assembled at 7.30, and having been put through a' preliminary drill by Captain R. Ashton, in the presence of the adjutant of the battalion, Captain Kerr, did justice to the good things pro- vided. After the cloth lead bun removed, the usual loyal toasts were drunk with enthusiasm, and also the healths of Captain Kerr Captain R. Ashton, the hosts, Lieutenants Henry and darrison ; and Sergeant FlanaTan, the drill in- structor, each of whom suitably replied. The baud of the company was in attendance and played a number of selections and several members also enlivened tha proceedings by singing suitable songs, and altogether a very pleasant evening was spent. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, FRODSHAM.—SERMON AND LEctunE.—On Wednesday the Rev. W. Jones, of Dcrby, preached a sermon in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Frodsham, in aid of the trust funds, and a public tea was afterwards provided in the scheol-room. the evening the same gentleman delivered, in the chapel, his popular lecture! entitled " Garfield, the martyred president." The chair was announced to be taken by Henry Linaker, Esq., but a letter, explaining his unavoidable absence, was read by the Rev. J. Picltwell, of Ruccorn, the superintenlent of the circuit. There was a good attendance and the lecture was listened to with the closest attention, the lecturer drawing valuable lessons from the indomitable per- severance of the late president which enabled him to rise from an obscure position to the highest honour which could ha conferred upon him. A vote of thanks, proposed by the Rev. D. Schofield, seconded by Mr. Thomas Hough, was unanimously accorded to the lecturer, chairman, and the ladies, who had presided at the tea in the afternoon.

On Tuesday morning a serious accident occurred on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, near IA igan Station. A pilot engine ran into a goods engine which was standing on the up line, and before an alarm could be given the debris was run into by a special train from Liverpool. A large amount of damage was done to the rolling stock, and a guard named Gannon was seriously injured.

div.head: ,Tatttro to the 6ditor.
div.p: ,Tatttro to the 6ditor.

THE NEXT GENERAL ELECTION. Sir,—l have read with satisfaction of the forethought of the Liberal party in Cheshire in providing themselves with good plain-spoken candidates for the nest general election, be it sooner or later. lamat a loss what to think of their neighbours and fellow politicians in South-West Lancashire for not doing likewise. Let them remember work done in time is done well, a.nd enthusiasm without organisation will not return Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues to office. T. W.
THE WATCH COMMITTEE AND THE BOROUGH
-P-O-LICE CLOTHING,

Sir,—The very wide dissatisfaction which the action of the Watch Committee has occasioned in reference to this I matter is only dimly reflected in our local Parliament. • The explanation our worthy Mayor gave at the last meetirT, of the Council would appear to partially justify their action deciding, as they usually are supposed to do, upon the advice of "a gentleman well qualified to give an opinion on such matters." From close enquiry it appears that, to sl,y the least, the statement as to the fit of our borough police clothing during past years are not justified by the facts, as the reports issued at the annual inspections for the last 10 or 12 years, taken as a whole, will testify; and as to cost, I am informed upon competent authority that the Watch Committee have been better served by local tradesmen in every way than they will find will be the case by the very doubtful course they have now taken. Again, what is to be understood by the 83. 61. argument? It seems very am- biguous, and may, upon examination by practical men, prove nothing but inferiority. The Watch Committee (as advised) have doubtless done what they considered best for the ratepayers' interests, but I am convinced that in local requirements of this ordinary character it is a miitake, and an unjust reflection upon the town, hastily to cast such an aspersion upon its own tradesmen, and which in this instance appears so unnecessary. The simple fact is explained by the committee having selected an inferior article (as a test of economy ?),,which Warrington itself could have supplied. —Yours truly, TOWN TRADE.

ST. HELENS JUNIOR PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. Sir,—Having read a letter from Mr. R. M. Prescott, in your issue of last week, I deem it my duty to answer the charges which he has thought fit to bring forward. In the first place, he begins by stating that the society was formed by Mr. J. C. Westworth. Now, sir, the present society has been formed by a party of young men with whom Messrs. Prescott and Westworth have had not the slightest connec- tion, and worked on an entirely different basis than the pre- ceding one. He also says, "The principal Conservative members have for the past month absented themselves," which he considers a "disgraceful proceeding," and then he gives reasons, which would make it appear that the Conser- vative party being beaten in argument were afraid to put in an appearance. No doubt Mr. R. M. Prescott thinks himself a" mighty debater," and that it is owing to his marvellous oratorical powers that the Conservative members have been driven from the society. Now, sir, it is quite true that Mr. Prescott has done a great deal towards furthering that un- fortunate episode, but in quite a different way than his letter leads people to believe. The behaviour of that gentleman has been such that any one who had any respect for his position in society must have severed his connection with the Junior Debating Society. Do not think, sir, that I am advancing this on my own responsibility; it has been men- tioned to me more than once by members of the Liberal party he eulogises in such glowing Language. To give an instance of his conduct I may mention that while I was a member he apologised three times for his misconduct. On one occasion he set at defiance the Speaker, and told him "he would please himself." So unseemly was his Conduct that en another occasion the Premier moved "that he be ex- pelled from the society," but he "apologised," as usual, and the matter passed over. He also resigned his position as Home Secretary because, to use his own words, "he could not consider himself an orderly Cabinet Minister," and Joined the independent party, where he was in a position of "greater freedom and less responsibility." Again, if further proof be needed of the influence he has had in driving mem- bers away from the society, I think the following will amply suffice. Night after nieht Mr. R. M. Prescott, in conjunc- tion with bis faithful and inseparable colleague of the inde- pendent party, Mr. J. C. Westworth, wasted valuable time in introducing debate on subjects referring personally to themselves, and which, no doubt, were considered of vital importance by those two inspired and egotistical individuals (and which could not strictly be ruled out of order), but which to the rest of the members, who had come to listen to interesting and instructive debate on public affairs, and not to listen to the dismal spouting on the grievances of those two important (in their own opinion) members, was insuffer- ably dry. Finding the time occupied in such a manner, their interest in the society began to die away, and naturally. Many 9f t/I,n 10ft thoroughly disgusted. lie again tries to be misleading. He states that "night after night Mr. ' Matthews has been in his place arguing measures which ot4er Caservative members introduced. This is entirely. 'misleading. The only measitrO (9_9t measures) introduced by another Conservative which Mr. Matthew argued, was the Irish motion. Thus, sir, you will see from the above that the Conservative party, instead of acting from the cowardly motive which he would have you believe, have acted from motives creditable to themselves as members .of that party so well known as the "party of order." Hoping you will excuse me trespassing upon your valuable space, I remain, yours truly, "PEACE WITH HONOUR." February 7th, 1881.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

MUSICAL ENTERTAINMENT AT WINSFORD. Till's rock band visited Winsford, on Tuesday last, and gave a much appreciated entertainmnnt, the Town Hall being well filled. In addition to singing of a quality one lire.es to hear' there was the rock barmonicon which consists of a series of pro- perly graduated stones from the Cumbrian Mountains, and which is played by the Messrs. Till with surprising effect. We may specially instance "Home, sweet home" with variations as pleasurable in the extreme. A SUDDEN DEATH AT _WINSFORD:--Mr. Thomas Light- foot, of Station-road, Winsford, came to a sudden end of life last Saturday. He had gone to Winsford market and was seized with an apoplectic fit, which, within the hour, carried him off. He was the trusted president or the Salt Boilers' Association, and was much respected in the town by all who knew him, Uviie foLICE Comr.—Before Captain Turner, J.P., I there was brought up charged with begging, TI-Lomas Lewis, I of Herefordshire, a lab4urer. The case was proved by P.C. Pearson. The prisoner, who had but recently come out of Manchester gaol for a ,similar offence, was sentenced to seven days' imprisonment at Knutsford with hard labour.—Philip Dodson, a farmer's son, was charged with stealing a ham, the property of Mr. Jamos Barlow, of Egerton Arms, Little Budworth. After the depositions of several witnesses had been taken, Dodson was committed to take his trial at Knutsford. OVER SCHOOL BOARD.—The first meeting of this newly- elected board was held on Tuesday, when there were present the Revs. J. T. Maxwell and Wm. Turner, and Messrs. Daggatt, Hoole, Hulse, Oakes, Smallwood, J. If, Z.ooke. and William Ste-e- ssttendmiCe. ?frrr').—The Clerk explained that the first duty of the board was to appoint the president and vice-president ; and in order to do this a chairman should be elected pro. fem.—The Rev. W. Turner was appointed unanimously for the time, whereupon he proposed, and Mr. thole seconded, that the Rev. J. T. Max- well be the chairman for ,the next three years.—As an amendment Mr. Hulse proposed Mr, Daggatt, which Nr, Smallwood seconl dvs9 i.oard then ivided ; or amend- • - "nsent Mr. Hulse voted, for the motion Mr. Turner and Mr. bole, the others remaining neutral.—Mr. Maxwell was therefore declared the chairman. He said he felt great reluctance in accepting the post, as the voting was so very Knall. The position of chairman was a very difficult one, and he should have at least a majority of the board in his favour. Mr. Hulse and Mr. Daggatt both avowed their in- tention of working with him to the best of their ability. On those conditions he would accept the post, and would do his duty satisfactorily. There would be differences of opinion in a board composed of seven members; but during the last six years they had only had about six divisions, and had worked together with harmony and good will.—Mr. Daggatt was unanimously elected the vice-chairman for the three years; and he thanked ths Board for the honour they had done him.—The remaining time was occupied in read-' log and confirming the minutes of the Fast me2ting, and hearing and deciding cases of non-attendance of children at school. In a few cases the fees were excused till March 25th, provided the parents did not obtain work earlier. But in many of the cases the attendance officer was directed to take proceedings unless a better attendance was made during the week.—The board then adjourned till March 7th.

------ Many facts in support of an inquiry into the case of Amelia Jordan, who was sentenced to 14 years' penal servi- tude for arson and robbery, have been obtained during the past few days, and a substantial fund is being raised at Hast- ings to meet the expenses incidental to the preliminary stages necessary to secure an official investigation. THE FATAL PRIZE FIGHT.—Lard Jnstice BagaHay had oefore him at the Warwick Assizes, on Wednesday, a case in which James Hodgkiss,Harry Bagnall, William 'Price, and John Broom were indicted for having on the 7th of October last, at the parish of Wishaw, taken part in and aided and abetted a prize fight. A second count charged these men, in conjunction with James Carney, with having, at the same I time and place, feloniously IZiiled and slain James High- land. The jury returned a verdict of "manslaughter" against all the prisoners. Sentence was deferred until Thursday, when his 15rdship said it was idle on the part of those who indulged in prize fights to talk of them as illus- trations of British pluck and endurance. They were nothing of the kind. It could not be too generally recognised that they were riotous, disgusting, and -degrading spectacles, their natural consequences being violence and drunkenness, and the law could not tolerate them. Carney, one of the principals in the fight, was sentenced to six and the other prisoners to four months' hard labour. Tax TEMPLE OF DIANA.—At Ephesus, was 435 feet high, and its erection required the labour of 200 years! The largest of the Pyramids of Egypt Is 431 feet high—covering 13 acres of ground. The stones are about 30 feet irs length, and the layers 206 in 'limber. It could not now be built for less than £30,000,000. div.head: RUNCORN BREACH OF PROMISE
div.p: A RUNCORN BREACH OF PROMISE
CASE. ACTION AGAINST A PUBLICAN. Mr. Justice Chitty and a special jury were occupied several hours on Tuesday, at the Liverpool Assizes, in hear-

ing a Runcorn breach of promise case. The action was brought by Susannah Banner, domestic servant, Runcorn, against John James Waterworth, liscensed victualler, Run- corn. Mr. Walton (instructed by Messrs. Crowther and Miller) appeared for the plaintiff; and Mr. Gully' QC., and Mr. Shand (instructed by Messrs. Ashton and Jolliffe, of Runcorn) appeared for the defendant. Mr. Walton, in his opening statement said the plaintiff, being a-minor, sued by her next friend, to recover damages for preach of promise to marry from the defendant, who denied the promise. The case was one in which there were some very painful features, and he had hoped at the last moment the defendant would have taken a course which would have saved the jury the disagreeable task of trying it. His Lordship : Must it be tried, Mr. Gully ? Mr. Gully: I think so, my lord. Mr. Walton, continuing, said the plaintiff was now 17 years of age. She was 15 years old when she went as domestic servant to the house of defendant, who kept an Hotel in Runcorn. At that time the defendant was married. Early in January of last year Mrs. Waterworth died. The plaintiff's father then told the defendant that he thought it would be better for the plaintiff to leave, as people might talk about the fact of a young girl remaining in a house with a widower where there was no other older female, and the defen- dant in reply to these scruples said "You have known me a long time. I am a respectable man, and you cannot suppose for a moment that any harm can attend your girl so long as she is in my house." -Believing the defendant, and trusting him, the father allowed the girl to continue in his service. Two , or three months after his wife's death, tke defendant spoke ' to the girl's father about marrying the plaintiff, saying that he required some one to look after the house; and after that he paid her considerable attentions, and these went on until the 15th April, when the defendant went into the plaintiff's bedroom in the middle of the night, and having the girl at his mercy, succeeded at last in seducing her. The engagement went on, and defendant treated the plaintiff before everyone as his intended wife, and their engagement was the talk of the town. Plaintiff continued to live in defendant's house until the end of December,lBBl, when defendant, having changed his mind, married another woman. It was, the learned counsel remarked, for this mean and unmanly conduct on the part of the defendant that the Iplaintiff asked for damages. The Plaintiff, a nice looking girl, who was neatly attired lin mourning, and gave her evidence in a very intelligent manner, examined by Mr. Walton, said: I shall be 18 years .of age on the Ist of next May. I went into the service of the defendant as servant when I was 15. Defendant's wife was then living. She died on the Ist of January, 1881. I continued in defendant's service after that time, and assisted in the bar and also in the housework.—When did defendant first say anything to you about marriage? On the 15th April.—Was anything said before that? Yes; one day when we were in the kitchen, about a week or a fortnight before.—What did he say? His sister was about to leave the house then, and I said " what shall we do about the missus then," and he:said "1 shall marry the servant."— His Lordship: Were there any other servants in the house? No.—Mr. Walton: After or about this time did you notice any change in defendant's manner towards yore? Yes, sir; he began to pay his addresses to me.—And did that go on until the date you mentioned the 15th April ? Yes, sir.—Was there any conversation in which he said anything about people talking, before the 15th April? Yes, once or twice. He saic-1 people were talking about me and him going to get married, and be said I must take no notice of it as long as he did not care.—On the 15th April, I believe he said something more, about three o'clock in the morniag ? Yes.— Where was it? In my bed-room, sir.— Were you asleep? Yes, sir.— Did he wake you? Yes, about three in the morning. What did he say? He did not say anything, but he attempted to seduce me.—Did he say anything about marriage? I said "You will perhaps be looking out for • for some one better, with money ;" and he said he did not want one with a fortune with her; he would rather have one with a fortune in her. He said I did not need to he frightened because he wished I was as safe of going to heaven as I was of going to be his wife. I remember that sometime after th's the defendant bought a trap, and took me into the yard to look it it.—What did he say? He said the first two that would ride out in that trap would be him and me, and that would be to get married.—Towards the latter part of the year did you notice any change in his manner towards von ? Yes; about September. He did not seem to bid me a.gooa night," or anything of that sort. I asked him the reason, and he said Ile intended to break his promise of marrying me, because he had so much unhappiness both with his mother and sister. I said what did it matter about-them so that I did my duty to him. He said they had to be looked at as well as himself.—Soon after this did you find he was paying attention to some young lady? Yee, and I gave him notice eid left his Ptvige,----Anet, he got married on the 24th • hat ia ti November? Yes.-1 forgot to ase you, " dAfare dent? He is a publican, and at that time he kept the Boathouse Hotel, in Mersey-street, Runcorn. 'He now occupies the Egerton Arms, which seems a larger place.—Cross-examined by Mr. Gully: Have you ever said till to-day that there was any promise to marry before the occasion when defendattt went into your bedroom? Yes, he did mention it to me ; but I used to laugh it off.— Have not you always said until to-day that he first promised to marry you on the 15th April? I have said it all along.— You . are asked to state the day and hour, time or times when, and the place or places where, the agreement to marry alleged by you in the second paragraph of the statement of claim was entered into ; was the agaeement verbal or in writing ? You say to that," the agreement to marry was first made on the 15th April, 1881, about three o'clock." You say you laughed it off? Yes, before the 15th April.— You say, he did say that you were to take no notice of people talking about you? Yes.—l understand you allege this prcmise to have taken place on the night between the 14th and 15th April. Now on the 14th April had the defendant been away all day? He had been away in the afternoon, from one o'clock until 11 at night.—Were his sister and brother-in-laNv living in the house? Yes, sir.—And had been for some time? Yes.—Was his uncle staying in the house? Yes; he was barman at the time. His name is Thomas Waterworili. The brother-in-law and sister are named Mr. and Mrs. Whinyates. A Mr. Collier came back with the defendant that night, but he elid not stay for supper. The defendant went part way home with Mr. Collier.—Did the brother-in-law and the sister, the uncle, and the defendant, and you yourself all sleep on the same floor—were your bed- -rooms alt ell on the same floor? Yes, sir. Mr. and Mrs. Whin- yatee, the uncle the defendant, and I occupied separate bed- rooms.—Was there anyone else in the house? No, sir; only defendant's daughter, a baby.--His wife had been dead about three months? Yes.—And bed defendant a li.t:-.1;c0.r, a cousin of his, steeping in the Mille hetheeni with him? Not at that time.—Had you Fottrttlt. a little sister sleeping with you ? No ; not limit his sister and brother-in-law left the liouse.—How old le your sister? About ten years of age.—l unieltand you to say that defendant seduced you pa tlels night? Yes, sir.—Am I right in supposing that you don't allege that he did so at any other time ? Not before, sir. —Do you mean to say that he has. since? Yes, on three ocelsions.—Yon stayed as his servant until October? Yes. It was on the sth September he told me he intended to break his promise of marrying me. I gave notice on the 19th September. I did not ask to be allowed to stop after I bad given botice. I am positive of that.—Were you keepina company with a young inln named Wakefield? -,e7ee, just before defendant seducAl me, but not aitetWards. He tola me to break it off.—Were you not keeping company with Wakefield last summer:par- ticularly in May and June, and going out walk 3 with him ? No, sir; not at all. I never walked out with him once afterwards.—When you gave notice, did you know that de- Pendant was going to be married again? Well, I did not know; but I knew he was keeping company with a young lady at that time.—Did not 'ycfu understand that he was engaged to her with a view to marriage? When I spoke to him he said courting was not marrying.—Did not Mr. Collier say to you "I hear you are going to leave, Susie ; how is that?" Yes.—Did you say," the reason is I can't please master whatever I do. I suppose it is because be is going to be married aajn" ? Yes, I did. I also said I would net rerna'n with another mistress in the house. Defendant's sister had been my mistress up to April.—Did Mr. Collier ' say to you in a chaffing way, "We must get up a petition to ask you to keep you on. Perhaps you might become the mistress, there is no telling"? No, he did not.—And did I not yon say, "Oh, there's no fear of that;" No; it was not mentioned. I know Mrs. Grice, thedefendant's aunt. I was in the service ot defendant's brother when I left defendant's service. The brother lives at the Boathouse Hotel, which he took when defendant went to the Egerton Arms. In December last I left the Boathouse. My mother died, and then I bad to go and keep house for my father. At that time my father was about to instruct his solicitor to write to the defendant about his breach of promise. Messrs. Crowther. and Miller's letter on the 30th December was the first application made. I remember Mrs. Grice asking me at that time if the defendant had really ever promised to marry me. I told her he had. I never asked the defendant to take me out in the trap.—Re-examined : Mr. and Mrs. Whinyates came to live with defendant about a week er a fortnight before his wife was confined, and they remained until soon after the 14th April. After they went away I had charge of the house untll I left. Defendant raised -my wages is. per week just "to be his housekeeper and altoge- ther." My little sister came to sleep with me the night Mr. and Mrs. Whinyates went away.—When was it you spoke to defendant and he said that "courting Was not marry- ing"—referring to his keeping company with another young woman ? It was on the n'ght that I gave him notice—the 19th September.—What did you see' ? I found a note, sir, under his dressing table cover ; and I told him that his sister , had sent to him to meet this Young girl at her house. He. I did not deny it; and when I told him he was keeping com- pany with Miss Coleburn he said mating was not marry- ing. I said it looked very much like it. When Mr. Collier wanted to know why I was leavinz the defendant I did not tell him. Mr. Collier is a friend of the defendant's. Mr. Gully, in reply to His Lordship, said the defendant met the case with a most distinct denial, and intended to go into the witness box. William Banner, plaintiff's father, said : I am a boatman. I remember the defendant's wife dying in 1881. I spoke to him about my daughter. I wanted to take her away as I did not think it was prudent for my daughter to stay in a house with a young man. Defendant said he was left in a very awkward' position in his business, my daughter was acquainted the business, and he beggei for her to stay. I have

had seen a letter from the young lady? She did not.— Did you say to her, "Oh, very well; but you know court- ing is not marrying ?" Decidedly not. I never gave her such freedom.—Did you ever go to her bedroom at night? Yes.—When? The month that she and sister were together

been acquainted with the family all my life, and I consented to her staying. After my daughter left defendant's service in October I saw the defendant. It was not until then that I found out what had taken place. I went to the defendant on the 10th December and asked him what sort cei a game he had been acting, and whether he called him- self a man or not. He did not answer but went quite pale. • On the 12th December I went and acquainted his mother about it.—Cross-examinea by Mr. Gully: Did you ever charge him with having promised to marry the girl until the lawyer's letter that you seat him on the 30th December? No, sir. The first time I heard of him talking about marry- ing, his "step-grandfather "—(laughter)---told me about it in his bar. Richard Davies, boatman, said : I know the defendant, and have known him for a long time. I remember the plain- tiff being in the defendant's service after his wife's death. Defendant spoke to me about her. Between the 17th and 29th July last we were at the defendant's mother's house, the Anchor Inn, playing at bagatelle. During the conversa- tion defendant said he had buried the best woman that ever was tied to a man. He asked how my family was getting on, and I said "You have got a veiy good servant, John." He said "Yes, I have, Richard, and I intend to make her my wife." The servant was Susannah Banner. A day or two afterwards, I went into defendant's house at dinner time. The plaintiff and defendant were Offing dinner together, and I went into the kitchen to them. I said " You are doing well." He said "Yes, come and have some with us," and I sat down. There was a knock in the bar, and defendant got up, put his arm round plaintiff's neck, said "My love," and passed on. I followed him out with the bread and meat in my band, and said "John, you are very loving." He re- plied "I am at home." A day or two after that I called at his house again for a glass of beer, and mentioned his ser- vant again saying she was a geed girl. Defendant said there was not a better girl in England.—Did you ever notice how he behaved towards her? I have always seen them very friendly together. The first time I ever took notice was in July. I have not seen them since then. I have heard remarks paseed at the counter about the courtship. It was said they would make a very good pair. I heard it said to defendant and he sail he might do worse.—Cross-examined : I live at Toxteth Park, Liverpool. I was master of a steamer when I was at Run- corn, and it was there under repair. I have known the de- fendant ever since he was a boy, and I know the plaintiff and her father.—When defendant said he intended to make her his wife were you chaffing him about girls? There was nothing said about girls except about my family, his family and the girl.—His Lordship : Was it serious conver- sation ? I took it to be genuine. Mary Hand, widow, residing at Runcorn, said: One day during last summer I was at the defendant's house when there was a man named Woodcock there. Defendant pro- mised that if I would " have " Wm. Woodcock, he would give me a wedding breakfast and said that it should be at his house, and we should stand for each other.—By His Lordship: He wanted me to marry Woodcock. (Laughter.) —Have you ever noticed anything special in his manner towards you ? Yes, I have seen him kiss her many times. The first time would be in May. I have seen de- fendant give her the keys, and all the privileges of the house. —Did you ever hear anyone speak of his getting married in his presence ? It was the common talk of the customers and throughout the town. This was the plaintiff's case. Mr. Gully, Q.C., in addressing the jury for the defence, said this was a case no doubt which would present a very serious conflict of evidence. It was a case in which a girl charged a man with improper conduct towards her, and these were charges which it was extremely difficult for any man, however conscious he might be of his own innocence, to meet. When a rather interesting-looking young girl got in- to the box and told a story of this sort against a man,one could not help feeling that, however innocent he might be of what was said against him, he was weighted with great difficul- ties in disproving such charges. But he begged of the jury to bear in mind that in these cases it was the duty et the plaintiff affirmatively to make out her case, and to satisfy them beyond all doubt that the case was the correct one. The story was that the girl was in defendant's service when his wife was living. She died in January, 1881, and the girl remained in the defendant's service until October. According to her account, in April, a fortnight or so before there was any actual promise of marriage, he said some words to her in the kitchen suggesting marriage, but which she said she laughed off, and which she considered as amounting to no promise. The defendant would tell the jury that he never made any premise of marriage at any time. But it was quite possible in that class of life that a man keeping company might say a good many things, a good many strong things in chaff, perhaps, to the servant girl in his house, which would not indicate any serious intention to marry, and would pass from the minds of each unless it was followed by some- thing much more serious. He did not understand that the . plaintiff said there was any promise of marriage until the night of the 14th April, when she said defendant went into her bedroom and seduced her, and that that was repeated upon several occasion. It was not pretended the plaintiff had a child, or that there was any evidence of a 'circum- stance Of that kind. Was plaintiff's conduct such as they ivould expect under the circumstances? The learned counsel pointed out that the plaintiff did not consult her friends as to the ergegement, that there was no public recog- nition of her as engaged to the defendant, that there were no presents, no letters, and he contended plaintiff's subse- quent conduct was inconsistent with her evidence. If de- fendant had gone into her room, he must have expected, one would have thought, to have met with some resistance, and the possibility of noise and a struggle. But sleeping on the same floor in different rooms were the defendant's brother-in-law, and his sister, his uncle, the de- fendant and his little cousin, and the plaintiff, with whom slept her little sister, who plaintiff said came a few days after. Did the jury think it was probable defen- dant would go into the room of a girl who had a child ten years of age sleeping with her, and others sleeping in bed- rooms close by, and would then effect what she said was effected that night? Defendent denied it altogether. He would also call a witness, who. when plaintiff was about to leave her place, asked her about her going, and why she was 2oing. She then told him she was going because she did not want to stay there with a new mistress, and she denied to him that he was going to marry her or that he had ever thought of it. He said in chaff, "We must get up a petition and ask John to keep you on. Perhaps you might be the mistress; there is no telling." Mr. Collier was chaffing her about John getting married, and she answered "There is no fear of that ; master would not have me." If what Mr. Collier would state was true, it was absolutely incredible that a girl, who felt she was injured and outraged, and knew her master was going to marry another woman, should have l'inwr_vd in that way to Mr. Collier. If that. I.enoe Was true it 'would be conclusive to show tha_t: teetnttirra AU:aunt was not true. Since the beginning of January this year, I have been at the Egerton Arms. Plaintiff entered my employ in January, 1879. At that time I was married. My wife died on the 15th January' 1881.—Have you at any time promised to . marry the plaintiff ? You must have gone to be at home.—Do I understand you to say that the whole out with the expectation that you would be engaged in some of her evidence as to the conversation between you and her, deadly affray, in which it would be necessary to take out from beginning to end, is absolutely untrue?
