I nevcr oaths, on an inquiry before the magistrates, deposed to facts usually put letters under the cover.—Did she tell you sle which were not only material but vital to the charge against

_ land brother-in-law used to go to the bedroom to look how baby was, mild sister, before we went to bed.—Did you ever go to plaintiff's bedroom when your sister left? NO ; I never did.—l know the plaintiff's sister came at the end of February, because sister and brother-in-law were sleeping together. From that time until the plaintiff left my service her little sister slept with her every night. Mr. and Mrs. Whinyates left my house the last day or the last but one in April. It is not a fact that the little sister came to keep plaintiff company after Mr. and Mrs. Whinyates left ;.it was before then. I know Mrs. Hand and the man Wood- cock. He is a customer of mine. They used to "chaff together" about getting married, .but they never really meant to get married—(laughter)—because Woodcock is a cripple.—Did you once say to Mrs. Hand, "When you and Woodcock get married I will give you the wedding break- fast, and Susie and I can stand for you, and you can stand for Susie and me ?",.Never. What Mrs. Hand said is utterly false.—Did you ever kiss plaintiff in the bar? Never in my life did I kiss her. I never took any liberties with plaintiff. I
have known Richard Davies a long time. Do you remember

his telling you you hadgot a good servant? We may have had a conversation of that sort, but I did not say, "I am going to make her my wife." What Davies said is utterly false. I did not on one occasion when Davies was present
put my arm round plaintiff's neck and say, "My love." I might have said, "I am at home," because I was at home. Davies never said such words as "You are very loving, _ _ _

John." It is false from beginning to ered.—Did you say there was never a better ser eant in England, or a better girl? I don't dispute that.—Yon said, I think, there was some talk about you marrying her? Reports had been up and down and i have always denied them to my frienils.—His Lordship: Have you ever said to Davies that you might do worse than marry her ?—Defendant: I may have said it. I don't dispute it.—Mr. Walton : Did you ever make her a present ?—Defendant: I made her a present of a suit of mourning On the death of my wife, but nothing else. lam tenant of the Egerton Arms, but I have no lease. The rent is £6O or £65 a year. I have been in business on my own account for nearly five years. The weekly takings average perhaps £2O; £25 is the highest average. James Collier, assistant overseer for the township of Run- corn, said that on the 14th April he came home with the defendant. Plaintiff told him she wa's going to give notice, and he asked her why she was leaving. She replied that in whatever she did she could not please the master. On another occasion he said, " We shall have to go and petition John, and see if we can't keep you on," and sail in a joking manner that she might became the mistress herself. She said, "There is no fear of that, as I am not good enough for master. He thinks more of some one else." He believed plaintiff said she had heard that defendant was going to be married, and she would not remain in the house cinder another mistress. James Whinvates, brother-in-law of the defendant, said he went to the defendant's house shortly before the wife of the defendant died in January, 1881, and remained there until the end of April. At that time plaintiff was in de- fendant's service. There was nothing in the conduct of plaintiff and defendant that led him to suppose there was any contract to marry or anything of that kind. On the night of the 14th April they went to bed about half-past twelve o'clock. He was not awakened by any noise that night.—Cross-examined: He was not positive that plain- tiff's sister was that night sleeping with plaintiff.—Re-ex- amined He believed it was about the time he went to sleep with his wife that the girl came to sleep with her sister. Mrs. 'Whinyates stated that the plaintiff's sister came at the end of February, and on the 14th of April slept with her sister. There was nothing that night to call her atten- tion to anything being wrong in any way. She never saw any signs of affection between the defendant and the girl.— Cross-examined : The plaintiff's sister never failed to come a single night. She saw her either night or morning. Mrs. Sarah Pendlehury, formerly charwoman at the Boat- house, deposed that she remembered the plaintiff and a young man named Wakefield keeping company. On Whit- Monday she fetched the plaintiff from the Boathouse to see the procession of clubs, and they met Wakefield, with whom they walked to the fair ground, and there left him. Mrs. Ann Grice, widow, and aunt of defendant, said she asked plaintiff if defendant had ever offered her marriage. She said "Nu," and then witness asked her if she had any letters to show or anything else. Plaintiff said she had not, and they were nothing but a pack of fools for trying to do anything.—Cross-examined: Plaintiff wanted her to speak to defendant's mother about the matter but she did not. Plaintiff asked her to ask the defendant's mother to come down as she wanted to see her. The learned counsel on both sides haying addressed the jury, ,His Lordship, in sumtning up, said this was to some extent a remarkable case, and he doubted whether they could have heard a greater conflict of testimony than had oceurred between the plaintiff and the defendant. The action was for breach of promise of marriage. It was not an action for seduction, and the jury would have to throw out of their minds altogether the evidence that the girl was s2duced by the defendant. The plaintiff must make out her Case in the afiirmative. Here they had rot what they generally did have, and that might be of course explained by the circumstances in life of the parties, and the position in which they stood towards one another, viz., that of master and servant ;—they had no letters, they had no presents, except the present of the suit of mourning upon which nothing turned. There was no arrangement with the parents on the other side ; they bad no interviews with the friends. His Lordship pointed out this singular circumstance against the plaintiff—she did not appear to have disclosed the cir- cumstance that the promise was made, either to her mother or her father. The father became aware of it some little time before the letter was written on the 30th December. The answer that was given on plaintiff's part was that she did not tell her father of the promise because that would necessarily involve her telling of her disgrace and what had been done to her. It was for the jury to say whether that was a satisfactory answer to the point which was a strong one against her, because though she was 17, one would have expected .in the ordinary course of life she would have communicated any promise on the part of the defendant to marry her to her father. After reviewing the evidence, his Lordship concluded by remarking, that he had gone through the case with some care, because it was a jury persona most otshtey nlust intimatelybe matter of considerable importance in respect to the testimony ed the minds affirmatively beforc! sledded. —Lev must take the whole ,!! the particulars of the car; and put them to- otifonthtwogether as well as they could—whether there was a promise or whether there was no promise—and consider all the sur- rounding circumstances, the position of the girl, her being a servant, her having her wages raised, and what Mrs. Hand said abant her having the keys and privileges of the house. The jury must put the probabilities as far as they could around the direct testimony, and then it was for them to say whether they did or did not consider the plaintiff had proved her case. If the jury thought she had proved her case, then came the question of damages. He did not sup- pose that would give them at y great difficulty. If they thought she had proved her nee the loss of some establish- ment in life on the part of the plaintiff such as she would have had if the defendant had married her as he promised, was a matter which they would have to take into considera- tion, and al sa any temporary damages in respect to her feel- ings in the matter. She was young and probably would find a husband. The jury found for the plaintiff with eCISO damages, and his Lordship refusal an application to stay execution.

the poachers—namely, that neither you nor any of your party had firearms on that occasion. So far as I can see, Ricketts was the first to advance this story, because as early as four or five o'clock in the morning, he being told that one of the poachers had been wounded and was probably dead at that time, and, being most solemnly and seriously asked by . . .

Police-sergeant Harrington whether he or any of his party had firearms, he repeatelly and indignantly denied it. And although that is not part of the perjury with which you are charged, when I come to the consideration of your moral guilt it is a most serious part of it, because it appeared from Bickett's own statement, made on oath, that not only was he conscious of his having a revolver himself, but had actually seen Percival's revolver and seen Percival fire his revolver in the direction of a poacher lying on the ground. As far as has been proved in evidence, you seem to have together concerted this plan of not disclosing the fact that there were firearms amongst your party, being fully aware of the gravity of it ; and you followed up that resolutien and determination by giving evidence each of von separately and independently, at different days, after long intervals, and in the case of one of you (Percival) with the circumstance of the concealment of his own revol- ver, which showed deliberation as to what he was doing— giving false testimony before the justices on a charge of murder. 'rhe jury have stated in reference to one of you that they did not believe, and I will say with reference to all of you that I cannot believe for one instant, and do not believe that you meant to compass the death of these poachers by this false testimony. I cannot for one moment think it possible that three men like you—decent, respect- able, and well-brought up men—could have thought for an instant of the frightful thing you were doing. If I thought that you had done that—that you had given this false evidence with the view of hanging these three poachers—l , can venture to think there is no punishment allowed by our law for perjury that is anything near being sufficient for such an offence. As it is proposed—and I state this in sup- port of the view I now express—that in the new criminal code for the crime of perjury committed with regard to a capital charge shall be double what the law now allows. But I dismsss from your case that you had any such inten- tion. At the same time, I cannot shut out from my eyes the fact that you committed this perjury, not in a moment of haste or unconsciousness of what it was, but carefully, deliberately, and in concert with one another. Therefore it is an off,mce which deserves a very severe sentence indeed I can draw no substantial distinction between any of you, and the sentence which I therefore think it right, after the most careful and anxious consideration, to pass on each of you is that of imprisonment for 18 months with, hard labour. I have to say with regard to one of you (Percival). that you were charged also with the offence of manslaughter. Of that offence you were acquitted, and I think it right to say now—l might have said it last night, but I prefer to say it now after more consideration—that, in my judgment, you were most properly acquitted of that charge; and I am very glad for your sake, and for the sake of your family, that you went through the trial, for this reason—that from my experience and observation a great number of persons will judge of your offence and of the charge of which you have been acquitted, not from this trial, not from the evidence brought before the jury, but, unluckily, owing to the vast multiplicity of the press of this country, from the full reports of evidence given before the magistrates, and will not, perhaps, think it worth while to observe that the evidence given there was not given here; for the evidence given before the magistrates made it diffi- cult to understand how it could have been otherwise than that you had caused the death of that unfortunate man. It was stated there that you had been seen to fire Your revolver off at the poacher when he was on the ground; and it is right and fair.to say that that evidence did not come out at the trial here. The witness who proved that before the magistrates was put into the witness box, and he shrank from it and did not prove it. That entirely altered the char- acter of the case; it altered it in every particular. First of all, it altered it as to the time and manner of the firing, and raised a doubt which probably influenced the jury as to whether or not it was really your revolver that fired the fatal bullet. The jury might have the thought it was another revolver that fired the fatal bullet; they might have also taken another view—the view that you fired it under cir- cumstances which satisfied them that it was a defensive action on your part, and not an aggressive act. I wish to say this for your sake, for the sake of your family, and for the sake of truth—that the jury gave a most sound and just vet diet in acquitting you of that charge of manslaughter. Before I part altogether from this anxious and painful case, I think I would not be doing my duty if I did not express my sense of the conduct of the police in this case. I must say, at least it struck me, that they acted with and showed in their conduct the highest possible care, discretion, and judgment; and that they had every anxiety to get at the truth and what was right. I cannot find language to express my admiration'of their conduct. It would be invidious to mention names, but for each one, from Captain Little down- wards to the humblest of those who were called before me, I can express lout one feeling of admiration of their conduct, their intelligence, their integrity, and care in the execution of their duty. The police often have lectures on the dis- charge of their duty, and it is only just as an encouragement to them that they should have this expression of opinion. I only regret that I cannot show them my sense of apprecia- tion in a more substantial manner.

div.head: OPENING OF A LIBERAL CUB AT
div.p: OPENING OF A LIBERAL CUB AT
PRESCOT,

On Wednesday evening the opening of a club in connection with the Liberal Association of Prescot, was inaugurated at the Crown Hotel, Prescot, when a mis- cellaneous entertainment,. consisting of instrumental and vocal music and adreeses by several prominent local Liberals, took place. The club, which owes its existence to the exertions of a few gentlemen connected with the Prescot Liberal Association, now numbers upwards of 100 members, and has obtained suitable accommodotion and rooms in the Crown Hotel. Mr. A. Eccles (president of the association) occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance of ladies and gentlemen, including Messrs. W. Tyrer (vice- president), C. W. Rawlins, C. Rawlins, T. P. Hewitt, John NVycherley, J. Saunders, G. Beecham, J. Twist, W. Davies, H. Fogg, D. Prescott, and W. Gerrard. The room was very tastefully and appropriately embellished for the occasion with plants, &c., and on the walls were hung portraits of Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Bright, the Earl of Dalhousie, and other Liberal statesmen. After a selection Of music by Atherton Brothers' band, The ettltnrstAN said he had looked forward with expec- tancy and pleasure to the time when they would be strong enough tcl farm an association of that kind in Prescot, and he hoped that in every way it would be a success. (Applause.) Although it was only a nucleus of what they hoped to see in years to come, they were sanguine enough to hope that in the not distant future theywould have a building of their own in which they could hold their meetings and accomodate their friends. As the association was not in a position to bring about this state of things immediately, they had thought it desirable to com- mence that way, and he congratulated them very much upon having secured such excellent premises. (Applause.) He hoped the club would have the effect of strengthening their political faith at a time like the present, when it was their duty to inquire into that faith and the reasons tor their political principles. They all knew that the watchwords of the Liberals were Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform—rapplause)—as opposed to war and objections to reform, which was the programme of their Conservative friends (Hear, hear.) They all knew the state of the country • during the last Conservative adminis- tration. They were constan,tly in a ferment of war. When- ever they opened their newspapers in a morning they were under an apprehension lest some catastrophe in this line had happened ; and gentlemen in business were perfectly in- capable of Laying their plans for fear of having them upset at a moment's notice. Since the accession to power of the Liberal party this undesirable state of things had vanished, and for the first time for many years the Queen, in her opening speech to Parliament, had been able to state that we were at peace with all the world. (Loud applause.) That was a strong and satisfactory position to take up in so short a time; and it was a most gratifying fact to know that we, as a nation, were at peace with all the world. Of course, retrenchment could not follow at once ; their Conservative friends had left them, among other things' a legacy of ex- penditure, and a number of bills which had to be paid. It was in the memory of all of them that when Mr. Gladstsme left the Treasucy there was a considerable surplus of revenue, which was very quickly mopped up by his successor, and another vast expenditure piled up, which was now being wiped off. Now that a Liberal Government was in power, they might look forward to having a reduction of taxation before long. (Applause.) Referring to the question of reform, he said that if they looked back they found a lon, roll of reforms brought about by the action of the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) First they had the Reform Bill, which conferred political power upon £lO householders; then they bad Free Trade, which was brought about by the strenuous work and energy of Mr. Cobden, to whom this country owed a deep debt of gratitude for carrying through that important measure ; and he strongly recommended all Liberals, who wished to thor- oughly understand the question of Free Trade to read Mr. John Morley's " Life of Mr. Cobden." Seeing that that club would have a library of literary works for the edification of the memoers, he would present them with a: copy of Mr. Jehn Morley's "Life of Cobden." (Hear, hear.) Having mentioned other beneficial measures passed by the Liberals, Mr. Eccles alluded to the obstruction in the House of Com- mons. He observed that, by the present rules of the House, members could, by technical means, such as moving the , adjournment of•debate, moving the previous question, &c., prolong useless discussions. They saw that practice resorted to continually in the late session of Parliament, and it was only by the very greatest persevereance on the part of Mr. Gladstone that the Irish Land Act was passed. (Hear, hear.) ' Mr. Gladstone, backed by the support of the whole of the Liberal party in this country, he believed,:had determined to put a stop to the prolongation of useless discussions. He had made up his mind that discussion in that House shoed be no longer a farce, and that reforms which were needed' should not be prevented by wilful obstruction. (Loud ap- plause.) It was absurd to say that the reforms pro- posed by Mr. Gladstone in the procedure of the House were inimical to liberty of speech, for he would be the last man in the world to propose anything of the kind. (Hear, hear.) _ The motion which Mr. Gladstone proposed was to give to a majority of the House of Commons the power of closing a debate. A very formidable opposition was threatened, and the leader of the opposition was the leader of the Conserva- tive party in the House of Commons. He maintained that Sir Stafford Northcote had taken up a false position, and quoted from a speech delivered by Sir Stafford Northcote on

the 26th February, 1880, to show that Mr. Gladstone might very fairly call upon the right hon. gentleman to second his motion. (Applause.) lie was very happy to say that it was quite clear to those behind the scenes that the opposi- tion would be signally defeated, and then the Obstruction in the House of Commons would be ended. (Renewed applause.) One of the most important questions to be considered during the present session was the reform of the land laws. They were all aware that the agricultural interests .of this country had for years past suffered very severely. Those interests had excited a great deal of atten- tion, and all sorts of remedies had been proposed. The ! agriculturists' want of success and prosperity could not could not be ascribed entirely to bad weather, although it had something to do with it. There was no doubt that the British farmer, in order to compete with India and America, would have to raise crops very much cheaper than he had done in the past. He thought the English agriculturist was very much behind his neighbours and had a great deal to learn in the wiy of cultivating land economically. There were, however, laws which affected the land, and sadly ina- peded him in his operations. The laws of primogeniture, entail, and settlement required reconsidering. Another subject which demanded immediate attention was the ques- tion of local taxation. They wished to see the equalisation of the franchise—(hear, hear,)—as there was no reason why a man, simply because he lived in the country and not in the town, should be at a disadvantage :politically. (Ap- plause.) He thought there was quite as much intelligence ! among the people residing in this district as among those who lived in the lower parts of our large towns. (Hear, hear.) Following this would be a redistribution of seats, but the Government would not put the country to the cost of anotker election until they considered it absolutely necessary. After again congratulating them upon the forma- tion of the club, Mr. Eccles said he had great .pleasure in declaring the club open. (Loud and continued applause.) Mr. TYRER (vice-president) mentioned in detail the pro- visions made by the association for the enlightenment and edification of the members in Liberal' principles, and said he hoped the club would soon have a large accession of mem- bers, and that they would shortly be in a building of their own. (Applause.) He trusted that the club would tend to the spread of Liberal principles in the neighbourhood. (Hear, hear.) On the motion of Mr. HENRY FOGG, seconded by Mr. W. MACKENZIE, a vote of thanks was unanimously accorded to .he Chairman and Mr. Tyrer, both of whom briefly replied. The proceedings-then terminated.

NEWTON AND EARL ESTOWN. DISPUTE ABOUT • THE PEDIGREE OF A GREYHOUND. At the Liverpool Assizes on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Chitty and a special jury, Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton Park, Newton-le-Willows, brought an action against John Thompson, trainer, living at Spennymoor, Durham, to re- cover £lOO damages for breach of warranty of a greyhound bitch. The defendant denied giving a warranty, and pleaded that the animal was of the age and pedigree stated. Mr. Russell, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. M‘Connell were for the
plaintiff, and Mr. -C-ully, Q.C., and Mr. Segar for the de- fendant. Mr: Russell, in opening the _ease, stated that the . _

action involved very serious questions indeed affecting the defendant and his conduct. It related to the sale of a grey- hound bitch purchased by the plaintiff from the defendant, at Brigg, after the coursing .neeting in November list. The question for consideration was whether the greyhound in question was a bitch pupped in May, 1879, and bred thus— by Lifeboat out of Alice. The defendant alleged that there were two distinct hounds, and the plaintiff alleged that the bitch sold to him was the pup by Weardale out of Myrtle, and pupped in 1879. The bitch which the plaintiff bought from the defendant ran at Brigg, last year, and won a stake, . .
and the plaintiff was so struck by its look, and make, and breeding, that he spoke to the defendant about it. The de- fendant said he was ready. to sell it, and described it as _ _ _ . .
being by Lifeboat out of Alice, and he described Lifeboat as being by Contango and Alice as by King Death. Contango was_a dog that had a successful career at coursing meetings. _ _ _
Ele had not won what was considered the blue ribbon of the

coursing plains, viz , the Waterloo Cup, but he had divided the Waterloo purse. However, he was still more successful as a stud dog, and in this respect he was stated to be the most successful dog in modern times. If the breeding, there- fore, of the bitch was what he had mentioned, apart from its
coursing merits it would have been worth the greater part of the money that was paid for it for stud purposes. Upon these representations, the plaintiff gave one hundred

• guineas for the bitch. Some days after the purchase, the plaintiff received an anonymous letter giving quite a different history of the dog. The animal herself also pre- sented some indications that she was not of the age which the plaintiff was led to believe. After the dog had run at Brigg, an objection was entered against her that she was not of the proper age, and the stakes were not paid over to the defendant. Finding that this was the case, the
plaintiff instituted an inquiry, and the result of that was that he discovered what he believed was the
:rue history of this dog—that it was pupped upon . the pre-

mises of Mr. Watson,—a saddler at Darlington, on the 28th May, 1879, and was by Wekrclale, out of Myrtle, a breed which was of no value for stud purposes with the Cohtango and King Death breed. The pup seemed to have been about Mr. Watson's premises until July of 1879, when it was handed over to a man named M'Leod, a tanner, living in Darlington, to rear. She remained with M.Lcod up to October in the same year, and whilst there was thrown down, and ,a cart wheel passed over her left foreleg and crushed it, leaving an enduring mark. The dog which was sold to the plaintiff as one which had been pupped in March, 1880, had that mark. The defendant alleged that the mark upon the bitch he sold to the plaintiff was the result of a scald; but the jury would be told by skilled witnesses that the appear- ance the dog's leg presented could not be the result of a scald. This accident having taken place in October, later in the same month, Watson, the owner of the dog, resumed possession of it, and the dog continued with him until the 6th December, 1880, when it was again returned to INl‘Leod's care. She continued with 111‘Lcod until the 19th March, 1881, when the defendant Thompson went to 31'Leod and told him that the owner (Watson) had authorised him to take the dog away, and he did so, but the defendant, he understood, would say that he had destroyed that bitch. There was also another significant circumstance, and some of the jury would probably know that coursing greykounds had two sets of names. One was their kennel name and the other their coursing name. The kennel name of the bitch pupped at Watson's was Blos- som, and the kennel name of the bitch sold by the defendant to the plaintiff was Blossom. The coursing name of the bitch pupped at Watson's was Myrtle Bud, and the coursing name of the bitch sold •by the defendant Bird Jennie. The bitch taken possession of at IlPLeod's by the defendant in March, 1881, ran in December, 1880, at Thirsk, under the name of Myrtle Bud, and Was described as being by Wear- dale out of Myrtle; at Plumpton in March, 1881, and at Dar- lington, in the same month, her owner being described as J. Dearing. In October, 1881, she ran in the Covington Stakes for bitch puppies, at Carmichael, Lanarkshire, under the name of Bird Jenny, and described as being by Lifeboat out of Alice, and there she ran in the name of J. S. Robinson. In the same month, she, ran for another puppy stakes at Gos- forth, and there she was described as the property of S. J. .Robinson. Next she ran for the Stanley and Oxhill Stakes, her owner being described as 11. Smith. Then on the 24th November of last year she ran at the Brig,g meeting, and there she appeared under another ownership, viz., that of R. J. Nelson. With regard to Lifeboat and Alice the coursing records had been searched in vain. The name Alice might be found, but not by King Death; and Lifeboat might be found, but not by Contango ; so that if the plaintiff showed that this warranty was given apart altogether from the grosser fraud, it would be a breach of the warranty which the defendant gave at the time of the sale. Several witnesses were called in support of Mr. Russell's statement. On Monday, upon the appearance of his lordship on the bench,

Mr. Gully said: Since the adjournment on Saturday I have considered the evidence in this case which I shall have to call, and your lotdship says it will he incumbent on me, in order to claim a verdict, to establish a pedigree of this dog. , His lordship : Yes; it would. Mr. Gully: I feel, upon looking at the evidence, that it will not establish a pedigree in the way in which 1 think it would be satisfactory. Under those circumstances, my lord, I feel I could not resist a verdict. His Lordship: Very well. Mr. Russell : A. verdict for £lOO. His lordship also certified for a special jury.

On Thursday afternoon, an explosion occurred at Trundon Grange colliery, Durham, by which, it is feared, some 60 or 70 lives have been lost. About 130 men and boys were at work at the time. A number of these were rescued—suffer- ing from the effects of the after-damp—but the task of ex- ploration growing more and more difficult the great majority of the colliers were still in the mine on Thursday evening. The after-damp was driven into the workings of another colliery two miles away, and here four men perished. The first intimation of the explosion to those on the bank was a loud report, and simultaneous outburst of flames and rub- bish up the Harvey shaft. The resident viewer, Mr. Wood, accompanied by John Lawrence (fore overman), Mr. Cooke ' (under viewer), and other officials, hastened to the pit heap, and speedily as possible organised means for the relief of the sufferers. The cage was found to have jammed some 30 yards from the bottom of the shaft ; therefore, fully half an hour's delay took place before a kibble could be rigged for the rescue party to descend, which was done with all pos- sible speed. The gentleman named being first to descend, meantime the excitement among the night shift men and families of those below was painfully intense, and dense ' crowds soon began to arrive on the scene from surrounding collieriel. including rescuers and other officials. The ex- plorers reached the Harvey searriby the low main shaft, and about four o'clock they effected communication with the high Main. Presently two persons were brought up to the bank, namely, Henry Ramshaw and Ralph Wynn ; then three others named Henry Mercer and William Taylor, and John Priestly, boys. Edward. Maloney, who had been nearly an hour clinging to the top of the cage, came next, followed by Thomas Thompsln and George Robson and Peter Brown, furnacemen. Subscquently Matthew Hunter, John Collier, Wm. Young, John Wynn, and Jos. Joseph Hepple were brought to the bank all. alive, but suffering more or less seriously from after-damp. Dr. Russell was I soon on the spot, and under his superintendence the poor fellows were removed to their homes, and appear generally •to be in a fair was of recovery. After this, the work of rescuing the sufferers, proceeded only slowly owing to the (1(:!)-tis encountered by the exploring party.

• proud to call him, upon having such an assembly around him, and at his side a son who he firmly believed would follow in the worthy footsteps of his father. His father deserved all respect. Those in his employ would all acknow- ledge that during the great depression in trade of the last few years, when many other works where discharging their workmen, Mr. Baxter's hands were kept fully employed. Any person going through Mr. Batter's works, could testify . . _

to his ability:- and enerdY in furthering the cause of labour in this neighbourhood. He (the speaker) had great personal reasons for feeling grateful to Mr. Baxter. He had had ' other masters in the neighbourhood who bad warmly sup- ported him in the work of his church and other churches, but he bad never gone to one from whom he had received more cordial and willing help than Mr. Baxter. (Applause.) Different from others who had just received him said "yes" or "no," and then given him a bow, Mr. Baxter had kinily entered into the object set before him, and when once satis- fied never refused to help it. Mr. Baxter's son could not • follow a more worthy example than his father set him, and at some future time he hoped Mr Ernest Baxter would be

conducting large and profitable works. The 11.-V. W. FLAHERTY also reponded. It was true that manufacturers' works had been the store-houses to which the people had been privileged to go when trade was bad, and there was unquestionably a large amount of respon- sibility resting upon workmen as well as the masters. It was sometimes said that the workmen had. made him what he was. Nothin, of the kind. If the master had trst had fore- thought, energy, perseverence, capability and tact, he would never have been the master. Every advantage was on the Part of the men who had energy, capability and tact. He hoped that as they were met together under such auspicious cir- cumstances, that it might only be the begining of a long, prosperous, and happy future, in which master and men would be brought more :'closely together; that men would feel the responsibility resting upon them, and masters recog- nise their responsibility and act towards their men as -duty . dictated.

The CHAIRMAN said the next toast .was very much like a Wigan toast "Our noble selves," the " Town and trade of St. Helens." He thought the good times were very near; in fact they were close to the front door.

The tast having been --- Mr. LUCAS said he believed trade was slightly improving, because in the towns where he went he could find new works being erected in different branches cf trade. That looked very much like improvement. That was what he should like to see round about 31. Helens. The glass trade was pretty good, he believed, and so they told him was the copper trade, but he could not speak about the chemical trade. He should like to see the prosperity of 1874 and 1375 return. (Cheers.) Mr. McNicint, in proposing the toast of the evening, "Health to Mr. Earnest Baxter," said life generally was hum- drum and monotonous, but there were a few events which made it somewhat agreeable. In a man's life there was not a coming of age often; only once. Getting married was a very happy event. (Laughter.) But in that case there was a church and a parson, and a lady, always an interesting object. The present was a very happy occasion, and he did not wonder at the enthusiasm manifested by some of the ladies. (Laughter.) When a young gentleman carna.. of age, pissed the rubicon, assumed the manly toga, and entered into the battle of life, it was a very important event indeed. The young gentleman whose health they were about to drink, he knew very well. He knew him at one of the very earliest periods of 'his existence. (Laughter.) He had seen him through his happy childhood, and a good part of his boy- hood. While he might not have been born with a silver spoon in his mouth, a bright star blazed forth which had kept over the paternal roof to this day. Now, he entered upon a path of his own, and he would not expect it to be all smooth if he was a sensible young man—he knew be was; he had had the advantages and ought to be, for besides his early culture and training he had had the advantage of being at one of the highest schools in the land. If a young gentleman had any exquisite sensibilities and generous sympathies, they were nowhere as highly promoted and brought forth as at one of the higher schools of the land. There he was taught honourable feel- ings, and that which was right to serve him throughout life. Because they were going to drink health and prosperity to him he was nor going to say that Mr. Baxter, jun., would have his own way through life, but like a ship he would encounter storms which might sweep over the deck; but if he was made of good English oak be would ride over all the storms which fortune or misfortune might send against him, and make a good voyage to the end of his career. Referring to Mr. Baxter, he said he knew there was not a more worthy gentleman in St. Helens. He (the speaker) had had to do with his workmen more or less a. good many years in plaster- ing up their wounds and other little good offices he had been permitted to do—(laughter);—and he had never heard one of them who did not speak of Mr. Baxter with the highest degree of respect. A man might be nice to his equals, but how he behaved to those below him was the test of a good man. Mr. Baxter was one of the most generous men to .his workmen he had ever met with, and he hoped that the young barque would follow in the wake of the old ship. He • believed he was tackling business in a right good fashion. He (the speaker) might not see the end of his career, but they would all join in wishing him a good time of it. He proposed the toast, which was drunk with enthusiasm. Mr. JOHN SHENTON then presented a silver goblet to Mr. Ernest Baxter, with a few appropriate words. The goblet bore the following inscription:—" Presented to Ernest Baxter, Esq., on his 21st birthday, by 207 of the employes of his father's copper and alkali works, as a mark of their esteem and regard. oth Ftbruary, 1832." Mr. WALKEn, the manager, also made comae suitable remarks. •

Mr. ERNEST BAxTErt, who was received with enthusiastic cheering, thanked them very much for the way in which they had drunk his health, and for the splendid presentation made him. He could not express his feelings adequately' • ' in fact, he did not believe there were words in the English dictionary that could express the pleasure he experienced in accepting from them such a present. He had only been amongst them two years' and he took it that the present was more an expression of the esteem in which his father was held than the esteem which they bore towards him. He hoped, however, that in time be would be able to merit a share of their esteem. (Cheers.) He did not hope to band the present down to his family just yet—(laughter)—but it would give him the greatest delight for years to come, he hoped, to show it to his friends and to be nble to say that two hundred and seven of his father's workmen had pre- sented him with it. In looking round he recognised a great many faces that he remembered as far back as his memory would take him—to the time when he was about three years old, and he was glad to know that some of those were amongst the two hundred and seven. He believed their workmen were sterling sort of fellows, the backbone of the country, and the mainstay of England. (Cheers.) It gave him the greatest delight in saying that his father's workmen did their work thoroughly, and that the best workmen that could be found in the United Kingdom were there that night; and the ladies present might consider themselves fortunate in having secured proper sort of husbands. (Laughter.) He remarked that his mother was sorry to be unable to be present, especially as she had suggested the gathering. (Cheers.) Mr. SHENTON proposed the health of Mr. Baxter, who responded, and endorsed the expressions of his son in regard to his workmen.
Cheers were given for the Baxter family. After the tables had been cleared dancing commenced.

CONVERSAZIONE AT HU YTON.—On Monday evening, a social gathering of the parishioners of Huyton and Roby, principally organised by Mrs. Segar, took place in the Huyton and Roby Schools, Damhouse-lane,:and was in every respect a complete and .gratifying success. The rooms were very tastefully and appropriately decorated for the occasion with evergreens, flowering plants, &c. The gas chandeliers and window sills were adorned with holly, ivy, and sprigs of other hardy shrubs ; the sombre hues of which were grate- fully relieved by large, beautifully tinted flowers ; flags and bannetettes were suspended from the ceiling in different parts of the room ; and the walls were graced with suitable texts, such as" Let brotherly love continue," "Bear ye one another's burdens," &c. The decorations were carried out under the personal superintendence of the Rey. A. T.NVarne and Mr. E. Bridge, and among the helpers were the Misses Segar, Busby, and Mr. Moss. The beautiful flowers on the table were lent by Mrs. Parrington, and other pots of fLwers in the windows by Mrs. Crook. Evergreens and dowers were given by the Rev. 0. 11. L. Penrhyn, Mrs. Jowett, Mrs. Segar, and Mr. Busby. About six o'c:ock over 160 •persons sat down to an excellent tea provided by Mrs. Griffiths, whose catering for entertainments of this character is so highly appreciated in the locality. After full justice had been done to the good things. provided, a conversazione was held, the audience forming into groups, some of whom occupied their time by conversing on parochial and other subjects: while others busied themselves in looking and examining the many curiosities and novelties provided for their delectation and edification. Dr. Packer lent two magnificent microscopes, which he exhibited himself. Mr. J: 'l'. Saiith lent a power- ful microscope, and exhibited (assisted by Mr. J. Johnson) some beautiful experiments with Geissler's vacuum tubes. Much amusement was caused by the appearance of a youth in Esquimaux costume (lent by Mr. J. Caw). Stereoscopes, musical boxes, pictures, and other interesting objects placed round the room were lent by Mrs. Penrhyn, Mrs. Packer, Mrs. Segar, Mrs. Evans, Mrs. Moss, Mrs. Barber, Mrs. Bailey, Miss Yeoman, Mrs. Harrison, and Mrs. Higgin. The Rev. A. T. Warne exhibited and operated with a galvanic battery, which caused much amusement. Great praise is due to Mr. Jas. Hodgson, the talented organist and choirmaster of Huyton church, and to the members of the choir for their beautiful rendering of the following glees :—" sing on, • sing on" (Mendelssohn),' "A rose in heaven" (Fr. Abt.), " Humpty Dumpty " tCaldi- cott). The Huyton Orchestral Society gave an effective rendering of the following popular pieces :—" Marche aux Flambeaux " (Sc. Clark), " The lost chord" (Sullivan), arranged for small orchestra by Rev. W. T. Southward, the air being played most expressively as a cornet solo by Mr. Brown; "March from Le Prophete (Meyerbeer). Mr. Airy sang "The king and the beggar maid." Mr. Dawson sang "The White Squall" and "Once again." Masters Robinson and Lowe did them great credit in their vocal duet. The Rev. Canon Penrhyn, vicar of Huyton, presided, and there was a very large attendance of ladies and gentlemen residing in the neighbourhood. The proceedings terminated with a speech by the vicar, and the singing of " God save the , Queen."
