div.head: WIDNES TRADERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WIDNES TRADERS' ASSOCIATION.

ANNUAL MEETING. On Tuesday, at noon, the annual meeting of the Widnes Traders' Association was held at the Officers' Room, Volun- teer Hall, Widnes. Mr. E. K. Muspratt (of Liverpool) the president, occupied the chair, and there were also present:— Major Cross, Messrs. S. K. Muspratt, H. Brunner, Clare, and H. Wade-Deacon (the secretary). lhe SECRETARY read the report of the Executive Corn-
mittee for the past year. This stated that the plans for
lengthening the canal and forming anew entrance to it and

the dock'were prepared by Major Cross, as authorised by the last general meeting, and were submitted to and ap- proved by the committee. They were then laid before the London and North-Western Railway Co., who were urged to take the matter in hand, and were reminded of the fact that the traders would be quite willing to take into consideration the advisableness of paying extra tolls on all goods using such extension. The Railway Co., however, declin2d to move in the matter, and for the present, at all events, there appeared no prospect of obtaining increased facilities. The Midland Railway Co. declined to put in their Bill the proviso to elaase 30, approved by the last meeting of the Association, stating that their Parliamentary agents advised them that there was no necessity to do so, as the meaning was clear without it, and the committee did not consider it necessary to take any further proceedings in the matter. The South Garston Dock and Railway Bill was dropped. A select committee was appointed by the House of Commons to enquire intee alia into the charges of railway companies and canal companies, for the conveyance of merchandise, Sze.; into the laws affecting such charges, and into the working of the Railway Commissioners of 1873, and to report upon any amendments of the laws and the powers of the commis- sioners that might be deemed desirable. The President of the Association (Mr. E. K. Muspratt) gave evidence before the committee on behalf of the Widnes Traders' Association, ' and at the close of the session, the committee found that there was so much evidence still to be taken that they were unable to report, and recommended their re-appointment. A , Bill was to be introduced this session by the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, and Cheshire Lines Railway Companies, in which it was proposed to obtain power to divide railways and canals into districts, and charge equal group rates for coals and minerals. The committee believed that this power (if granted) would be opposed to the interests of traders, and they, therefore, recommended that a memorial be sent to the Board of Trade drawing attention to the clause in the Bill, and asking them to interfere for the protection of traders. The report was signed by Mr. T. Sntton-Timmis, chairman of the Executive Committee. The financial statement showed a balance in hand of XlO7 83. 7d. The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, re- marked that, unfortunately, although the committee had had several interviews with the London and North-Western _ _

_ Railway Company, and done their very best to get the entrance to the canal improved, all their suggestions had fallen through. The committee had done their utmost in this matter, and he did not think there was anything further to report with regard to it. Major CROSS thought it might be as well to state that Messrs. Hutehinsons' trustees had let the contract for the extension of the West Bank dock, which would afford much greater facilities to the traders of Widnes. The CHAIRMAN: I did not know that. Major CROSS: it is a matter of great importance to the traders of the town.

Mr. S. MUSPRATT said he had also noticed that during the past year the London and North-Wtstern Railway Company ha l done something in the way of dredging, which was a matter of great importance. Mr. CLARE scarcely knew whether what the company had done could rightly be described as of great importance. It was certainly a move in the right direction, but it was no use saying too much about it as yet. The CHAIRMIIi said he wished to make a few observa- tions upon what he considered an important point, viz, the action of the Select Committee on Railway Rates. He gave , evidence before that body, both on the part of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce and the Widnes Traders' Association. He drew the attention of the committee to the want of a new

classification of goods, and especially so as regarded chemi- I cals ; and, in reference to that particular point, even Sir Edward Watkin admitted that there was a very good case made out. He hoped the result of this action would be that they would have a reclassification of goods, and when that took place there was not the slightest doubt that they would have a better place in the classification than they had at present. It was certainly monstrous that chemicals should be classed with fish, feathers, fur, C., and that they should be subject to a maximum rate of 31d. per ton per mile upon dry chemicals. The association desired that chemicals should be classified as iron, damagable and undamagable, when carried at owner's risk, and then they would come under the maximum clauses of Id. per ton per mile, which would be a very great protection to the trade. He might say that at the present time he had been in communication with the London and North-Western Railway Company as to the charge for the carriage of saltcake from Widnes to 'Liverpool. The present charge was 4d. per ton, and the company justified themselves for so charging by the fact that they were within the maximum rates. There was no denying the truthfulness of this statement, but still it was a very high charge upon an article which was only worth at the present time 355. per ton. There was another matter to which he wished to draw the attention of the committee of the association, and that was that coal and fuel could be carried to Garston—past Widnes—when exported, at a very much lower rate than it could be carried for use of works in Widnes. The late Mr. Deacon, when he was president of that association, brought evidence before the Railway Com- mittee, and he (the speaker) in what he said followed the line of that evidence. He certainly thought they had a very just cause of complaint. They would notice in the report that the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company had asked for powers in clause 15 of their bill to group collieries, mines, &c., so as to charge a uniform rate, irrespective of distance. This was just what the committee had to complain of in the Lanca- shire Union rate, and now the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire were going in for the same powers. When the question was tried before the commissioners by a certain well-known colliery, they found that the grouping of quarries and collieries was illegal and could not be main- tained irrespective of distance. It was to the interest of the association to oppose the alteration of the law, and he trusted that other bodies in St. Helens and Liverpool would join them in so doing. If such a principle were once introduced, it would form a precedent, and would be applied not only to minerals, but to other merchandise, in which case every town which was favoured by its geographical position would be at the mercy of the rail eray company, who could levy rates irrespective of such position. He therefore, recommended that they should memorialize the Board of Trade upon this and other matters in the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Bill, which the committee of the association thought would be detrimental to trade. Perhaps they would take into consideration that day whether it was desirable they should also memorialize the Board of Trade upon the matter of classification. Major CROss had pleasure in seconding the motion moved by the chairman. He thought it was desirable that the at- tention of the executive should be called to the action being taken by the Wolverhampton Chamber of Commerce, who were commencing an agitation having for its object the en- tire separation of the water ways from the control of the railway companies. This was certainly a movement in the right direction, and it was one which the executive of the association would do well to most carefully watch. The CHAIRMAN was glad that Major Cross had called their ; attention to the action of the Wolverhampton Chamber of Commerce, which he had intended referring to in the course of his own remarks. They, in Widnes, certainly ought to snpport such a proposal. It would perhaps be well for the Executive Committee to draft a memorial to the Board of Trade, supporting:the action of the Wolverhampton chamber, and calling the attention of the Railway Rates' Committee to the question of the reclassification of goods. This action would be a sort of reminder, because there was no question that Mr. Chamberlain would be induced to look more thoroughly into the matter in dispute, if he found that a number of trades throughout the country were taking action in regard to it. Mr. CLARE said he did not see what particulir course the Wolverhampton chamber could suggest as to the canals, because most of them already belonged to the railway companies. The CHAIRMAN: You could buy the canals up. This would not be such a vast preposal as buying up the railways themselves. The canals c tuld be vested in trustees and worked by them for the pnolic good. There is no reason why in many places we should not have new csnals made with which to compete with railway companies. Major Crtoss said water carriage was the cheapest which could be obtained. It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. BRUNNER, that the memorial should be adopted. The following are the impor- ant clauses in the document : That amongst other railways your memorialists use the railways of the Cheshire Lines Committee, and that the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, and Cheshire Lines Railway Companies, are jointly introducing a Bill into Parliament this session, entitled A. Bill for conferring addi- tional powers on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, and on the Cheshire Lines Committee, and for other purposes. That by clause 15 of the said Bill, it is Proposed that power shall be granted the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway Company to divide into districts any part, or parts, of the railways or canals for the time being owned, or worked, by the company, either separ- ately or jointly, with any other company or person, and to charge equal group rates for coals and minerals. That the powers asked for would, if granted, give the railway com- panies authority to divide the railways and canals into dis- tricts of unlimited size, in a most arbitrary manner. That your memorialists consider that each colliery, quarry, mine, atc., should have the full benefit of its geographical position, and should not be placed in a group with, and its products charged the same sum for conveyance as those of another colliery, quarry, mine, &co not so favourably situated. That your memorialists fear that the power, if granted, of forming collieries, quarries, mines, &c., into groups may form a mis- chievous precedent which may be used in order to extend the principle so as to embrace all other works, manufactor- ies, ,Szc., and thus deprive them of any natural advantages they derive from their position." It was resolved, on the proposition of Major CROSS, seconded by Mr. CLARE, that the executive should be in- structed to support, by memorial, the action of the Wol- verhampton chamber, also refer to the re-classification of goods. This terminated the proceedings.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

IMPORTANT MEETING. The monthly meeting of the Widnes Local Board was held on Tuesday afternoon. Major Cross presided, and there were also present : Messrs. Booth, Sadler, Carey, Brown, Pank- hurst, Heyes, Forster, Gossage, Matthews, Handley. O'Keeffe, Kershaw, Gaskell. Shuttlewertb, Allen (clerk), Roberts (engineer), Higtinson (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance inspector). THE PRICE OF GAS. The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee were read, and their confirmation was moved by Mr. GOS3AGE. They stated that there were from 250 to 300 tons of coke now in stock, which was offered to the public at a lower rate than usual. A letter had been received from Mr. E. Timmins relating to the sale of the gear used at the Netherley works. Tke committee recommended that £4OO be offered for the gear, as it stood, as from the 31st November last. The com- mittee recommended that the offer of .Z 205 from Thomas Johnson for the spare pumping plant, be not accepted. Also that the price of gas within the township of Widnes should, in future, be 4s. per I,ooo' ft., subject to the following dis- counts for cash within the first mouth following:—Con- sumers of below 100,000 feet per annum, 61. per 1,000 feet; of 100,000 to 3,000,000 feet, Is. per 1,000 feet; and of above 3,000,000 feet, is. 3d. per 1,000 feet. The consumers beyond the township, a discount of 61. per 1,000 upon their present rates. The application of the Highway Committee for a reduction in the price for public lighting had been considered, and the committee recommended that the charge (555. per lamp per year) be continued for this quarter, and that the Highway Committee take the sabject of attending to the lighting and repairs into consideration for the next financial year. Mr. Timmins wrote on the Bth inst., accepting the offer of the Board of £4OO for the pump at Netherley. Mr. HANDLEY moved, and Mr. SADLER seconded, an amendment in favour of the charge per lamp being 475. in- stead of 555. Mr. KERSHAW proposed that the discounts to be allowed on gas be one-half of those above stated. but the resolution was not seconded. The CHAIRMAN said that the recommendations of the committee as the price of gas would have to be altered within the limit of the Act of 1807, which provided that the districts named should be charged the same as Widnes itself. Mr. GOSSAGE, in reply, said the gear at Netherley was of a very simple nature, and not likely to get out of order, so that he considered the best course which the Board could adopt would be to buy it. The price of gas had been put as low as it could at present be placed, as the sales had for some time been decreasing. Mr. Handley's amendment was carried, after which the min ites were passed. HIGHWAY COMMITTEE. " The minutes showed that the property owners in Market- street having refused to enter into an agreement to pay is. per annum, the street being a private one, the surveyor had been instructed that the thoroughfare must not in future be scavenged. The Sheffield and Midland Railway Company were preparing to erect screens at Moss Bank- , road, so as to hide passing engines from horses.—lt was recommended that a reply to the London and North-Western Railway Company's letter, of the 23rd November last year, be forwarded, distinctly disputino• the claim therein set up, and referring them to their letter of Ist January, 1874, to the Board of Tra4e, after the enquiry by that Local Board. Also that the Railway Co. be asked, as a temporary measure, to make the gates the full width of the road, doing away with the wicket gate, and form a parapet opposite the cottages on the south-westerly side of the crossing, estimated to cost about £2O; that notice be given that this Board will insist upon all shunting at this crossing being discontinued—that the Railway Co. be informed that in the opinion of the Board, the time has arrived when it is absolutely necessary a bridge should be substituted for the crossing. Mr. KERSILAW moved, and Mr. PANKRURST seconded the proposition for the adoption of the minutes, which was agreed to.

div.head: BYE-LAMS.
div.p: THE BYE-LAMS.
The j int Highway and Health Committees minutes were passed, on the proposition of Mr. CAREY, seconded by Mr. KERSHAW.

Mr. CAREY said that substantial progress had been made with the revision of the bye-laws, and the committee hoped that at the next meeting of the Board they would be able to present them in a finished state.

THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. The Health Committee presented the monthly report of the Medical Officer, which showed that the births had been 95, or 45.6 per 1,000; and the deaths 42, or 20-1 per 1,000, including those of eleven under one year, and nine between one and five years. The annual report of Dr. Cooper was also laid before the Board, from which we extract the fol- lowing :—" During the past year the number of deaths regis- tered in the township of Widnes was 423, and calculating on a population of 25,000 persons to the middle of the Year 1881, this will give a death-rate of 1092 per 1,000 of population for that year. From the principal zymotic diseases 39 deaths were recorded, and calcu- lated on the same population, these give a death-rate of 1.56 per 1,000 from that case of diseases. They were as follows :—Measles, 8; scarlatina, 3; diptheria, 1; typhoid fever, 12; diarrhoei, 15; total, 39. The deaths of children under 1 year (including premature births) num- bered 138, giving a death-rate of 5.52 per thousand of population. The following is art epitome of the ages at which the deaths occurred throughout the township : Deaths of persons under 1 year, 138; over 1 and under 5 years, 95; over 5 and under 15 years, 26; over 15 and under 25 years, 27; over 25 and under 60 years, 89; over 60 years, 48; total at all ages, 423. The grouping into various ages in the above is in accordance with the ages fixed in the forms furnished by the Local Government Board, which are duly filled up and accompany this report. The births during 1881 num- bered 1,095, giving a birth-rate of 43.8 per thousand of population." The report next referred to the outbreak of zvmotic diseases, and the steps taken to arrest the progress of them. Dr. Cooper concluded his report as follows :—"No serious difficulty has arisen during the past year in connec- tion with offensive trades. In one instance complaint was made, but the owner of the works complained of, has dis- continued the process which caused the nuisance. In con- eltpien I niay say, on teYiewing the work of the year, that considerable progt as has been made in carrying out useful sanitary work. Also that the health department of my Board has devoted itself very zealously during the year to arrang- ing new bye-laws on the basis of the model bye-laws, furnished to them by the Local Government Board, and that they hope very shortly to submit satne to that body for their confirmation." A letter had been received from Mr. Alfred Fletcher, dated the 12th January, stating that no effort should be wanting on his part to suppress the evil caused by the alleged escape of sulphurretted hydrogen in ! the West Bank district. Mr. Dickson, nuisance inspector, piesented a detailed statementas to the work which bad been i done during the year. Mr. CAnEY, in proposing the adoption of the minutes, said ; he thought the district compared very favourably in respect to health with England and Wales. The quarterly return of the Registrar-General showed that in England and Wales the birth rate had been 55.3, the total death rate 18 9, deaths from zymotic diseases 2-2-1, and the children who had died under one year 1.29. In Widnes the birth rate had been 43.8, the death rate 16.9, deaths from zymotic disease 1.56, i and the deaths of children under one year 1.26.

div.head: FINANCE.-MR. BEASLEY'S- ACCOUNTS.
div.p: FINANCE.-MR. BEASLEY'S- ACCOUNTS.

It appeared from the Finance minutes, that the corn- mittee recommended that the offer of £40,000 to £50,000, at 4 per cent., be accepted, provided the matter was settled at once. The Clerk had been instructed to take proceedings for the recovery of several property improvement accounts. The following accounts were ordered to be debited with legal expenses and interest :—T. Wedgwood, £4O 14s. 91; .1. 111idwood, £26 14s. 7d.; J. Hedley, £l5 175.; B. Dutton, £25 7s. 76.; W. J. Hargreaves, £l3 16s. ; and W. Collinge Taylor, .£7 2s. 86. The account of Mr. Beasley, late Law Clerk to the Board, not having been rendered, Mr. Allen had instructed Messrs. Collins and Co. to take proceedings to ' obtain it. Recommended that cheques drawn on the 13th July, last year, for counsel's and agent's fees be cancelleJ, and that the treasurer's account be debited and legal ex- penses credited as follows :—Lewin and Gregory, £2lO lie. 46.; Segar, £7O 18s. Gd.; Kennedy, £l2 Os.; Pickford, lls. ; C. H. Beloe, £lO 18s. The summary of accounts showed £l,lOO 19s. gas fund; £6lB 13s. 96. water fund; £453 17s. 106. water extension; and general fund, £1,495 3s. 86. Mr. HEYES proposed that the minutes be passed. , Mr. HANDLEY, in seconding the motion, explained that I the large loan referred to in the minutes was not a new but a consolidated one. The resolution was carried. APPOINTMENT OF RETURNING OFFICER.—THE FINANCIAL

div.head: OUTLOOK.
div.p: OUTLOOK.

The CHAIRMAN explained that this was the twelfth year he had been connected with the Board, and the tenth of his chairmanship, and he should be glad if they would appoint some other gentleman to the position of returning officer. Last year they were about £22,000 ia debt, and now the Board's accounts were on the right side. After a brief discussion, it was determined, on the motion of Mr. GOS;AGE, seconded by Mr. SHurn.rworcru, that Mr. Kershaw should be elected returning officer.
THE TWO SURVEYORS.-THE BOARD STAND BY MR. HIGGINSON.

Mr. CAREY moved that, as the public business was now terminated, the Board go into committee. Mr. SHUTTLEWORTH proposed, and Mr. SADLER seconded, a proposition in favour of the representatives of the press being allowed to remain, which was agreed to without even being pot to the vote. • Mr. SnurrLEwonnt : I beg to move tkat Mr. Higginson be not called upon to resign. The CHAIRMAN: Would it not be better if that motion took the form "That no alteration be made in the surveyor's ' department?" You are speaking as if there had been a resolution proposed that there should be a change in the surveyor's department, which there has not. Mr. SrtrrmEwouTw understood that there was a motion of that kind passed at the private meeting of the members in committee, a month ago. A MEMBER: No there was not. The CHAIRMAN: I beg to say distinctlr that there was not. A resolution was moved that Mr. Higginson should be asked to resign, and an amendment was moved to the effect that Mr. Copland (sewerage scheme surveyor) should be asked to resign. A further amendment was submitted that the consideration of the subject be postponed for a month; but ultimately no decision was come to. Mr. SHurnEwoßTEt: I am quite willing to alter the resolution.

The CHAIRMAN said he did not wish Mr. Shuttleworth to alter his motion; let him put it in his own way. It was, however, right that he should know that the Board in com- mittee did not pass any resolution asking Mr. Higginson to resign. Mr. SADLER seconded the proposition. Mr. KERSHAW remarked that the reason why be originally brought this question before the Board was that they were about to undertake the sewerage of the town, and he con- sidered it important that the work should be thoroughly and honestly done. In order that they might lttain to this point they must have attention, and things must not be "slipped over," or done in any roughshod fashion. His experience during the last five years, had led him to the t onclusion that there was not attention given to the work in the sur- veyor's department which there ought to be. Work was allowed to be finished, and then it was condemned, instead of this action being taken before. In carrying out the sewer- age scheme, all the work ought to be inspected, thoroughly examined, and passed by the surveyor, before it was certified and paid for. Well, they knew that Mr. Higginson had re-,. used in that room to give any information in eonnectiois with the scheme. The sewerage proposals brought for by Mr. Higginson were such, in his opinion, as no man in his sober senses would ever have brought forward, if he had only sat down and considered the matter for quarter of hour. He had as much respect for their surveyor as any man at that Board, so far as his own personal personal feel- ings went, and he should like to "pull hand in hand" with him if he could have done so. Charges had been thrown out in that room in connection with the sewerage scheme reflect- ing improperly upon the Hutchinson estate trustees. The Highway Committee had now got their expenditure down to £l2O a month, and his conviction was that they were not even getting half the value in work which that sum repre- sented. The speaker then gave a number of instances where he alleged Mr. Higginson was very blameworthy. One of ' these was the putting of such a wide parapet to Sankey's hotel; the state of the road ins various portions of the dis- trict, neglected parapets, and such like matters. In his opinion, Mr. Higginson and Mr. Copland could never work together. Mr. Copland (the sewerage surveyor) had nothing against Mr. Higginson—indeed, he had never heard him say a word against that official. Neither had he heard Mr. Higginson say a word against Mr. Copland; but he had re- marked that his services could not be dispensed with. In conclusion, he moved that Mr. Higginson be asked to resign. Mr. FORSTER seconded the amendment, on the ground that he thought, after the longlist of charges brought against Mr. Higginson, "they could not work together." Mr. BROWN did not propose to argue that some of the _ _ _ _

charges made by Mr. Kershaw were not well founded, but, in a place like Widnes, there always would be some parts of the roads to which exception might be taken. It had always been so, no matter who had been the surveyor. The High- way Committee were quite as responsible for many of the things concerning which complaint had been made as the surveyor. [Mr. KERSHAW : Oh.] They knew there was no man who, if he was subject to a severe hostile criticism, could not be shown how many things might have been done batter' and especially so after- the event. The work could be done better in the interests of the ratepayers by a man like Mr. Higginson than even by a surveyor who was, perhaps, better educated, but would only use Widnes as a stepping stone by which he might rise "to higher things." He felt some little delicacy in opposing the Chairman of the Highway Committee (Mr. Kershaw) in this matter, but he should certainly vote for the retention of the surveyor's services, on the ground that

he had committed no such unpardonable sin ai to prevent his being made into a very useful servant of the Board in future. Either Mr. Higginson was their surveyor, or he was not; and if he was, it was the duty of the Highway Com- mittee to see that he was properly treated by those who were his subordinates, and not his equals. Dr. O'KEEFFE said that with regard to the charge of hav- ing flagged in a superior manner opposite certain places of worship- Mr. KERSHAW : I did not mention any place of worship, sir.

Dr. O'KEEFFE : You mentioned Sankey's publichouse. (Loud laughter, in which the speaker joined heartily.) The fl.wging at the front of the Albert-road Wesleyan Chapel, was quite as wide "as that in front of Sankey's place of worship." (Renewed laughter.) Such flagging was certainly ornamental, and, from the length of time which it was likely to last, it would prove a good investment. Cowley's path- way had been mentioned by Mr. Kershaw; but if the sur- veyor interfered with that, he might incur the resentment of Mr. Cowley, who was a ponderous man indeed ! In his opinion, the surveyor had not been consulted as he ought to have been at the time when the sewerage scheme was initiated, and the matter had rather been put into the hands of his assistant than into his own. Certainly the assistant survevor had had a good deal of experience as to sewers, and would probably prove an efficient man to carry out the work, which, however, ought of course, to be superintended by Mr. lli2ineOn.

Mr, BOOTH remarked that he most decidedly supported the remarks of Mr. Brown and the last speaker. Mr. CAREY said that a little time ago he certainly had one or two bones to pick with the Surveyor, and he really had the opinion that it was impossible for him to carry on the duties of 'his situation successfully, and to the satisfaction of the public. One of these " bones " was the apparent obsti- nacy of Mr. Hig2;inson—he really did not know what else to call it—as to the sewerage scheme. The surveyor had, however, explained that he had never had any intention of refusing to look into the figures as to the plans which were put forward in opposition to his own. He had not done so simply because he took them to be correct. Mr. Higginson I had always carried out in •a fairly satisfactory manner the I wishes of the Health Committee ; though he certainly thought him wanting in organising and business power. He thought that the surveyor was capable of improvement in this respect—with care. Mr. Higginson was then calle4 into the room, and replied to the various charges brought forward by Mr. Kershaw, in a manner which apparently gave much satisfaction. Mr. Kershaw's amendmend was put, and only three mem- bers voted for it. The original motion of Mr. Shuttleworth was, therefore, passed by a very large %majority. Tiae proceedings then terminated.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1882.

Edge Hill ; and Mr. Wm. James Taberner, booking clerk at the same station, were called to prove the case.—The defen- dant, in reply to the Bench, said he did not possess a single can which would hold 15 gallons, and it was not reasonable to suppose that, under such circumstances, he should put 18 gallons on the consignment note.—The Chairman remarked that the only evidence upon which the Company could rely in this case was a ticket found in the can, and which had ui•on it what appeared to be the words eighteen shillings, and not 18 gallons. There was no evidence of the milk Flaying been measured at Edge Hill, and, in the absence of such proof, the summons would be dismissed.---Wm. Wilkinson, farmer, Sutton, was charged with being guilty of a similar fraud upon the company, in the case of milk which was being carried between Sutton Weaver and Edge Hill, on the Bth and 9th.—Mr. Preston said that on defend- ant's cans being examined at Edge Hill, they were found to contain ten gallons more than had been paid fop on each of the dates mentioned.—Defendant said he was 60 years of age, could neither read nor write, and had to trust to his boys in sending off the milk. Some time after the milk had been sent away, he heard that a complaint had been made that the correct number of gallons had not been paid for. He spoke to one of the boys about having misstated the number of gallons, on which he said, " Well, I believe they all do it." He would not have countenanced such a pro- ceeding if he had been aware of it.—Mr. Cooper, station master, Sutton Weaver, gave evidence in support of the prosecution. Mr. Salisbury, Liverpool, said he received the milk in question from defendant, whose con- signments he did not measure, as he had faith in his state- ments.—The Chairman said the circumstances in Wilkin- son's case were somewhat different to those of the other defendants. He would be fined 10s. and costs in each case. CHARGE Or ROBBERY IN A PUBLIC-HOllSE.—William Howell and Sarah Howell, husband and wife, who obtain a livelihood by singing and playing in public-houses, were charged with stealing a bag, the property of Thomas Salkeld, labourer, Pennington's-row.—The prosecutor stated that on Saturday night, he was in the Glass Barrel public- house, somewhat under the influence of liquor, and whilst the prisoners were sitting near him, he missed the bag and money. He went out and gave the couple into the custody of P.C. Kelly.—Thomas Powell, labourer, stated that after the prisoners had been taken away, he found the , purse and money in a ginger beer case near where they and . the prosecutor had been sitting, and gave them to Thomas Ashton, the landlord.—P.C. Kelly and the female searcher at the police station also gave evidence. The latter stated that she found a florin in the female prisoner's shoe, though , she had previously stated she had no money upon her.— ' The magistrates discharged the prisoners. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Wm. Bankes.

A VIOLENT FEMALE.—EIiz tbeth Perry was charged with wilfully damaging a window and door, belonging to the Guardians of the Runcorn Union. The evidence of Mr. Jones, the workhouse master, showed that for several days the prisoner was suffering so badly from disease, that she had to be confined in a room. While there she broke all the glass in one window, and two or three panes in another, took the lock off the door, and got out. The damage to the door amounted to lls.—The prisoner said she did not know for what reason she was being kept in the room. She did not like it, and getting vexed, she broke the windows and got out.—Mr. Bankes sentenced the prisoner to 14 days im- prisonment with hard labour. YESTERDAY.-13410re Messrs. W. Bankes (chairman) and C.
W. Hazlehurst.

ASSAULT ON A CHILD BY A DRUNKEN WOMAN.—Agnes Ford was fined ss. and 6s. 6d. costs for drunkenness. She was also charged with assaulting the child Of Mr. Richard- son, butcher, Church-street, on the 16th inst.—The father said that he observed the prisoner drunk in Church-street, and as she passed along she was followed by a number of children, who were teazing her. Ford became angry, rushed upon the children, and seized hold of his little child, who happened to be in the way, knocking it down, and beating its head against the ground.—Harry Richardson, aged seven years, corroborated this statement.—Yrisoner, who said she only " smacked " the child, was fined 103. and 93. 6d. costs. _

COAL STEALING AT SUTTON DOCK.—Thomas Johnson and William Stubbs were charged with having been found on premises belonging to Mr. Donald Lee, at Sutton Dock, for an unlawful purpose.—Superintendent Williamson said he had received a number of reports concerning people steal- ing coal at Sutton Dock, near Frodsham, and he instructed Sergeant Lowndes and P. C. Egerton to watch the place in plain clothes. On the previous night, the officers concealed themselves near the spot, and saw the prisoners go upon the premises, with some bags in their possession. Egerton suc- ceeded in securing Stubbs, but Johnson escaped, and was apprehended about ten o'clock the same night. When the prisoners visited the place, a number of women were waiting near an adjoining bridge—it is supposed with the object of taking the coal they stole.—The two police officers gave evidence in support of this statement. The prisoner John- son was likewise charged with assaulting P.C. Egerton. The constable stated that when he took Johnson into custody, he struck him twice, once on the cheek and a second time on the eye.—ln the coal stealing case, each of the prisoners was committed for one month with hard labour, and Johnson was ordered to be iTprisoned one month for the assault.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. INIONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit (chairman) and Mr. James Reynolds.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. INIONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit (chairman) and Mr. James Reynolds.

ASSAULT ON A YOUNG MAN.—Peter Massey was charged with assaulting a young man named John Nichols, on 'the 4th inst.—Complainant said that after leaving a certain beerhouse, on the night referred to, he found the door of his own dwelling closed. He went to the house of a neighbour named Hill to make some enquiries, when the defendant set upon him, kicked him, knocked him against a pair of drawers, and struck him twice. Defendant also threatened he would knock his remaining eye out, and so make him blind.—Defendant was fined 10s. and 9s. 61. costs. TIIE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—The followitg people were summoned by the Runcorn School Board, who were represented by Mr. Bowyer, school attendance officer. and were each ordered to pay 55., including costs, for not sending their children to school :—Edwin Lewis, Jane Hicks, Charlotte Done, Thomas Sharkey, John Critchley, James Massey, Patrick Haverty, Thomas Webb, James Dawson, Elie ibeth Maddocks, Richard Clynch, James Riley, Ellen Johnson, John Filkin, Samuel Foster, Joseph Worthington, Wm. 3Lirshall, and Benjamin Wright. THE RAILWAY CO. AND THE MILK DEALERS.—ALLEGED FitAuDS —Mr. George Percival, of Sutton, was summoned for having, on the 15th December, 1881, whilst the owner of certain milk passing on the London and North-Western Railway, between Sutton Weaver and Liverpool, given a false account of the weight and quantity of it, with intent to defraud the company. A. similar charge was preferred against defendant in relation to'the 19th of the same month. —Mr. A. C. Preston (Liverpool and Chester) appeared on behalf of the company, and Mr. Ferrand (from the solicitors' department, Lime-street) was also present.—Mr. Preston said the summonses against defendant were issued under the 8 and 9 Vic., c 20, sec. 99, in which any owner of goods failing to give an account, to produce his bill of Wine.", or giving a false account with a view to avoid payment of the tolls payable, should be guilty of a contravention of the Act, and for every such offence should forfeit a sum not exceeding I£lo for every ton of goods, or for every parcel exceeding one hundredweight, such penalty being in addition to the toll. The circumstances of the cases were somewhat peculiar, and revealed a practice which it appeared had been going on upon the line for some time, not only at Sutton Weave; but in other districts round Liverpool. - For the accommo- dation of milk dealers and dairymen in the country, they were allowed to send their milk into that city, and other large towns at the rate of one penny per gallon, exclusive of the weight of the can. Consignment notes were provided which the persons sending the milk had .to fill up in their own handwriting, stating the exact number of gallons carried in the cans. Lately it had been found that some of the milk dealers were in the habit of making false declara- tion as te the contents of the cans—for instance, stating that a can containing 16 gallons had only 12 in it. This conduct defrauded the company of 3d. or 4d., as the case might be. That was a small amount, but the loss on the h hundreds of tons sent into the city must be a serious sum. The company bad, therefore, made a great effort to put an end to such a course of proceeding. Oa the 15th December the defendant sent to the station two cans, and on the note requesting that they might be forwarded to the Liverpool Dairy Company was a statement that the number of gallons in each can was twelve. On the arrival of the cans at Edge Hill station they were opened and examined by one of the company's officials, and each of them was found to contain 18 gallons. A tally was put in the cans from the consignor to the consignee, as a guide when the accounts were settled at the end of the months, and this stated that the cans contained 32 imperial gallons, which fact clearly proved that defendant intended to defraud the company. As defendant had pleaded guilty, he would only put in formal evidence. On tllel9th Decem- ber defendant' forwarded two cans, and, on being examined at Edge Hill, they were each found to contain 16 gallons, though according to the declaration there were only 12 gal- lons—The Chairman said he did not consider it necessary to call evidence in this particular case, as defendant had pleaded guilty.—The defendant was subsequently fined 20s. and costs in each case.—Thomas Massey was charged with a similar offence, on the 3rd ult, at Sutton Weaver.—Mr. Prep- ton said that in this case defendant forwarded a can of milk from Sutton Weaver to Edge Hill, and when examined at that station it ws found to contain 18 gallons, though in the declaration Massey said there were only 12 gallons. The milk was cmsigned to J. W. Warner, Edge Hill. This , would save the defendant sixpence.—Mr. Cooper, station master, Sutton Weaver ; Mr. James Stewart, station master,

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. F. H. Gossage (chairman) and
John Brock.

CHARGE OF BREAKING INTO AN OFFICE. Peter Riley was charged, on remand, with breaking into the office of Messrs. Golding, Davis, and Company, on Saturday night, and stealing two coats, value us. Late on Saturday night the prisoner was found on the premises by the watchman, who ordered him to go away. He refused, became very abusive, threw half a brick at the watchman, and threatened to shoot him. It was some time before he went away. Next morning the office was found to have been broken open and entered by means of the window, in which a pane of glass was smashed. All tli; drawers and cupboards had been ran- sacked, and an attempt had teen made to force tha lock of the iron safe, but the fastening had successfully resisted the efforts of the burglar. Superintendent Barker said that the stolen property had not yet been recovered, and, as the prisoner had already served five years in a reformatory, he had to ask that he might be remanded until Wednesday next. —The magistrates granted the application. THE TENANCY OF WEST BAN,K HOTEL.—The Bench con- sented to the temporary transference of the license of West Bank Hotel from John Barclay Reynolds (who was convicted of having been drunk on his licensed premises last week), to James McGovern. _ _ _ _

TIIE BEGGAR AND THE MAGISTRATE.—Sarah Redman, a girl, was convicted, on the evidence of Sergeant Clarkson, of begging in Victoria-road, on Tuesday afternoon. The prisoner denied her guilt, on which Mr. Gossage said he had not the slightest doubt about it, as she had frequently asked alms of him. She would be imprisoned until the rising of the court. —Mr. Lewin, Deputy Magistrates' Clerk, warned the mother of the prisoner that if her daughter was brought up on a similar charge again, the Bench would probably send her to an industrial school, in which, case the parents would be compelled to contribute towards her maintenance. Between the 4th and 11th .insts., the cloth was missed by the prosecutor, who had seen the pi:isoncr Morley at the shop, but had no reason for suspecting her honesty. On Wednesday, however, from information re- ceived, P.S. Robinson visited Dalton's house, and there found a piece of the missing cloth, which she stated she had purchased from Morley, who, in turn, said she had bought it from a travelling draper. COMMISSIONERS.

The adjourned meeting was held on Thursday morning. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present, Messrs. Meadowcroft, Lake, P. Speakman, Mc.Dougall, Taylor, Williams, Norman, Linaker (law clerk), and Brookes (sec- retary).—The CHAIRMAN stated that the adjournment had taken place for the purpose of filing the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. Lyon. He would not make any sug- gestion in the way of names, but leave the members to pur- sue their own course.—Mr. NORMAN and Mr. MEADOWCROFT immediately rose; and the CHAIRMAN ruled that the former gentleman was upon his feet first—Mr. NORMAN proposed that Mr. Dobson, who had been a member of the Board for many years, and against whom he was sure none of them could have anything to say of a depreciatory character,, should be elected to fill the vacancy. 11lr. Dobson had frequently been chairman of cotnmittees, and had .filledotber important positions in the connection with the transaction of their business.—Mr. WILLIAMS seconded the resolution.— Mr. MEADowcnorr remarked that he had also a name to submit to their consideration, and in doing so he wished it to be clearly understood that his remarks were made in no spirit of opposition to Mr. Dobson. He, however, most cer- tainly thought that the gentleman whose name he had to submit to then, to fill the vacancy, was one who would prove a great acquisition to the Board, as he was a man of wide commercial experience; one who could give an intelligent expression to his opinions, and who was intimately known to every member. The gentleman to whom he referred, was Mr. George Rhodes, who resided in an important part of the town, viz t Duke's- field, which was rapidly ex- tending. It was felt by the inhibitants of that part of Runcorn that they had very large interests involved in the local government of the town, and that they were certainly entitled to a distinct representation upon the Board.—Mr. NORMAN wished to know if Mr. Rhodes would stand if ' elected ?—Mr. MEADOWCROFT said he should not have taken upon himself the responsibility of submitting such a motion to the Board, unless he had been quite satisfied upon that point.—Mr. FISHER seconded the amendment, and said he could endorse every word to which Mr. Meadocroft had given utterance. Considering the way in which Duke's-field was extending, it would only be common justice to the rate- payers in that part of the town to give them a representative who could look after their interest. He seconded the pro- posal without any feeling of opposition to Mr. Dobson, whom he had known for some years.—The CHAIRMAN: We have two very good names before us, gentlemen. I should be glad to se either or both of them, upon the Board.—There voted for Mr. Rhodes : Dr. McDougall, Messrs. Fisher, Taylor, Lake, and Meadowcroft.-5. For Mr. Dobson: the Chair- man, and Messrs. P. Speakman, Williams, and Norman-4. —On the amendment being put as the substantive motion, it was ',carried unanimously—Mr. Norman said that, of course, no gentlemon present had any objection to Mr. Rhodes being appointed.—The proceedings then terminated.
FORMATION OF A RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION AT PRESCuT,

A few weeks ago the question was mooted of the forma- tion of an association to look after and study the interests and welfare of the ratepayers of Prescot generally at the different public boards connected with the town, especially with regard to the increase of rates, official salaries, Jec. Several preliminary meetings of a number of ratepayers were subsequently held, and after due deliberation it was considered desirable that a ratepayers' association should be formed, and that a public meeting should be convened with a view to the establishment of such an association. The meeting was accordingly held on Monday evening, in the Town Hall, when there was a tolerably large attendance of ratepayers. Mr. James Hewitt presided, and there were also present on the platform, Messrs. J. Berry, J. Pratt, J. A. Browne, W. Brown, J. Haydon, and others.—The CHAIR- MAN, having read the notice convening the meeting, said it was intended to form an association to protect the interests of the ratepayers generally, and to prevent, if possible, a repetition of such acts of what he might term folly as had lately been perpetrated by the Local Board of Prescot. The association would not entertain anything of a party political character; its efforts and attention would be strictly con- fined to the furtherance of the interests of the ratepayers of Prescot, and if any political crisis arose they might depend upon it the association would not be made use of for any political purpose whatever. (Hear.) He might also say that the association would be irreligious, or rather non- sectarian, and would embrace persons of all denominations who had the well-being of the ratepayers at heart. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman then read a statement of the objects of the association, which were as follows :—" (1) To protect the interests of the ratepayers with regard to the expendi- ture of the Local Board and School Board, and to create a healty public opinion on local government. Its duty will be to initiate and support all necessary reforms, and to return to various boards and governing bodies men whose opinions are in accordance with those of the rate- payers' association. (2.) To take such steps as will prevent any undue influence or over representation of any class. (3.) The association will not be confined to watching the proceedings of the Local Board and School Board, but aim , at securing an efficient representation on the Board of Guardians, upon whom devolves the control of a large ex- penditure of the rates in the relief of the poor, and in pay- ment of official salaries. (4.) Also to interest itself in obtaining a cheaper supply of gas, and in any other way to protect the interests of the ratepayers generally. (5.) The association disclaims anything of a religious or party- political character, its sole object being to deal with the man- agement of local affairs, and the promotion of the true interests of the Local Board district."—The Chairman then called upon Mr. James Berry to moved the first resolution. Before doing so, Mr. BERRY said he had heard that there were rumours floating about the town that the reason he and some other friends were taking an active part in promoting that association, was simply because they wanted to get in public office. He strongly denied that that was so; their desire was to do something that would be the means of pro- moting the true interests of the town in which they lived. The resolution he had to propose was as follows:—" That this meeting, having learned the objects of the proposed Ratepayers' Association, do hereby resolve to form such an association for the Local Board district of Prescot." The chairman had already placed before them the objects of the association. and he ventured to say those objects were of a cellar-I-lendable character. Referring to the Local Board, be asked whether that body had discharged their duties in such a manner as to entitle them to the confidence of the ratepayers? He was sure that neither he nor his associates had any wish to say anything disrespectful or disparaging about the members of the Local Board, but they had a right, as ratepayers, to criticise their proceedings, and to use, if possible, such influence as might be the means of , causing them to act somewhat differently to what they had done, and more in accordance with the views they enter- tained. It was unnecessary to recount all the blunders committed by the Local Board since its formation, as they were pretty well known in:the town, but he would, however, like to refer to one in particular. In the early part of 1880, the gas company of Present sought for pawers in the House of Commons to enable them to enlarge their works. At the time the application was made the company had carried out the greater portion of the work, so that to a certain extent, it was a farce to seek for powers to do what they had already done. What course did the Local Board adopt? They held a meeting, and it was pretty well understood that they would oppose the company' d bill, in order that the town might have gas at a cheaper rate. What was the result ? The opposition collapsed, though how it was brought about the ratepayers could not ascertain. It was true that en the Local Board there was a large "element of gas," and he supposed the larger lights extinguished the farthing "dips." (Hear, hear, and laughter.) One gentleman, Mr. W. L. Evans, to whom great credit was due, interested himself in opposing the bill, hut it was hardly to be expected that be would undertake the whole responsibility and expense, as it was pretty well knowe that opposing a bill in the House of Commons or the House of Lords was a very expensive matter. A sort of compromise was effected, and if they re- membered they were congratulated by one of the local papers on the compromise being effected, and the gas cm- piny allowed to dip into their pockits at the rate of ss. 4d. per thousand cubic feet of gas. He contended that that was a most exorbitant charge, and read a list of prices charged in various towns in England, similar in size to Pres- cot, but lacking the same advantages, showing that gas could be supplied at a much cheaper rate. He asked them, as sensible men, whether they had just cause to complain of the extravagant charges of the Prescot Gas Company; and he ventured to say if they had had a ratepayers' association three years ago, the company would not have been allowed to get their bill passed so easily. The ratepayers would have been prevented from being imposed upon in such a disgrace- ful manner, for it was a disgrace that, considering the many advantages of the Prescot Gas Company, they should charge such an extravagant price. Referring to the School Board, he thought it a costly "luxury," and was of opinion that some means might have been adopted at the outset which would have saved the town the expense of a School Board. He had no hesitation in saying that the salaries paid to the officers of the board were very much too high—[A. voice: They are.]—and if the members of that board would only look a little more to the interests of the ratepayers they would not pay such high salaries. It was absurd to say they could not have efficiency without paying heavily for it. They could have efficiency with economy, or economy with effciency, which ever way they liked to put it, at a consider- ately less price than was now paid by the Prescot School Board, and hoped that when the next election took place some pressure would be brought to bear upon the candidates with respect to this matter. Mr. Berry then touched upon the expendituLe of the Guardians. He observed that from 1878 to 1880 the cost of in-door maintenance had advanced from £2,875 to £3,297, and of out-door relief from £3,573 to £5,329, an increase of £1,756. Was not something required to be done to check such reckless expenditure A that? It was quite true the Union was growing, but the increase of expense was very much out of proportion to the growth of the population ; and he ventured to say that the increase in salaries for this year would amount to considerably over £3OO. 'Was it not requisite that an association should be formed to watch the proceedings of the Guardians, and to take such steps as might be considered necessary with a view to the reduction of that vast expense? At the present time the rates of Prescot amounted to something like 7s. in the pound, and was it reasonable to expect that people would come and build and reside in the town with the rates at that figure? He did not think it was.—Mr. WILLIAM BnowN seconded, and Mr. HENRY WHITFIELD, in an minus- lug speech, supported the resolution, which on being put to

the meeting was carried unanimously.—Mr. JOSEPH PRATT] then moved "That a committee consisting of eighteen rate- p Ayers, including the president, vice-president, treasurer, and secretary be formed to make the requisite rules and carry out the subject of this meeting." After remarking that he considered it partly the fault of theratepayers that the rates we're 7s. in the pound, Mr. Pratt referred to the ques- tion of the Court Leet. He did not think it was a credit to the town that they should be brought up into that hall every year to answer to their names and pay 2d. each. He thought that was a question which only wanted bringing before the proper authorities to get it put right. If he was rightly in- formed a person who failed to pay one year would have to pay double the next year, and if the money was not paid then the amount was doubled each succeeding year it was not paid, and the person was liable to be distrained for the money. This was a condition of things he thought ought to be seen to.—Mr. J. A. BROWNE seconded the motion, which was agreed to. The following committee was then appointed to carry out the necessary arrangements : Messrs. C. B. Johnson, James Hewitt, James Berry, Robert Henry Menzies, William Meredith, John Alcock, Thomas Taylor, George Rigby, Henry Whitfield, Wm. Beesley Wm. Brown, James Case, Peter Pendleton, Thos. Prescott, Appleton, James Stockley, J. A. Browne, and Joseph Batt.—lt was understood that a meeting of the committee would shortly be held to appoint the various officers.—A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings.

ORDER OF SONS OF TEMPERANCE. MEETING AT RUNCORN. On Monday evening, a public meeting, in connection with the Order of the Sons of Temperance, was held in the Mill Brow Sunday School. Mr. S. Coventry occupied the chair, and was supported by Messrs. Cook, Boyle, Parker Faulkner, and Jones. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the meeting, said temperance was not sufficiently thought about by the masses. It was certainly one of the greatest questions of the day, and he thought that if it was carefully studied and examined from all points they must be brought to the conclusion that it was the greatest matter outside religion with which they had to do. Ile did not wish them to suppose that he was putting temperance before religion but he knew of many cases where religion had entirely lost its elevating power over men and women because, unaided by temperance, they had not retained their hold upon it. He had no doubt that many of those present had recollections of the ravages of drink, both in their own homes and amongst their friends. The recollections of his own early days were exceedingly painful. His childhood had been blighted by the cursed liquor, and long before he heard about temperance he made up his mind never to take any of that which had made his family so miserable. The scenes of his boyhood had had a very beneficial effect upon his life, because when he saw the wretchedness caused by drink in the home of his youth, he made a resolution, which he thanked God he had been able to keep that his home should never be cursed through indulgence in alcoholic beverages. He wished all present to take the subject to heart, to think about it, talk to their friends about it, and do their best to promote the cause of temperance in their midst, depending upon God for assistance. Mr. PARKER (Weston) said it was about 11 years since he first joined the temperance band, and he had every reason to look back to that time with pleasure and thankfulness to God. The English were wise in many branches of know- ledge, but when he considered the habits'of the country, he could not help thinking that they were a very foolish people. Which ever way he looked upon the drink he could not conceive it to be anything but a curse. If he studied its effects upon the homes of the people, he saw that there was nothing so deadly in its effects as drink. Painful thoughts flitted through his mind as he recalled what took place in his home when he was a boy ; and he was reminded that such scenes were constantly occurring in other homes at the present day. After what he had witnessed in komes where the parents had gone to an early grave, killed by drink, and where the children were left destitute, he felt he could not say a single word in favour of so devastating a traffic. Some people talked about moderation ; but moderation, in its true sense, meant a moderate use of all necessary things, and he failed to see where the necessity for drink lay. He believed many men only took it because they were fond of it, many of them well knowing, and even candidly admitting, that it was all the time doing them great beirm. If men would only put away these depraving appetites they would add to the number of the years of their lives. The cause whose prin- ciples tbey were there to spread was a noble cause, and well worthy of their assistance. He hoped they would all give the matter their earnest consideration, and do their utmost to suppress the giant evil in their midst. Mr. BOYLE said they were living in an age of science. Wonderful inventions had been discovered, properties never before dreamt of had been found in the simplest things, and great questions, such as the origin of man, were being dis- cussed. He considered that temperance was what might be called an economical science. When a man took his money to the grocer's, clothier's, the fruits of it enabled him to work for more; but supposing he spent it at the public-house he get no adequate return for it. He defaced his manly beauty, drowned his reason, and became a wife's sorrow and the chil- dren's woe, and he most probably ended his career either in the workhouse or the asylum. There were in this country 185,000 public-house licensed for the sale of alcoholic liquors, and he asked them what benefit were they to the country? He attributed nearly all the crime in the land, directly or indirectly, to the drink traffic. He stated that during the last week in the old year and in the first wssk in the new year 360 cases of murder, manslaughter, attempted suicides, wife-beating, &c., were tried, all of which were attributable to the effects of drink. He thought it was the duty of all patriotic men and women to raise their voices against the heinous traffic. It was often said that teetotallers were fanatics, and meddled with other people's business; but they merely wished people to see how economical it was to be abstainers. Temperance was a good thing because it in- creased work. If £5 were spent in boots, £1 17s. was paid as wages; for the same amount spent in earthenware, £2 was for labour; and for linen, .E 2 6s. went to pay the workmen for their labour. If they spent the same in woollen goods, £3 of it was paid in wages ; and if those goods were made into clothing, the workingmen received £3 Ils, as their share of the money. But out of £5 spent in drink, only half-a-crown went in labour. As an illustration of this, he said that in Scotland there was a large distillery, where about £1,000,000 worth of liquor was manufactured annually, and in the making of which they employed only 150 men. Near to the distillery stood an iron works, which sent out in iron about the same value yearly as the distillery in drink, but they had in their employment 1,400 men. The public. houses were so numerous that it was an impossibility for some men to pass them. He thought it was a monstrous thing to put so many man-traps in the way of the working- man, and it was for the purpose of doing their utmost to put a stop to so abominable a practice that the Order of Sons of Temperance was instituted. It had its origin in one of the States of Americi. It was commenced by two natural brothers, on the 29th of Sept., 1842. The rules and regulations of the order met with great approbation, and it rapidly spread through the States, and acrqss the Atlantic, until it extended into Germany, Africa, and all parts of the world. They had a membership of about 3,000,000, and many great and noble men had been associated with them, President Lincoln in the number. Mr. Boyle then spoke at some length of the benefits of the club. He said it was a great advantage to hold their meetings in a room not connected with a public- house. In conclusion, he urged all to join the order, as it was really the best thing they could do for themselves and also for their families. Mr. FAULKNER said that a great portion of the evil effects of drink fell upon the ladies, but if every young lady would make up her mind to say, when a young man began to pay his attentions to her, " the lips that touch liquor shall never touch mine," there would be a vast improvement in the town. They need not feel afraid as to the results, because it was an established fact that ycung men would come after the young women=-(laughter)—and if the young man re- fused to give up his glass for the sake of one, he was not worth troubling about. The married women also had great power over their husbands, and it was their duty to do their best to make the home attractive in readiness for the husband's return from work, to have the children clean, the hearth tidy, and the tea things set as though they were waiting for someone she loved ; and if she would greet her husband with a smiling face, he would not feel so great an inclination to go to the public-house. When a man returned from his work, and found the house dirty, and his wife a slatternly woman, not worth looking at, it was only likely he should go to a place where he could be comfortable. The landlords always took care to have the bar-rooms clean, to have a cheerful fire burning in the grate, and they were always ready to greet their customers with good humour. It was the best thing a wife could do to try and keep her husband at home, and he hoped they would all try it, and he felt surs good would then be done. Mr. MALCOLM JONES also said a few words to the young men, advising them to give up all companions who were ad- dicted to drink. The usual vote of thanks brought the meeting to a con- clusion.

"Boon SERVANTS OF THE MOTHER OF GOD." An in- stitution wholly new to St. Helens has noiselessly risen up within the last few days, which, however, promises to be- come one of no small interest and importance., Some have bees struck by the unwonted appearance of certain modest figures gliding quietly among the poor at the East end ; and our readers may be interested to know a little more about them. They are, it seems, nuns of an order called the Poor Servants of the Mother of God, who consecrate their lives, first to earning their own living by labour, and secondly to work amongst the poor • so that the labour of those at home tends to support the others who are busy with works of mercy. Their ministrations comprise the visitation of the poor, more especially with a view to promote the cleanli- ness, comfort, and modesty of home life, and at " Mother's meetings" they contrive to teach not only economy, but to substantially encourage it. The service of the sick is not overlooked, and the supervision of children with a par- ticular regard to attendance at school, is a notable matter of their care. They also take charge of orphans to train them to habits of industry and virtue • and, when expedient, open what is popularly known as the creche, where babies are looked after, while the mothers are at work. All this is energy well directed to local needs; and the ministrations of the sisters are not confined to their own co-religionists, but freely dispensed without regard to religion. The fathers at Holy Cross have been fortunate enough to secure this boon to the many poor of their district; but it is hoped that soon the numbers of the little community in George- street will grow large enough to enable them to widen the sphere of their charity, everywhere so much wanted.
